Calculus may be retarded in its progress, and prevented from creating much distress, by the internal use of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> and lime-water, by soap less taken in milk or in veal-broth, or by the use of aerated alkaline water, which may perhaps be considered as being both more safe and more efficacious, and at the same time more pleasant, than any of the other practices. The scurvy may be prevented by warm clothing and perseverance in brisk exercise, by drinking wine or cider, and eating freely of such vegetable substances as can be had in these situations where this disease is most apt to show itself. In constitutions where there is an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> disposition to the scrophula, if early precautions be taken to strengthen the solids by cold bathing, a nourishing course of diet, and moderate use of wine, the constitution which gives rise to the disease will probably be prevented from producing any very bad effects. The other kinds of morbid matter, which are of the specific nature, are received into the body by infection or contagion. The infection of a putrid fever or dysentery is best prevented by immediately taking an emetic on the first attack of the sickness or shivering; and if that do not completely answer, let a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> blister be applied between the shoulders: by this method the nurses and other attendants on the sick in the naval hospitals have often been preserved. As to other infectious morbid matter, we must refer to what has already been said when treating of hydrophobia, poisons, gonorrhoea, &c. The ill effects which may arise from the different species of salivary, are to be obviated, in general, by the prudent administration of emetics, and carefully abstaining from such kinds of food as are known to cause the accumulation of noxious matters in the first passages. Crude vegetables, milk, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, and other oily substances, are to be avoided by persons troubled with a fowling in the stomach; brisk exercise, especially riding, is to be used, and they are to refrain from fermented liquors: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> drink should be pure water; or water with a very little of some ardent spirit, such as rum or brandy. Seltzer and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRMONT">Pyrmont</a> waters are to be drunk medicinally; and aromatic bitters, infusions, or tinctures, acidulated with sulphuric acid, will be found serviceable, in order to strengthen the fibres of the stomach, and promote the expulsion of its contents, thereby preventing the too hasty <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a> of the alimentary mixture. In order to procure immediate relief, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNESIA">magnesia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBA">alba</a>, or creta preparata, will seldom fail; the magnesia, as well as the chalk, may be made into lozenges, with a little <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> and mucilage; and in that form may be carried about and taken occasionally by people afflicted with the acid salivary. In constitutions where there is an exuberance or stagnation of bile, and a troublesome bitterness in the mouth, it is necessary to keep the bowels always free, by taking occasionally small doses of pure aloes, olym ricini. Appendix. M E D I C I N E. Means of preserving Health. When there is a tendency to the empyreumatic and rancid fuburra, people should carefully avoid all the various kinds of those oily and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-seasoned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of diet generally termed made-dishes, and eat sparingly of plain meat, without rich sauces or much gravy; and in these cases the most proper drink is pure water. II. Rules for those who enjoy perfect Health. There can be no doubt, that, in general, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> is the true foundation of health; and yet the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> physicians, as we may see in the rules laid down by Celsus, did not scruple to recommend indulgence now and then, and allowed people to exceed both in eating and drinking: but it is safer to proceed to excess in drink than in meat; and if the debauch should create any extraordinary or distressing degree of pain or sickness, and a temporary fever should ensue, there are two ways of shaking it off, either to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> and encourage perspiration, or to get on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-back and by brisk exercise restore the body to its natural state. The choice of these two methods must always be determined by the peculiar circumstances of the parties concerned, and from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> which they may before have had which agrees best with them. If a person should commit excess in eating, especially of high-seasoned things, with rich sauces, a draught of cold water, acidulated with sulphuric acid, will take off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> at the stomach, and assist digestion by moderating and keeping within bounds the alimentary fermentation, and thus preventing the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> of too much flatus. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> of ices may be here of real service at the tables of the great, as producing similar effects with the cold water acidulated. Persons in these circumstances ought not to lay themselves down to sleep, but should keep up and use gentle exercise until they are sensible that the stomach is unloaded, and that they no longer feel any oppressive weight about the praecordia. If a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> be obliged to fast, he ought, if possible, during that time, to avoid laborious work: after suffering severe <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>, people ought not at once to gorge and fill themselves; nor is it proper, after being overfilled, to enjoy an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> fast: neither is it safe to indulge in a state of total rest immediately after excessive labour, nor suddenly fall hard to work after having been long without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>: in a word, all changes should be made by gentle degrees; for though the constitution of the human body be such that it can bear many alterations and irregularities without much danger, yet, when the transitions are extremely sudden, there is a great risk of producing some degree of disorder. It is also the advice of Celsus to vary the scenes of life, and not confine ourselves to any settled rules: but as inaction renders the body weak and listless, and exercise gives vigour and strength, people should never long omit riding, walking, or going abroad in a carriage. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FENCING">Fencing</a>, playing at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENNIS">tennis</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, or other similar engagements, which afford both exercise and amusement, as each shall be found most agreeable or convenient, are to be used in turn, according to the circumstances and tendency to any particular species of disease. But when the weaknesses of old age shall have rendered the body incapable of all these, then dry frictions with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> will be very requisite to preserve health, by accelerating the flow of humours through the smallest orders of vessels, and preventing the fluids from stagnating too long in the cellular interstices of the fleshy parts. Sleep is the great restorer of strength; for, during this time, the nutritious particles appear to be chiefly applied to repair the waste, and replace those that have been abraded and washed off by the labour and exercise of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; but too much indulgence in sleep has many inconveniences, both with respect to body and mind, as it blunts the senses, and encourages the fluids to stagnate in the cellular membrane; whence corpulency, and its necessary consequences languor and weakness. The proper time for sleep is the night, when darkness and silence naturally bring it on: sleep in the daytime, from noise and other circumstances, is in general not so found or refreshing; and to some people is really distasteful, as creating an unusual giddiness and languor, especially in persons addicted to literary pursuits. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">Custom</a>, however, frequently renders sleep in the day necessary; and in those constitutions where it is found to give real refreshment, the propensity to it ought to be indulged, particularly in very advanced age. With regard to the general regimen of diet, it has always been held as a rule, that the softer and milder kinds of aliment are most proper for children and younger subjects: that grown persons should eat what is more substantial; and old people lessen their quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> food, and increase that of their drink both of the diluent and cordial kind.

MEDICI

Pages 90-93

LORENZO DE, filled, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> propriety, the Magnificent, was the grandson of Cosmo, and about 16 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> at his decease. In 1469 his father died, and he succeeded to his authority as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it had constituted a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his fortune. In the year 1474, Lorenzo incurred the displeasure of the pope for the opposition he he made to some of his encroachments on the petty princes of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and for this reason he deprived him of the office of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of the Roman see, which he conferred on one Pazzi, connected with a Florentine family, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of which he thus secured, and intended to sacrifice Lorenzo and Giuliano to his private <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>. Their assassination was fixed for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>, April 26, 1478, and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> was the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in which a monitor of an archbishop had resolved to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> them by the instigation of the pope. When the people <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> one of their favourites (Giuliano) expiring, and the other (Lorenzo) covered with blood, their rage was not to be expressed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. The interference of the magistrates was finally victorious, who had the courage and virtue to hang the archbishop from one of the windows, arrayed in his pontifical robes, which made <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> resound with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCLAMATION">acclamation</a>—Medici! Medic! <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with their enemies! Lorenzo was delivered from that part of the cathedral to which he had fled for refuge, and was triumphantly carried home, where his wounds were attended to by men of ability. His friends in the meantime pursued the conspirators, and spared none who happened to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in their way. In a word, the generality of them were either hanged <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> decapitated, and very few had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> to escape their uncommon vigilance. Much to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Lorenzo, he exerted all his influence to prevent the indiscriminate massacre of his cruel enemies, and restrain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> indignation of the people, begging that they would trust the magistrates with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of the guilty; and the respect in which he was held had the most astonishing effect in restraining the vengeance of popular indignation. No sooner had hostilities ceased between Pope Sixtus and the Florentine republic, then Lorenzo began to develop plans for securing the internal peace and tranquillity of Italy, by which the highest honour has been conferred on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. But the life of this great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was again brought into imminent danger by the intrigues of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Riaro, and some Florentine exiles, who determined to assassinate him in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of the Carmelites, on the festival of the Ascension 1481; but the plot was happily discovered, the conspirators were executed, and after this Lorenzo very seldom went abroad without being surrounded by a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of friends in whom he could securely confide. When we attentively examine the character of Lorenzo, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not perhaps appear astonishing, that Italy, Christendom, and even the Mahometans themselves, conferred upon him the most flattering approbation. Even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRANDOLA">Mirandola</a> chose Florence as the place of his residence entirely upon his account, and there ended his mortal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a>. To a most engaging person Lorenzo added almost every other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCOMPLISHMENT">accomplishment</a>. He was the favourite of the ladies, the envy of his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, and the admiration of all. He was declared to be unrivalled in chivalry, and one of the most eminent orators that the world in any age has produced. According to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of his contemporaries, he was even superior to Julius Caesar himself, except as a general, yet he would also have proved a most consummate commander had not peace been always the darling of his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>. We recollect a memorable passage in the Rambler, which may here be appropriately introduced. A great man condescending to do little things, is like the Medicis. Fun in his western declination; he remits his splendor, but retains his magnitude, and pleases more though he dazzles less. To such little things did Lorenzo frequently submit, often seeking <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in his nursery, and spending hours there in all the frivolous pranks of childish diversion. The gravity of his life, if contrasted with its levity, must make him appear as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of two different persons, incompatible, and, as it were, impossible to be joined the one with the other. Such were the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and veneration of the citizens for Lorenzo, that the physician who attended him on his deathbed, terrified to return to Florence, left the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in a state of distraction, and plunged himself into a well. When Ferdinand <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> was informed of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, he cried out, "This man has lived <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> enough for his own <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, but too short a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> for Italy." He died on the 8th of April 1492, amidst a number of his weeping friends, who appeared deeply conscious of such an irreparable loss. Medicis, John de, on account of his bravery and knowledge in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> affairs, was surnamed the Invincible. He was the son of John, otherwise called Fourdun, de Medicis. His only son Cosmo I. styled the Great, was chosen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Florence after the murder of Alexander de Medicis, A.D. 1537. He first carried arms under Laurence de Medicis against the duke of Urbino, afterwards under Pope Leo X. Upon the death of Leo, he entered into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of Francis I., which he quitted to follow the fortune of Francis Sforza duke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>. When Francis I. formed an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the pope and the Venetians against the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, he returned to his service. He was wounded in the knee at Governola, a small town in the Mantuan territory, by a musket <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>; and being carried to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, he died the 29th of November 1526, aged 28. Brantome relates, that when his leg was to be cut off, and when he was informed that he needed some person to support him, "Proceed without fear (said he), I need nobody!" and he held the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> himself during the operation. This anecdote is also mentioned by Varchi. John de Medicis was above the middle stature, strong, and nervous. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, to express their affection for him and their concern for his loss, assumed a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a> dress and standards, which gave the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> band to the Tuscan troops whom he commanded. Medicis, Laurence, or Laurencius de, was descended from a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Cosmo the Great, and affected the name of popular. In 1537, he killed Alexander de Medicis, whom <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. had made duke of Florence, and who was believed to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> son of Laurence de Medicis duke of Urbino. He was jealous of Alexander's power, and disguised this jealousy under the specious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a> of love to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. He loved men of learning, and cultivated literature. His works are, 1. Lamenti, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a>, 12mo. 2. Acidoso Commedia, Florence 1595, 12mo. He died without issue. Medicis, Hypolitus de, natural son of Julian de Medicis and a lady of Urbino, was early remarkable for the brilliancy of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and the graces of his person. Pope Clement VII. his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a>, made him cardinal in 1529, and sent him as legate into Germany to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Charles V. When that prince went into Italy, Medicis, yielding to his warlike disposition, appeared. Medici appeared in the dress of an officer, and advanced before the emperor, followed by several respectable gentlemen of the court. Charles, naturally suspicious, and afraid that the legate intended to do him some ill offices with the pope, sent after him and caused him to be apprehended. But when he understood that it was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> fallacy of humour in the young cardinal, he set him at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> in a few days. The character which Medici obtained by the happy success of this appointment was of essential service to him. He was considered as one of the supports of the Holy See; and a little before Clement's death, when the corsair Barbarossa made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> into Italy to the great terror of Rome, which was only defended by 200 of the pope's guards, Medici was despatched to protect the coasts from the fury of the barbarians. On his arrival at the place of destination, he was fortunate enough to find that Barbarossa had withdrawn himself at that critical moment; which allowed him to claim the honour of the retreat without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> his person or his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. When he returned to Rome, he was of great service in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of Paul III., who nevertheless refused to make him legate to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCONA">Ancona</a>, though that office had been promised to him in the conclave. Enraged also that the pope had bestowed the principality of Florence on Alexander de Medici, supposed to be the natural son of Laurence duke of Urbino, he was prompted by his ambition to believe that he might succeed to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> by the destruction of Alexander. He entered into a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> against him, and determined to carry him off by a mine; but the plot was discovered before he had accomplished his purpose. Octavian Zanga, one of his guards, was arrested as his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCOMPLICE">accomplice</a>. Hyppolitus de Medici, apprehensive for his own safety, retired to a castle near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIVOLI">Tivoli</a>. On his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to Naples, he fell sick at Itri in the territory of Fondi, and died August 13, 1535, in his 24th year, not without suspicion of being poisoned. His house was an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> for the unfortunate, and frequently for those who were guilty of the blackest crimes. It was open to men of all nations; and he was frequently addressed in twenty different languages. He had a natural son named Andrea de Medici, who was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>. This anecdote proves that his manners were more military than ecclesiastic. He wore a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and never put on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of cardinal except on occasions of public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>. He was wholly devoted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, hunting, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. Medici, Alexander de, first duke of Florence in 1539, was natural son of Laurence de Medici, further named the Younger, and nephew of Pope Clement VII. He owed his elevation to the intrigues of his uncle and to the arms of Charles V. This prince having made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Florence after an obstinate siege, conferred the sovereignty of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> on Alexander, and afterwards gave him in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> Margaret of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a> his natural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>. According to the terms of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a> granted to the Florentines, the new duke was to be only <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> doge, and his authority was tempered by councils, which left them at least a shadow of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> liberty. But Alexander, who felt himself supported by the emperor and the pope, was no sooner in possession of his new dignity, than he began to govern like a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>; being guided by no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> but his own caprice, indulging the most brutal passions, and making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of discouraging families, and of violating even the asylum of the cloisters to gratify his lust. Among the confidants of his debauchery was a relation of his own, Laurence de Medici. This young man, who was only 22 years of age, at the instigation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> Strozzi, a zealous republican, conceived the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of assassinating Alexander, and thereby of delivering his country from oppression. From the moment when he first became attached to him, he tried to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> his confidence, for no other reason but that he might the better have it in his power to take away his life. A considerable time elapsed before he found such an opportunity as he desired. At length, under pretence of procuring the duke a tête-à-tête with a lady of whom he was deeply enamoured, he brought him alone and unattended into his chamber, and put him under his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>. He went out, under pretence of introducing the object of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>; and returned along with an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSASSIN">assassin</a> by profession, to whom alone he had entrusted his design, only to stab him. This cruel <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> happened on the night betwixt the 5th and 6th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1537. Alexander was only 26 years of age. The Florentines derived no advantage from this crime of Laurence, for they failed in their attempt to recover their liberty. The party of the Medici prevailed, and Alexander was succeeded by Cosmo; whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, it must be confessed, was as just and moderate, as that of his predecessor had been violent and tyrannical. Laurence de Medici fled to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, to some of the leaders of the malecontents at Florence, who had taken refuge there; but not thinking himself in sufficient security, he went to Constantinople, whence he returned sometime after to Venice. He was there assassinated in 1547, ten years after the duke's murder, by two soldiers, one of whom had formerly been in Alexander's guards: And these soldiers were generous enough to refuse a considerable sum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, which was the price put upon his head. Medici, Cosmo de, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> duke of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, joined Charles V. against the French, after trying in vain to continue neutral. As a reward for his services, the emperor added to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Tuscany <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PIOMBINO">Piombino</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELBA">Elba</a>, and other states. Cosmo soon after received from Pope Pius IV. the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of grand duke; and had it not been opposed by all the princes of Italy, this pontiff, who was entirely devoted to Cosmo, because he had thought proper to acknowledge him to be of his house, would have conferred on him the title of king. There never was a more zealous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of learning. Ambitious of imitating the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Cæsar, he like him, was fond of learned men, kept them near his person, and founded for them the university of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a>. He died in 1574, at the age of 55, after governing with equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and glory. In 1562 he instituted the military order of St. Stephen. His son, Francis <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> who died in 1587, was the father of Mary of Medici, the wife of Henry the Great and of Ferdinand I., who died in 1608. Medietas linguae, in Law, signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a>, or inquest impanelled, of which the one half are natives of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> and the other foreigners. This jury is never used except where one of the parties in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> is a stranger and the other a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENIZEN">denizen</a>. In petit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, murder, Medinatus murder, and felony, foreigners are allowed this privilege; but not in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> treason, because an alien in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> shall be tried according to the rules of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, and not by a medicias lingue. A grand jury ought not in any case to be of a medicias lingue; and the person that would have the advantage of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> in this way, is to pray the same, otherwise it will not be permitted on a challenge of the jurors.

MEDICINE

Pages 83-83

And there is every reason to hope, that this appointment <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be attended with many effects highly beneficial to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. A short view of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> and importance of this subject will, we presume, not be unacceptable to the intelligent reader. Whatever aid the science of medicine can contribute towards the good of the state, and the execution of its laws, has been by the Germans denominated State Medicine; a new, but not improper, appellation, for that branch of knowledge which many writers have termed Medical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURISPRUDENCE">Jurisprudence</a>. It comprehends both medical <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a> and juridical medicine. The former consists of the medical precepts which may be of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to the legislature <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to the magistracy. The latter is the aggregate of all the information, afforded by the different branches of medicine, which is necessary for elucidating doubtful questions in courts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. Although there are some traces of juridical medicine in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a> code; such as determining the real <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of birth, with a view to prevent the imposition of spurious children: it properly originated with the code of laws enacted by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. under the name of Constitutione criminalis Carolina; in which it is ordained, that the opinions of physicians should be taken, with regard to the danger of wounds, child <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, murder, poisoning, procured <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABORTION">abortion</a>, concealed pregnancy, &c. These directions, and the impossibility which was found of determining many questions by simply legal means, induced some legislators to enjoin, that all tribunals and judges should procure from sworn physicians, appointed to this office, their opinions concerning all the subjects to be mentioned hereafter. Since that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, it has been treated systematically by many learned men; such as Fortunatus Fidelis, Zacchias, Alberti, Hebenstreit, Haller, Ludwig, Plenck; and lastly, in the most masterly manner, by Metzger. Numberless dissertations have been written on all its parts; and among those who contributed to its advancement, we may reckon <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBROSE">Ambrose</a> Parry, Bolin, Butener, Morgagni, Camper, and Gruner. Collections of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, illustrating its principles, have been made by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMAN">Amman</a>, Daniel, Bucholz, Pyl, Scheff and Metzger. These are only a few of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> writers, who have attended to this science: to enumerate more would be unnecessary. From its very <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, it is evident how necessary a knowledge of this science must be to every medical practitioner, who is liable to be called upon to illustrate any question comprehended under it before a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. On his answers, the fate of the accused person must often depend; both judge and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a> regulating their decision by his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, while he is delivering his sentiments, his own reputation is before the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of the public. The acuteness of the gentlemen of the law is universally acknowledged; the versatility of their genius, and the quickness of their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>, are rendered almost inconceivable, by constant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>. It is their duty to make every possible exertion for the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of their client, and they seldom leave unnoticed any inaccurate or contradictory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>. How cautious must, then, a medical practitioner be, when examined before such men, when it is their duty to expose his errors, and magnify his uncertainties, till his evil influence seem contradictory and absurd? How often must he expose himself to such severe criticism, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he be not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the subject on which he is giving evidence, and have not arranged his thoughts on it according to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> principles? On the other hand, he may deserve and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> much <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, by so public a display of judgement and professional knowledge. Some acquaintance with this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of medical science must be useful at least, and sometimes necessary, to judges and lawyers. They will thus be enabled to estimate how much they may depend on the opinion of any physician, and will know how to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> their questions, so as to arrive at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and avoid being misled by his partiality or favourite opinions. To the lawyer who conducts the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of an accused person, in a criminal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, it is almost indispensible; without it, he cannot do justice to the cause of his client. Before criminal courts, the questions which occur most generally are, respecting 1. The cause of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, as ascertained from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of the body. 2. The sufficiency of the supposed cause to have produced death. 3. Probable event of wounds, contusions, &c. 4. The importance of the part injured. 5. Supposed child-murder; whether still-born or not. 6. Whether death accidental or intended. 7. Abortion; its having occurred, 8. Spontaneously, from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>; accidentally, from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> violence or passions of the mind; or intentionally, from the introduction of a sharp <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, use of certain drugs, &c. 9. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">Rape</a>; its being attempted or consummated; recent or previous deliration. 10. The responsibility of the accused for his actions. Before civil courts the questions generally regard, 1. The state of mind; madness, melancholy, idiocy. 2. Pregnancy; concealed, pretended. 3. Parturition; concealed, pretended, retarded, premature. 4. The first-born of twins. 5. Diseases; concealed, pretended, imputed. 6. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">Age</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Before consistorial courts, the subjects investigated are, 1. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPOTENCE">Impotence</a>; general, relative, curable, incurable. 2. Sterility; curable, relatively incurable, absolutely incurable. 3. Uncertainty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>; hermaphrodites. 4. Diseases preventing cohabitation; venereal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEPROSY">leprosy</a>, &c. [Merged from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">WORMS</a>, p.71] Those infesting the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body are chiefly of three kinds: the acarides, or small round and short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> worms; the teres, or round and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> worm; and the tania, or tape worm. The acarides have usually their seat in the rectum.—The teres or lumbrici are about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAN">span</a> long, round and smooth: they are seated for the most part in the upper small intestines; but sometimes they are lodged also in the stomach, and in any part of the intestines, even to the rectum.—The tape-worms are from two to forty feet long, according to the testimony of Platerus; they generally infest the whole tract of the intestines, but especially the ileum: they very much resemble a tape in their appearance, whence the name of tape-worm: but another <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of this genus, from the resemblance of each <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> to a gourd seed, has the name of the gourd worm. In the Medical Transactions, vol. 1st. Dr Heberden gives a very accurate account of the symptoms produced by the acarides, from an eminent physician who was troubled with them all his life. They brought on an uneasiness in the rectum, and an almost intolerable itching in the anus; which sensations most usually came on in the evening, and prevented <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> for several hours. They were attended with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, sometimes so considerable as to produce a swelling in the rectum both both internally and externally; and if these symptoms were not soon relieved, a tenesmus was brought on, with a mucous dejection. Sometimes there was a gripping pain in the lower part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>, a little above the os <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol0.html#article-PUBIS">pubis</a>. If this pain was very severe, a bloody mucus followed, in which there were often found acarides alive. They were also sometimes suspected of occasioning disturbed sleep, and some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of headache. On this case Dr Heberden observes, that the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> of the patient did not seem to have suffered from the long continuance of the disease, nor the immediate inconveniences of the disorder itself to have increased. "It is (says he) perhaps universally true, that this kind of worms, though as difficult to be cured as any, yet is the least dangerous of all. They have been known to accompany a person through the whole of a long life, without any reason to suspect that they had halved its end. As in this case there was no remarkable sickness, indigestion, giddiness, pain of the stomach, nor itching of the nose, possibly these symptoms, where they have happened to be joined with the acarides, did not properly belong to them, but arose from some other causes. There is indeed no one sign of these worms, but what in some patients will be wanting." The above mentioned patient used purging and irritating clysters with very little success. One dram and an half of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a> was infused in six ounces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and the strained liquor being given as a clyster, occasioned a violent pain in the lower part of the abdomen, with faintness and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> sweat: this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INJECTION">injection</a>, though retained only one minute, acted as a smart purge, but did little or no good. Lime-water was also used as a clyster; which brought on a catarrh, but had no good effect. Six grains of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> were dissolved in six ounces of water, and injected. This clyster in a few minutes occasioned an aching in the rectum, gripped a little without purging, and excited a tenesmus. Some few acarides were brought off with it; but all of them were alive. The uneasy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> in the rectum did not abate till some warm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a> was thrown up. Whenever the tenesmus or mucous stools were thought worth the taking notice of, warm milk and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> generally gave immediate relief. If purging was necessary, the lenient purges, such as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANNA">manna</a> with oil, were, in this particular case, made use of: <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-RHUBARB">rhubarb</a> was found too stimulating.—But, in general, the most useful purge, and which therefore was most usually taken, was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a> and rhubarb, of each half a drachm: this powder seldom failed to bring away a mucus as transparent as the white of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, and in this many acarides were moving about. The cinnamon frequently adhered to this mucus, which did not come off in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities, when a purge was taken without cinnamon. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALOMEL">Calomel</a> did no more than any other purge which operates briskly would have done; that is, it brought away acarides, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of mucus. Oil given as a clyster sometimes brought off the animalcules: the oil swam on the surface of the mucus, and the acarides were alive and moving in the mucus itself, which probably hindered the oil from coming in contact with them and killing them. Dr Heberden also observes, that mucus or slime is the proper nest of the acarides, in which they live, and is perhaps the food by which they are nourished; and it is this mucus which preserves them unhurt, though surrounded with many other liquors, the immediate touch of which would be fatal. It is hard to satisfy ourselves by what <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a> they find it out in the human body, and by what means they get at it; but it is observable in many other parts of nature, as well as here, that where there is a fit <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> for the hatching and growth of animals and vegetables, nature has taken sufficient care that their seeds should find the way thither. Worms are said to have been found in the intestines of still-born <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a>. Purges, by lessening this time, never fail to relieve the patient; and it is not unlikely, that the worms which are not forced away by this quickened <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the intestines, may, for want of a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of it, languish, and at last die; for if the acarides are taken out of their mucus, and exposed to the open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, they become motionless, and apparently die in a very short time. Dr Heberden supposes that the kind of purge made use of is of some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> in the cure of all other worms as well as acarides; the animals being always defended by the mucus from the immediate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of medicines; and that therefore those purges are the best which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> briskly, and of which a repetition can be most easily borne. Purging waters are of this sort, and jalap especially for children; two or more grains of which, mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, are most easily taken, and may be repeated daily. From Dr Heberden's observations, we may easily see why it is so difficult to destroy these animals; and why anthelmintics, greatly celebrated for some kinds, are yet far from being <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIFICS">specifics</a> in the disease. As the worms which reside in the cavities of the human body are never exposed to the air, by which all living creatures are invigorated, it is evident, that in themselves they must be the most tender and easily destructible creatures imaginable, and much less will be requisite to kill them than any of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> insects. The most pernicious substances to any of the common insects are oil, caustic fixed alkali, lime, and lime-water. The oil operates upon them by shutting up the pores of their bodies; the lime-water, lime, and caustic alkali, by dissolving their very substance. In the case of intestinal worms, however, the oil can have very little effect upon them, as they are defended from it by the moisture and mucus of the intestines; the like happens with lime-water: and therefore it is necessary that the medicine should be of such a nature as to destroy both mucus and insects together; for which purpose the caustic fixed alkali is at once safe and efficacious; nor is it probable that any case of worms whatever could resist the proper use of this medicine. A very large dose of any salt indeed will also destroy the mucus and destroy the worms; but it is apt to inflame and excoriate the stomach and intestines, and thus to produce worse distempers than that which it was intended to cure. Dr Heberden gives the following remarkable case of a patient cured of worms by enormous doses of common salt, after trying many other remedies in vain. In February 1757, the patient was seized with uncommon pains in his stomach, attended with nausea, vomiting, and constipation of bowels, and an almost total loss of sleep and appetite: Worms. He soon became much emaciated, and could neither stand nor walk upright; his belly grew small and hard, and closely retracted, insomuch that the sternum covered the navel, and the latter could scarce be discovered or felt by the finger: his urine was always milky, and soon deposited a thick white sediment; his excrements were very hard and lumpy, resembling those of sheep, only of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; nor had he ever a stool without some medicine or other to procure it. In this situation he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> four years; during which time he had been in an infirmary, attended by eminent physicians, but was disguised as incurable. At last he was advised by a neighbour to drink salt and water, as he said he knew one cured by it who had for many years been afflicted with the same kind of pains in the belly and stomach. As his distemper was now almost inapplicable, he willingly tried the experiment. Two pounds of common salt were dissolved in as little water as possible, all which he drank in less than an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. Soon afterwards he found himself greatly oppressed at the stomach, grew extremely sick, and vomited violently; on the fourth straining he brought up about half a pint of small worms, part acariides, and the rest resembling those worms which are called the botus, and frequently met with in the stomach of horses, but much smaller, and about the size of a grain of wheat. The salt soon began to operate downwards, and he had five or six very copious fetid stools, tinged with blood; and in them discharged near an equal quantity of the same kind of worms he had vomited. Being greatly fatigued with the violence of the operations, he fell into a calm sleep, which lasted two hours, during which he sweated profusely, and awoke much refreshed. Instead of his usual pains, he now only complained of a rawness and soreness of his gullet, stomach, and bowels, with an almost unquenchable thirst; to allay which, he drank large quantities of cold water, whey, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>-milk, or whatever he could get. The urine he now passed was small in quantity, and rendered with very great difficulty, being highly saturated with the salt, from whence arose a most troublesome dysuria and strangury. However, these symptoms gradually abated by a free use of the liquors above-mentioned; and on the third morning he was so well recovered, that he took two pounds more of salt, dissolved in the like quantity of water. The effects were nearly similar to the former; only that most of the worms were now burnt, and came away with a considerable quantity of lime and mucus. The drought, strangury, &c. returned with their former violence, but soon yielded to the old treatment. He sweated very copiously for three days, slept easily, and by that time could extend his body freely: on the fifth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> he left his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>, and, though very weak, could walk upright; his strength and appetite soon returned, and he became robust and well. The anthelmintic medicines which have been recommended by one person or other, are in a manner innumerable; but the principal are, 1. Quicksilver. This is very efficacious against all kinds of worms, either taken in the form of calomel or corrosive sublimate. Even the crude metal boiled in water, and the water drunk, has been recommended as an almost certain cure. But this, it is evident, can receive no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPREGNATION">impregnation</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>. If, therefore, it have any effect, it must be from some foreign and accidental impregnation. In most instances there can be no objection to mercury, but only that it is not endowed with any attenuating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> whereby the mucus in which these insects resides can be dissolved. It therefore fails in many cases, though it will most certainly destroy worms where it can get at them. 2. Powder of tin. This was for some time celebrated as a specific, and indeed we may reasonably expect good effects from it; as by its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and grittiness it rubs off the mucus and worms it contains from the coats of the intestinal canal, in which case they are easily evacuated by purgatives. In order to produce any considerable effects, it must be given in a large dose. 3. Geoffroa incrustis, or cabbage bark. This remedy is used by the inhabitants of Jamaica. The first account of it which appeared in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was published in the Physical and Literary Essays, vol. ii., by Mr Duguid surgeon in that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. He acquaints us, that the inhabitants of Jamaica, young and old, white and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, are much infested with worms, especially the long round sort; the reason of which, he thinks, is the quantity of sweet viscid vegetables which they eat. On dissecting a child of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> months old, who died of vomiting and convulsions, twelve large worms were found; one of them filled the appendix vermiformis, and three of them were entwined in such a manner as to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> up the valvula Tulpia, so that nothing could <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> from the small to the great guts.—The cabbage bark, however, he tells us, is a safe and effectual remedy, and the most powerful vermifuge yet known; and that it frequently brings away as many worms by stool as would fill a large hat. He owns that it has sometimes violent effects; but this he attributes to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> who make the decoction (in which form the bark is used) too strong, and not to the remedy itself. Mr Anderson, surgeon in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, has also given an account of this bark and its operation, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Dr Duncan, published in the Edinburgh Medical Commentaries, volume iv. p. 84. From this account it appears, that there are two different kinds of cabbage bark; the one much paler than the other: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> kind operates much more violently than the other. It often occasions loose stools, great nausea, and such like symptoms, attended with great uneasiness in the belly: in one or two instances it was suspected of inducing syncope. The darker coloured kind resembles the calca lignea, though it is of a much coarser texture. This kind, Mr Anderson thinks, may be exhibited in any case where an anthelmintic is necessary; the dangerous symptoms might have followed either from the use of the first kind, or from an over-dose of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>. The usual method of preparing the medicine is by boiling two ounces and a half of the bark in two quarts of water to a pint and a half. Of this a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a>-spoonful may be given at first in the morning, gradually increasing the quantity till we come to four or five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>-spoonfuls in a day. When exhibited in this manner, Mr Anderson informs us, that he never <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> it produce any violent symptoms, and has experienced the best effects from it as an anthelmintic. After the use of this decoction for eight or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> mornings successively, a dose of jalap with calomel must be given, which seldom fails to bring away the worms, some dead, some alive. If at any time the decoction produce more than one or two loose stools, a few drops of liquid laudanum may be given; and, in general, Mr Anderson gave 15 or 20 drops of the spirit of lavender with each dose. In a letter from Dr Ruth, professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a>, to Dr Duncan of Edinburgh, the following account is given of another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of this medicine. "It has long (says he) been a complaint among physicians, that we have no vermicide medicine which can be depended upon. Even calomel fails in many cases where there are the most pathognomonic signs of worms in the bowels. But this complaint, it is hoped, is now at an end. The physicians of Jamaica have lately found, that the cabbage bark, as it is called in the West Indies, made into a syrup with brown sugar, is an infallible antidote to them. I have used above 30 pounds of it, and have never found it fail in one instance. The syrup is pleasant; it sometimes pukes, and always purges, the first or second time it is given." The most accurate botanical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the geoffreana inermis, or the tree furnishing the worm bark, as it has often been called, is that which was published some years ago in the Philosophical Transactions by Dr Wright, formerly physician at Jamaica, now of Edinburgh, who also highly extols this remedy as an anthelmintic. Notwithstanding these encomiums, however, the cabbage bark has not come into general use in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. But diseases from the tereter, or lumbrici as they are often called, the species of worm against which this bark is employed, much less frequently occur in Britain than in some other countries. When they do occur, in almost every instance they readily yield to more gentle and safe anthelmintics; and the worms may not only be expelled by calomel, but by the vegetable bitters; as the powder of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTEMISIA">artemisia</a> fantonica, or the like. 4. Couhage, or cow itch. This is the Dolichos serus or pruriens of Linnæus; and the principles on which it acts have been already explained under the article Dolichos. It is somewhat similar to the powder of tin, but bids fair for being more efficacious. It might at first appear to occur as objections to this medicine, that by the hairs of it entangling themselves with one another, calculi might be formed in the intestines, or obstructions equally bad; or if the sharp <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> and hooks with which it abounds were to adhere to the nervous coats of the intestines themselves, they might occasion a fatal irritation, which could not be removed by any means whatever. But from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> of those who have employed it extensively in practice, it would appear, that these objections are entirely theoretical; and that it may be employed with perfect safety. The episcule, gently scraped off from a single pod, and mixed with syrup or molasses, are taken for a dose in the morning fasting. This dose is repeated in this manner for two or three days without any sensible operation; but even a very slight purgative taken afterwards has been found to discharge an almost incredible quantity of worms. And according to Dr Bancroft, who has given a very particular account of its use in his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUIANA">Guiana</a>, it is one of the safest and most certain anthelmintics yet discovered; but, as well as the bark of the Geoffrea, it has hitherto been very little used in Britain, probably from its not being necessary. 5. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> pink. This plant, which is the Spigelia marilandica of Linnæus, is also an American plant, and was first recommended in the Edinburgh Physical and Literary Essays by Dr Gardiner of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARLESTOWN">Charlestown</a> in South Carolina. He is of opinion that a vomit ought always to precede the use of it; and informs us, that half a dram of it purges as briskly as the same quantity of rhubarb. At other times he has known it produce no effect on the belly though given in very large quantity: In such cases it becomes necessary to add a grain or two of sweet mercury, or some grains of rhubarb; but then it is less efficacious than when it proves purgative without addition. The use of it, however, in small doses, is by no means safe; as it frequently produces giddiness, dimness of sight, convulsions, &c. The addition of a purgative, indeed, prevents these effects; but at the same time, as already observed, it diminishes the virtue of the medicine. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> therefore recommends large doses, as from them he never knew any other effect than the medicine's proving emetic or violently cathartic. The dose is from 12 to 60 or 70 grains of the root in substance, or two, three, or four drams of the infusion, twice a day. This medicine has also had its day, and is now very far from being considered as a specific. The long round worms seem to be the most dangerous which infest the human body, as they often pierce through the stomach and intestines, and thus bring on a miserable death. The common symptoms of them are nausea, vomiting, looseness, fainting, slender intermittent <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, itching of the nose, and epileptic fits. By the consumption of the chyle they produce <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>, paleness, weakness, coliciveness, tumor of the abdomen, eructations, and rumbling of the intestines; but it is from the perforation of the intestines that the disease proves so frequently fatal. A child may be known to have worms from his cold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERAMENT">temperament</a>, paleness of the countenance, livid eyelids, hollow eyes, itching of the nose, voracity, startings, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, in sleep; and more especially by a very fetid breath. Very frequently, however, they are voided by the mouth and anus, in which case there is no room for doubt. In the Medical Commentaries, vol. ii., we have an account of the intestines being perforated by a worm, and yet the patient recovered. The patient was a woman troubled with an inflammation in the lower part of the abdomen. The pain was so violent, that for six days she slept none at all; the tumor then broke, discharged upwards of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of thin watery faeces, immediately after which the excrements followed. The next day she was extremely low; her pulse could scarcely be felt; the extremities were cold; and there was a considerable discharge from the wound, which had already begun to mortify. She got a decoction of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CINCHONA">cinchona</a> with wine, which alleviated the symptoms; but in removing the mortified parts a worm was found among them nine inches long, and as thick as an eagle's quill. By proper applications, the discharge of excrements ceased, and she recovered perfect health. She was sensible of no accident giving rise to the Appendix.

MEDICIS

Pages 89-90

CORNO DE, was born in the year 1389, and was in the prime of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father, Giovanni. His conduct was distinguished for urbanity and kindness to the superior ranks of his fellow citizens, and by a constant <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the wants of the lower classes, whom his munificence abundantly relieved. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and moderation, however, could not repel the ambitious designs of the rival families, the Florentines and Medici; for in 1433, Rinaldo de Albizzi, at the head of a formidable party, carried the appointment of the magistracy. On returning from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> seat he was seized upon by his adversaries, and committed to prison. The conspirators not agreeing as to the proper method of dispatching their prisoner, one Peruzzi recommended <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, which was heard by Cosmo, who refused to take any other sustenance than a small portion of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. In this dismal situation he remained four days, shut up from all his kindred and friends, where he soon expected to be numbered with the dead. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> employed to take him off, unexpectedly proved his friend. Malavolta, the keeper of the prison, relented, and declared that he had no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> reason to be alarmed, as he hesitated not to eat of every thing that was brought him. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Lorenzo, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a> Averardo, raised a considerable body of men in Romagna and other districts; and being joined by the commander of the republican forces, they marched to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> to relieve him. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> was obtained from the magistracy, by which he was banished to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a> for ten years, his brother to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> for five, and several of their relations shared a similar fate. Padua was in the dominions of Venice, and he received a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPUTATION">deputation</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> before he reached it, promising him their protection and assistance in whatever he should desire. He rather experienced the treatment of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> than of an exile, as they entertained the highest expectations from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> commercial knowledge. From this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> his life may be considered as one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of uninterrupted prosperity, and his family received <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> equal to that of the greatest potentates. In his public and private charities he was almost unbounded, and perhaps possessed more wealth than any single individual in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> at that period. In his promotion of science and encouragement of learned men he was truly exemplary, and from this source he acquired the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and esteem. His fostering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> protected the arts as well as the sciences; and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, all flourished under his powerful protection. The countenance he shewed to these arts was not such as their professors generally receive from the great; for the sums of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> which he expended on pictures, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, and public buildings, appear almost incredible. When he approached the period of his mortal existence, his faculties were still unimpaired; and 20 days before he died, he requested Ficino to translate from the Greek the treatise of Xenocrates on death. He died on the 1st of August 1464, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 75, and gave strict injunctions, that his funeral should be conducted with as much privacy as possible. By public decree he was honoured with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Pater Patriae, an appellation which was <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> on his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>, and was declared by competent judges, to be founded in real merit.

MEDINA

Pages 93-93

Sir John, an eminent painter, was son of Medina de l'Afritius, a Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> who settled at Brufells, where the son was born in 1660. He was instructed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> by Du Chatel; under whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> he made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress; and applying himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of Rubens, made that eminent <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a>. He painted both <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a>; and was held in extraordinary esteem by most of the princes of Germany, who distinguished his merit by several marks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. He married young, and came into England in 1686, where he drew portraits for several years with great reputation; as he painted those subjects with remarkable freedom of touch, a delicate management of tints, and strong resemblance of the persons. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Leven encouraged him to go to Scotland, and procured him a subscription of £500, worth of business. He went, carrying a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of bodies and postures, to which he painted heads. He returned to England for a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but went back to Scotland, where he died, and was buried in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a> of the Grayfriars at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> in 1711, aged 52. He painted most of the Scotch <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. Two small history pieces, and the portraits of the professors, in the Surgeons <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">Hall</a> at Edinburgh, were also painted by him. At Wentworth castle is a large piece containing the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Argyll and his sons, the late two dukes John and Archibald, in Roman habits; the style Italian, and superior to most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> performers. The duke of Gordon presented Sir John Medina's head to the great duke of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a> for his collection of portraits done by the painters themselves; the duke of Gordon too was drawn by him, with his son the marquis of Huntley and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Lady Jane, in one piece. Medina was knighted by the duke of Queensberry, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a>; and was the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> made in Scotland before the union. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> in the octavo edition of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> were designed by him; and he composed another set for Ovid's Metamorphoses, but they were never engraved.

MEDINA-TALNARI

Pages 93-93

a famous town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Petraea, between Arabia Deserta and Arabia the Happy; celebrated for being the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of Mahomet. It stands at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>'s journey from the port of Jambo. It is of moderate size, surrounded by wretched walls, and situated in the midst of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> plain. It belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a>, although it had of late times a particular sovereign of the family of Dacii Barkad. At present, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> is confided by the sultan to a vizir, who must be taken from the family of the sovereign. Before Mahomet, this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> was called Intireb; but it got the name of Medinet en Nebbi, "the City of the Prophet," after Mahomet, being driven from Mecca by the Koreishites, had taken refuge there, and passed in it the rest of his days. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of Mahomet at Medina is respected by Muslims, but they are under no obligation to visit it for the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">caravans</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> alone, which on their return from Mecca <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> near Medina, go a little out of their way to see the tomb. It stands in a corner of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, whereas the Kaba is situated in the middle of that at Mecca. That the people may not perform some superstitious worship to the relics of the prophet, they are prevented from approaching the tomb by gates, through which they may look at it. It consists of a piece of plain masonry <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEST">chest</a>, without any other monument. The tomb is placed between two others, where the ashes of the two first caliphs repose. Although it is not more magnificent than the tombs of the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the founders of mosques, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> that covers it is decorated with a piece of green <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> stuff embroidered with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, which the pasha of Damascus renew every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years. It is guarded by 40 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a>, who watch the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> said to be deposited there. It is seated in a plain abounding with palm trees, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 39° 53'. N. Lat. 2° 53'. MEDINA Celi, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in Old Castile, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the same name; seated near the river Xalon, in W. Long. 2° 9'. N. Lat. 41° 15'. MEDINA de-las-Torres, a very ancient town of Spain, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESTREMADURA">Estremadura</a>, with an old castle, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a duchy. It is seated on the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, at the foot of a mountain near Bajadoz. MEDINA del Campo, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, rich, and ancient town of Spain, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Leon. The great square is very fine, and adorned with a superb fountain. It is a trading place, enjoys great privileges, and is seated in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> abounding with corn and wine. W. Long. 4° 20'. N. Lat. 41° 22'. MEDINA-del-rio-Secco, an ancient and rich town of Spain, in the kingdom of Leon, with the title of a duchy; seated on a plain, remarkable for its fine pastures. E. Long. 4° 33'. N. Lat. 42° 8'.

MEDINE

Pages 93-93

an Egyptian piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> silvered over, and about the size of a silver threepence.

MEDIOLANUM

Pages 93-94

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Insubres, built by the Gauls on their settlement in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; a municipium, and a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strength; and a seat of the liberal arts; whence it had the name of Novae Athene. Now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, capital of the Milanese, situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Olana and Lombro, E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 30'. N. Lat. 45° 25'.
