MEDIOLANUM Adiutrix, in Ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Gallia Celtica, which afterwards took the name of the Eburovicus Civitas (Antonine); corrupted to Civitas Ebrovicorum, and this last to Ebroica; whence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> appellation <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EVREUX">Evreux</a>, a city of Normandy. E. Long. 1° 12'. N. Lat. 49° 21'. MEDIOLANUM Gugernorum, in Ancient Geography, a town of Gallia <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELGICA">Belgica</a>; now the village Moyland, not far from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a>. MEDIOLANUM Ordovicum, in Ancient Geography, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, now Llan Vethlin, a market town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTGOMERYSHIRE">Montgomeryshire</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. MEDIOLANUM Santonum, in Ancient Geography, which afterwards taking the name of the people, was called called Santonica Urbs; also Santones and Santoni: A town of Aquitaine. Now <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAINTES">Saintes</a>, capital of Saintonge in Guerine, on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARENTE">Charente</a>.

MEDIOMATRICI

Pages 94-94

anciently a territory of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELGICA">Belgica</a>. Now the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METZ">Metz</a>.

MEDITATION

Pages 94-94

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> by which we consider anything closely, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> is employed in the search or consideration of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. In our <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, it is used to signify a consideration of the objects and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> truths of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. Mythic divines make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between meditation and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a>: the former consists in discursive acts of the soul, considering methodically and with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of faith and the precepts of morality; and is performed by reflections and reasonings, which leave behind them manifest impressions on the brain. The pure contemplative have no need of meditation, as seeing all things in God at a glance, and without any reflection. When a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, therefore, has once quitted meditation, and is arrived at contemplation, he returns no more; and, according to Alvarez, never resumes the oar of meditation, except when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> of contemplation is too weak to fill his sails.

MEDITERRANEAN

Pages 94-94

something enclosed within <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that is remote from the ocean. MEDITERRANEAN is more particularly used to signify that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> which flows between the continents of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, entering by the straits of Gibraltar, and reaching into <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, as far as the Euxine sea and the Palus Maeotis. The Mediterranean was anciently called the Grecian sea and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> sea. It is now cantoned out into several divisions, which bear several names. To the west of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> it is called the Ligurian or Tuscan sea; near <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, the Adriatic; towards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, the Ionic and Aegean; between the Hellespont and the Bosporus, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">White</a> sea, as being very safe; and beyond, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> sea, its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> being dangerous.

MEDITRINALIA

Pages 94-94

a Roman festival in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Meditrina, kept on the 30th of September. Both the deity and the festival were so called à medendo, because on this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> they began to drink new wine mixed with old by way of medicine. The mixture of wines, on this festival, was drank with much form and solemn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>.

MEDITULLIUM

Pages 94-94

is used by anatomists for that spongy substance between the two plates of the cranium, and in the interstices of all laminated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>. See ANATOMY, No. 1. 11.

MEDIUM

Pages 94-94

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, that space <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> region through which a body in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> passes to any point: thus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETHER">ether</a> is supposed to be the medium through which the heavenly bodies move; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, the medium wherein bodies move near our <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, the medium wherein fishes live and move; and glass is also a medium of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, as it affords it a free passage. That density or consistence in the parts of the medium, whereby the motion of bodies in it is retarded, is called the resistance of the medium; which, together with the force of gravity, is the cause of the cessation of the motion of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROJECTILES">projectiles</a>. Subtle or Ætherial Medium. Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton considers it probable, that, beside the particular æreal medium, wherein we live and breathe, there is another more universal one, which he calls an ætherial medium; vastly more rare, subtle, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, than air, and by that means freely permeating the pores and interstices of all other mediums, and diffusing itself through the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>; and by the intervention hereof he thinks it is that most of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> phenomena of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> are effected. See ÆTHER, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">ELECTRICITY</a>, FIRE, &c. Medium, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a>, any substance through which light is transmitted.

MEDLAR

Pages 94-94

See Mespilus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MEDULLA OSSUM

Pages 94-94
or MARROW of the bones. See ANATOMY, No. 5. Medulla cerebri and cerebelli, denotes the white soft part of the brain and cerebellum, covered on the outside with the cortical substance, which is of a dark or ash colour. See ANATOMY, No. 131—133. Medulla oblongata, is the medullary part of the brain and cerebellum, joined in one; the fore part of it coming from the brain, and the hind part from the cerebellum. See ANATOMY, No. 134. It lies on the basis of the skull, and is continued through the great perforation thereof into the hollow of the vertebre of the neck, back, and loins; though only so much of it retains the name oblongata as is included within the skull. After its exit thence it is distinguished by the name of medulla spinalis. Ibid. No. 135.

MEDUSA

Pages 94-95

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, one of the three Gorgons, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Phorcys and Ceto. She was the only one of the Gorgons who was subject to mortality. She is celebrated for her personal charms and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of her locks. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> became enamoured of her, and obtained her favours in the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>. This violation of the sanctity of the temple provoked Minerva; and she changed the beautiful locks of Medusa, which had inspired Neptune's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a>, the sight of which turned the beholders into <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>: but Perseus, armed with <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>'s axe, with which he killed Argus, cut off Medusa's head, from whose blood sprang Pegasus and Chrysaor, together with the innumerable serpents. ferments that infest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. The conqueror placed Medusa's head on the aegis of Minerva, which he had used in his expedition; and the head still retained the same petrifying powers as before. Medusa, a genus of vermes, belonging to the order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLLUSCA">mollusca</a>. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">Helminthology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MEDWAY

Pages 95-95

a river of England, rises in the Weald of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, and entering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a> near Ashurst, runs by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNBRIDGE">Tunbridge</a>, and thence continues its course towards <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAIDSTONE">Maidstone</a>. It is navigable for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ships to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, and thence for vessels and barges to Maidstone, the tide flowing up to that town. The distance between the mouth of this river, where the fort at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHEERNESS">Sheerness</a> is erected, and Rochester bridge, is between 16 and 18 miles. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the river, the channel is so deep, the banks so soft, and the reaches so short, that it is one of the best and safest harbours in the world; and ships of 80 guns ride abreast at low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, within musket <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> of Rochester bridge. Nor is there a single instance upon record, that any of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> ever suffered here by storms, except in the dreadful tempest which happened in November 1703, when the Royal Catherine was sunk and lost. On the shore of this river are two castles, one at Upnor, which guards two reaches of the river, and is supposed to defend all the ships which ride above, between that and the bridges; on the other side of the river is Gillingham castle, built for the same purpose, and well furnished with cannon, which commands the river. Besides these, there is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> of guns at a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> called the Swan, and another at Cockhamwood. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> fortification on this river is the castle at Sheerness.

MEEREN

Pages 95-95
or Meer, John Vander, called De Jonghe, an eminent landscape painter, is supposed to have been the son of the old John Vander Meer, and of whom he learned the first rudiments of the art; but being in his youth deprived of his instructor before he had made any great progress, he became a disciple of Nicholas Berghem, and was accounted the best of those who were educated in the school of that admired master. In the manner of his master, he painted landscapes and cattle; and his usual subjects are cottages, with peasants at their rural occupations and diversions. It is observed of him, that he very rarely introduced cows, horses, or any other species of animals, except goats and sheep; the latter of which are so highly finished, that one would imagine the wool might be felt by the softness of its appearance. His touch is scarce perceptible, and yet the colours are admirably united. He died in 1688. The genuine works of this Vander Meer bear a very high price, and are esteemed even in Italy, where they are admitted into the best collections; but the scarcity of them has occasioned many moderate copies after his works to be passed on the undiscerning for real originals. MEGALOPOlis, in Ancient Geography, dividely (Ptolemy, Pausanias); or conjunctly Megalopolis, (Strabo): A town of Arcadia, built under the auspices of Epaminondas, after the battle of Leuctra; many inconsiderable towns being joined together in one great city, the better to withstand the Spartans. It was the greatest city of Arcadia, according to Strabo.

MEGALESIA

Pages 95-95

and MEGALENSIS LUDI, feasts and games in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Cybele <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Rhea the mother of the gods, kept on the 12th of April by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and famous for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> rejoicings and diversions of various sorts. The Galii carried the image of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of drums and other music, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the noise they made to prevent <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> from hearing the cries of his infant son <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, when he was disposed to devour him.

MEGARA

Pages 96-96

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, formerly called Hybla, a town towards the east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>; extinct in Strabo's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, though the name Hybla remained on account of the excellence of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. It was a colony of Megareans from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. Rufus Megaricus denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> laugh.

MEGARIS

Pages 96-96

a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Tuscan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, joined to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, now called Capo dell'Ovo.

MEGASTHENES

Pages 96-96

a Greek historian in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of Seleucus Nicanor, about 300 years before Christ. He wrote about the oriental nations, and particularly the Indians. His <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is often quoted by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. What now passes as his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> is spurious.

MEGIDDO

Pages 96-96

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Galilee, recited (Joshua xvii. 11.) among the cities of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANASSEH">Manasseh</a>, in the tribe of Issachar <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Asher, on the west side of Jordan; famous for the defeat of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AHAZIAH">Ahaziah</a> and Joash, who perished there (2 Kings xxiii. 29.) near it was an open plain, fit for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARRAY">array</a>. It was situated to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, contrary to its position in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> maps. The Canaanites, being tributary to the Israelites, dwelt in it, Joshua xvii.—It was rebuilt by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, 1 Kings ix.

MEIBOMIUS

Pages 96-96

the name of several learned Germans.—John Henry Meibomius was professor of physic at Helmstadt, where he was born, and at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUBEC">Lubec</a>; he wrote the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of Maccenas, published at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> in 4to, 1653, with several other learned works. Henry, his son, was born at Lubec in 1638; became professor of physic at Helmstadt; and, besides works in his own profession, published Scriptores rerum Germanicarum, 3 vols. folio, 1688; a very useful collection, first begun by his father.—Marcus Meibomius, of the same family, published a collection of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> Greek authors who had written upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> music, with a Latin version by himself, dedicated to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTINA">Christina</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, who invited him to her <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. But the engaging him one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> to fing an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of ancient music, while somebody was ordered to dance to it, the immoderate mirth which this occasioned in the spectators so disgusted him, that he immediately left the court of Sweden. His edition of the Greek mythologists, and notes upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a> Laertius in Menage's edition, show him to have been a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of learning; but he suffered no little railing for his attempt to correct the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> text of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, by a kind of metre he fancied he had found out in those ancient writings.

MEISSEN

Pages 96-96

a considerable town of Germany, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, and in the margravate of Misnia, with a castle. It formerly belonged to the bishop, but is now secularized, and the inhabitants are Lutherans. In this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is a famous manufactory of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13° 33'. N. Lat. 51° 15'.

MELA

Pages 96-97

Pomponius, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Latin writer, was born in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Batavia in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and flourished in the reign of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Claudius. His three books of Cosmography, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> De situ orbis, are written in a concise, perspicuous, and elegant manner; and have been thought worthy of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and labours of the ablest critics. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Vossius gave an edition of them in 1658, 4to, with very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and copious notes. To this edition is added, "Julii Honorii oratoris excerptum cosmographicum," first published from the manuscript, and and Ethici cosmographia. Gronovius afterwards published another edition with illustrations by medals. In his last edition are added five books, De Geographia, written by some later author; by Jornandes, as Fabricius conjectures. MELÆNE, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">BLACK</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUX">FLUX</a>, in Medicine. See MEDICINE, No. 499.

MELALEUCA

Pages 97-97

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the polyadelphia class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">INDEX</a>.

MELAMPODIUM

Pages 97-97

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the syngenesia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 49th order, Compositae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">INDEX</a>.

MELAMPUS

Pages 97-97

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a celebrated footfayrer and physician of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a>, son of Amythaon and Idomenes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Dorippe. He lived at Pylos in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>. His servants once killed two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a> who had made their nests at the bottom of a large oak; and Melampus paid so much regard to their remains, that he raised a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> pile and burned them upon it. He also took particular care of their young ones, and fed them with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after this, the young serpents crept to Melampus as he slept on the grass near the oak; and, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> sensible of the favours of their benefactor, they wantonly played around him, and softly licked his ears. This awoke Melampus, who was astonished at the sudden change which his fens had undergone. He found himself acquainted with the chirping of the birds, and with all their rude notes, as they flew around him. He took advantage of this supernatural gift, and soon made himself perfect in the knowledge of futurity, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> also instructed him in the art of medicine. He had soon after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of curing the daughters of Proetus, by giving them hellebore, which from that circumstance has been called melampodium; and, as a reward for his trouble, he married the eldest of these princesses. The tyranny of his uncle Neleus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Pylos, obliged him to leave his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and Proetus, to show himself more sensible of his services, gave him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. About this time the personal charms of Pero, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Neleus, had gained many admirers; but the father promised his daughter only to him who brought into his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> the oxen of Iphicles. This condition displeased many; but Bias, who was also one of her admirers, engaged his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Melampus to steal the oxen and deliver them to him. Melampus was caught in the attempt, and imprisoned; and nothing but his services as a footfayrer and physician to Iphicles would have saved him from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. All this pleaded in the favour of Melampus; but when he had taught the children Iphicles how to become a father, he not only obtained his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, but also the oxen; and with them he compelled Neleus to give Pero in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> to Bias. A severe distemper, which had rendered the women of Argos insane, was totally removed by Melampus; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANAXAGORAS">Anaxagoras</a>, who then sat on the throne, rewarded his merit by giving him part of his kingdom, where he established himself, and where his posterity reigned during six successive generations. He received divine honours after death, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> were raised to his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>.

MELAMPYRUM

Pages 97-97

COW-WHEAT, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the didynamia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 40th order, Peronatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">INDEX</a>.

MELANCHOLY

Pages 97-97

a kind of delirium attended with gloomy thoughts, heaviness, and sorrow. See MEDICINE, No. 327.

MELANCTHON

Pages 97-98
Philip, born at Bretten in the Palatinate in 1495, was one of the wisest and most able men of his age among the reformers, though of a mild temper, and disposed to accommodate rather than to inflame disputes. In his youth he made an admirable progress in learning, and was made Greek professor at Wittenberg in 1509. Here his lectures upon Homer, and the Greek text of St Paul's Epistle to Titus, drew to him a great number of auditors, and entirely effaced the contempt to which his low stature and mean appearance had exposed him. Melanchthon reduced the sciences to systems; and acquired such reputation, that he had sometimes 2,500 auditors. He soon entered into an intimate friendship with Luther, who taught divinity in the same university; and in 1519 they went together to Leipzig, to dispute with Eicus. The following years he was continually engaged in various employments; he composed several books; he taught divinity; took several journeys, in order to found colleges and visit churches; and in 1530 drew up a confession of faith, which goes by the name of the Confession of Augsburg, because it was presented to the emperor at the diet held in that city. All Europe was convinced, that he was not, like Luther, backward to accommodate the differences between the various sects of Christians. He hated religious disputes, and was drawn into them only through the necessity of the part he was called to act in the world; and therefore would have sacrificed many things to have produced an union among the Protestants. For this reason, Francis I., the French king, wrote to desire him to come and confer with the doctors of the Sorbonne, in order to agree with them about putting an end to all controversies; but though Luther endeavoured to persuade the elector of Saxony to consent to that journey, and though Melanchthon himself desired it, that prince, whether he distrusted Melanchthon's moderation, or was afraid of quarrelling with the emperor Charles V., would never grant his permission. The king of England also vainly desired to see him. Melanchthon, in 1529, assisted at the conferences of Spire. In 1541, he was at the famous conferences at Ratibon. In 1543, he went to meet the archbishop of Cologne to assist him in introducing the reformation into his diocese; but that project came to nothing; and in 1548, he assisted at seven conferences on the subject of the interim of Charles V., and wrote a censure on that interim, and all the writings presented at these conferences. He was extremely affected at the divisions raised by Flacius Illyricus. His last conference with those of the Roman communion was at Worms, in 1557. He died at Wittenberg in 1560, and was interred near Luther. Some days before he died, he wrote upon a piece of paper the reasons which made him look upon death as a happiness; and the chief of them was, that it "delivered him from theological persecutions." Nature had given Melanchthon a peaceable temper, which was but ill suited to the time he was to live in. His moderation served only to be his cross. He was like a lamb in the midst of wolves. Nobody liked his mildness; it looked as if he was... was lukewarm; and even Luther himself was sometimes angry at it. Melanchthon was a man in whom many good as well as great qualities were wonderfully united. He had great parts, great learning, great sweetness of temper, moderation, contentedness, and the like, which would have made him very happy in any other times but those in which he lived. He never affected dignities, or honours, or riches, but was rather negligent of all these things; too much so in the opinion of some, considering he had a family; and his son-in-law Sabinus, who was of a more ambitious temper, was actually at variance with him upon this very account. Learning was infinitely obliged to him on many accounts; on none more than this, that, as already observed, he reduced almost all the sciences which had been taught before in a vague irregular manner, into systems. Considering the distractions of his life, and the infinity of disputes and tumults in which he was engaged, it is astonishing how he could find leisure to write so many books. Their number is prodigious, inasmuch that it was thought necessary to publish a chronological catalogue of them in the year 1582. His works indeed are not correct, and he himself owned it: but as he found them useful, he chose rather to print a great number, than to finish only a few: "which however (as Bayle says), was pollporing his own glory to the advantage of others." His constitution was very weak, and required great tenderness and management; which made Luther, as hot and zealous as he was, blame him for labouring too earnestly in the vineyard.

MELANIPPIDES

Pages 98-98

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a Greek poet about 520 years before Christ. His grandson of the same name flourished about 60 years after at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Perdiccas the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">Second</a>, of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>. Some fragments of their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> are still extant.

MELANTERIA

Pages 98-98

an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, which seems to have been applied to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> pyrites. The Greeks used it externally as a gentle eucharistic and a styptic, as an ingredient in their ointments for old ulcers, and also to sprinkle in the form of powder on fresh wounds in order to stop the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HAEMORRHAGE">haemorrhage</a>. MELASSES. See Molasses.

MELASTOMA

Pages 98-98

the American gooseberry-tree, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the decandra clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 7th order, Calycanthaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MELCHA

Pages 98-98

a small village of Barbary, situated about 30 miles from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>, built on the ruins of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, some of which are still visible.

MELCHISEDEC

Pages 98-99
or Melchizedek, king of Salem, and priest of the Most High. The scripture tells us nothing either of his father, or of his mother, or of his genealogy, or of his birth, or of his death. And in this sense he was a figure of Jesus Christ, as St Paul affirms, who is a priest for ever, according to the order of Melchisedec, and not according to the order of Aaron, whose original, life, and death, are known. When Abraham returned from pursuing the four confederate kings, who had defeated the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah, and had taken away Lot Abraham's nephew along with them (Gen. xiv. 17, 18, 19, &c.) Melchisedec came to meet Abraham as far as the valley of Shaveh, which was afterwards named the King's valley, presented him with the refreshment of bread and wine (or he offered bread and wine in sacrifice to the Lord, for he was a priest of the most high God), and blessed him. Abraham, being desirous to acknowledge in him the quality of priest of the Lord, offered him the tithes of all he had taken from the enemy. After this time, there is no mention made of the person of Melchisedec; only the Psalmist (cx. 4.) speaking of the Messiah, says, "Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec." St Paul, in his epistle to the Hebrews, unfolds the mystery which is concealed in what is said of Melchisedec in the Old Testament. See Heb. v. 6—10. An infinite number of difficulties and scruples have been started upon the subject of Melchisedec.—St Jerome thought that Salem, of which Melchisedec was king, was not Jerusalem, but the city of Salem near Scythopolis, where they still pretended to show the ruins of the palace of this prince. The greatness and extent of these ruins are a sufficient proof of the magnificence of this ancient building. He thinks it was at this city of Salem or Shalem, that Jacob arrived after his passage over Jordan, at his return from Mesopotamia (Gen. xxxiii. 18.). Some believe that Salem, where Melchisedec reigned, is the same as Salim spoken of in the gospel of St John, chap. iii. 23. From the time of Epiphanes there were names invented for the father and mother of Melchisedec. To his father was given the name of Heraclas or Heracles, and to his mother that of Alhtaroth or Astaria. It is generally agreed on by the learned, that when the apostle says, he was "without father and without mother," no more is meant, than that he is introduced into the history of Abraham without acquainting us who he was, or whence he came, where he lived, or when he died. Nevertheless, some have taken St Paul's words literally, and contended that he was not of human but divine nature. Origen and Didymus took him to be an angel; and the author of the Questions upon the Old and New Testament pretends, that he was the Holy Ghost, who appeared to Abraham in a human form. The Arabic Catena, upon the ninth chapter of Genesis, makes Melchisedec to be descended from Shem by his father, and from Japheth by his mother. Heraclas or Heraclim his father, was, they say, son or grandson of Phaleg, and son of Heber; and his mother named Salathiel, was daughter of Gomer son of Japheth. Cedrenus and others derive Melchisedec from an Egyptian stock. They say his father was called Sidon or Sida, and was the founder of the city of Sidon the capital of Phenicia. Suidas says he was of the cursed race of Canaan; for which reason the scripture does not mention his genealogy. The Jews and Samaritans believed Melchisedec to be the same Melchisedec was the patriarch Shem; which opinion has been followed by a great number of modern writers. M. Jurius undertook to prove that he is the same as Cham or Ham. It would be endless to set down all the opinions upon this matter; therefore we shall only add, that Peter Cuneus and Peter du Moulin have affirmed, that Melchisedec who appeared to Abraham was the Son of God, and that the patriarch worshipped him and acknowledged him for the Messiah. About the beginning of the third century arose the heresy of the Melchisedecians, who affirmed that Melchisedec was not a man, but a heavenly power, superior to Jesus Christ; for Melchisedec, they said, was the intercessor and mediator of the angels, but Jesus Christ was so only for men, and his priesthood only a copy of that of Melchisedec, who was the Holy Ghost. We shall only beg leave to add here one opinion more concerning Melchisedec, which is that of the learned Heidegger, who, as the author of the *Hihi Patriar*, thinks, has taken the right method of explaining the accounts of Moses and the apostle Paul relating to this extraordinary person. He supposes a twofold Melchisedec; the one historical, whereof Moses gives an account in the 14th chapter of Genesis, as that he was king as well as high priest of Jerusalem; the other allegorical, whom St Paul describes, and this allegorical person is Jesus Christ. As the history of this prince and priest is so little known, it is no wonder, as Selden observes, that many fabulous accounts have been invented of him; of which the following may suffice as a specimen. Eutychus patriarch of Alexandria relates, that the body of Adam having been embalmed according to his order, was deposited in a cave under a mountain of the children of Seth; but that Adam before his death had commanded that they should take away his remains from that place, and transport them to the middle of the earth: that Noah, to follow the orders of his ancestors, had preserved the bodies of Adam and all the patriarchs with him in the ark: that finding himself near his death, he ordered his son Shem to take the body of Adam, to furnish himself with bread and wine for his journey, to take with him Melchisedec the son of Phaleg, and to go to the place in which an angel would show them where to bury the first man: that Noah added this order, "Command Melchisedec to fix his residence in that place, and to live unmarried all his lifetime, because God has chosen him to do service in his presence; command him, that he build no temple, nor shed the blood of birds, nor four-footed beasts, or any other animal; and that he offer no other oblations to God but bread and wine." This is the reason, according to this author, why Melchisedec, when he met Abraham, brought forth only bread and wine. A Greek author, under the name of Athanasius, relates, that Melchisedec was the son of an idolatrous king called Melchi and of a queen called Salem.—Melchi, having resolved to offer a sacrifice to the gods, sent his son Melchisedec to fetch him seven calves. In the way the young prince was enlightened by God, and immediately returned to his father, to demonstrate to him the vanity of his idols. Melchi, in wrath, sent him back to fetch the victims. While he was absent, the king sacrificed his eldest son, and a great many Melchisedec's other children, to his gods. Melchisedec returning, and conceiving great horror at this butchery, retired to Mount Tabor, where he lived seven years, without clothes, and fed only on wild fruits. At the end of seven years, God appeared to Abraham, bid him go up to Mount Tabor, where he should find Melchisedec. He ordered him to clothe him, and to ask his blessing; which Abraham having done, Melchisedec anointed him with oil, and they came down together from the mountain.

MELCHITES

Pages 98-98

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the name given to the Syrian, Egyptian, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>. The Melchites, excepting some few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of little <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> no importance, which relate only to ceremonies and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, are in every respect professed Greeks; but they are governed by a particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a>, who resides at Damas, and assumes the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of patriarch of Antioch. They celebrate mats in the Arabian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> among the Melchites follow the rule of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> rule of all the Greek monks. They have four fine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> distant about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>'s journey from Damas, and never go out of the cloister.

MELCOMB REGIS

Pages 99-100

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a>, in England, 130 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, is situated at the mouth of the river Wey, by which it is parted from Weymouth. It appears from the name to have been anciently the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s demesne, and from the records to have paid quit-rent to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> all along after King Edward I. till it was bought off by the inhabitants before they were united to Weymouth. It lies on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the haven, on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> surrounded by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> except on the north. The streets are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and well paved, and many of the houses <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. It <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">lent</a> members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> in the reign of King Edward I. before Weymouth had that privilege. It was by parliament appointed a staple in the reign of Edward III. In the next reign the French burnt it; and it was thereby rendered so desolate, that the remaining inhabitants prayed and obtained a discharge from customs. On account of its quarrels with Weymouth, in the reign of Henry VI. its privileges as a port were removed to Poole; but in that of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> they were restored to it by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of parliament, which was confirmed in the next reign, on condition that Melcomb and Weymouth should make but one corporation, and enjoy their privileges in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>; and to this was owing the flourishing state of both. In the two reigns last mentioned, a wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> with seventeen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> was built from hence to Weymouth; to which, as well as its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> contributors were certain citizens of London; and upon its decay it was rebuilt in 1770. Here is a good market-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> and town-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, to which the members of the corporation of Weymouth come to attend public business, as the inhabitants do to its church for public worship. For several years past the sea has retired from it on the east, the priory formerly being bounded by the sea; but there is now a street beyond it, from which it is several paces to the high <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> mark. The priory was situated in the east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the town, in Maiden street, whose site occupied about an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>, now covered with tenements. On the south side are the remains of the chapel, now converted into a malt-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. Near it are the remains of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, formerly a nunnery. Here are three meeting houses and a workhouse for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. The church, which is in the middle of the town, has a wooden turret for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a>, and had been an old chapel. It was rebuilt in 1605, and made parochial, and is a handsome fabric, with a beautiful altarpiece painted and given by Sir James Thornhill. The port, which generally goes by the name of Weymouth, is said to be the best frequented in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, and is defended by Sandford and Portland castles. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> for both <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are Tuesdays and Fridays, but there are no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MELCOMB_REGIS">Melcomb-regis</a> is reckoned bigger, more thriving, and and populous than Weymouth. They are both but one corporation and borough, consisting of a mayor, recorder, two bailiffs, an uncertain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of aldermen, and twenty-four <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> burgesses. Whoever has been a mayor is ever after an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALDERMAN">alderman</a>. They send four burgesses to parliament, who are elected by such as have freeholds, whether they are inhabitants <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not; the number of voters is near 700. Every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a>, as in London, has the privilege of voting for four persons, who when chosen are returned, in two distinct indentures, as the burgesses of Weymouth and the burgesses of Melcombe-regis.

MELDAE

Pages 100-100

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Gallia Celtica, (called Meldorum Civitas in the Notitia), on the Matrona. Now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAUX">Meaux</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Champagne, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARNE">Marne</a>, in France.

MELEAGER

Pages 100-100

a Greek poet, the son of Eucrates, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SELEUCIA">Seleucia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, and flourished under the reign of Seleucus VI. the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Syria. He was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a>; and died in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Coos, anciently called Meropé. He there composed the Greek epigrams called by us the Anthologia. The disposition of the epigrams in this collection was often changed afterwards, and many additions have been made to them. The monk Planudes put them into the order they are in at present, in the year 1380.

MELEAGRIS

Pages 100-100

the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>; a genus of birds belonging to the order of gallinace. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MELES

Pages 100-100

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a fine river running by the walls of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>, with a cave at its head, where <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> is said to have written his poems. And from it Homer takes his original name Melichigenes, given him by his mother Critheis, as being born on its banks. (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>).

MELETIANS

Pages 100-100

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the name of a considerable party who adhered to the cause of Meletius bishop of Lycopolis, in Upper <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, after he was deposed, about the year 366, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of his having sacrificed to the gods, and having been guilty of other heinous crimes; though Epiphanius makes his only failing to have been an excessive severity against the lauded. This dispute, which was at first a personal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between Meletius and Peter, became a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> controversy; and the Meletian party subsisted in the fifth century, but was condemned by the first <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Nice.

MELIA

Pages 100-100

Azaderach, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Bead tree, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the decidua clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 23rd order Trihilatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MELIANTHUS

Pages 100-100
Honey-flower, a genus of plants belonging to the didynamia clas; and in the natural method ranking under the 24th order Corydaliae. See Botany Index.

MELIBOEA

Pages 100-100

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, at the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORONTES">Orontes</a>; which, before it falls into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, forms a spreading lake round it. This island was famous for its purple dye. Thought to be a colony of Thebians; and hence Lucretius's epithet, Thebaticus.

MELICA

Pages 100-100

ropegrass, a genus of the digynia order, belonging to the triandra clas of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 4th order <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAMINA">Gramina</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MELICERES

Pages 100-101

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, a kind of encysted tumour, MELICERTA mour, so called when their contents are of the con- sistence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. See TUMOUR, SURGERY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MELICERTA

Pages 101-101

MELICERTES, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Melicertus, in fa- bulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a son of Athamas and Ino. He was saved by his mother from the fury of his father, who prepared to dash him against a wall as he had done his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Leucrus. The mother was so terrified that she threw herself into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> with Melicerta in her arms. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> had compassion on the misfortunes of Ino and her son. He changed them both into sea deities. Ino was called Leucothoe or Matuta; and Melicerta was known among the Greeks by the name of Palamon, and among the Latins by that of Portunus. Some suppose that the Isthmian games were instituted in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Melicerta.

MELILLA

Pages 101-101

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>- dom of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEZ">Fez</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Garet. It was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-TA">ta</a>- ken by the Spaniards in 1469, but returned back to the Moors. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, 2. 9. N. Lat. 35° 20'. MELILLOT. See TRIFOLIUM, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> and AGRICUL- TURE <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MELINDA

Pages 101-101

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> on the east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, situated, according to some, between the third and fourth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of south latitude; though there is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> disagreement among geographers as to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. It is allowed by all, however, that the coasts are very dangerous; being full of rocks and shelves, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> at some seasons very liable to tempests. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>- dom of Melinda is for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> rich and fertile; producing almost all the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> except wheat and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, both which are brought thither from Cam- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAYA">baya</a> and other parts; and those who cannot purchase them make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of potatoes in their stead, which are here fine, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and in great plenty. They likewise abound with a great variety of fruit trees, roots, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, and other edibles, and with melons of exquisite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. They have also great plenty of venison, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>, oxen, sheep, hens, geese, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, &c. and one breed of sheep whose tails weigh between 30 and 40 pounds. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> is also called Melinda.

MELINUM

Pages 101-101

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">NATURAL</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">HISTORY</a>, the name of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> famous in the earliest ages of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, being the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> painters of antiquity; and, according to Pliny's account, one of the three colours with which alone they performed all their works. From the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> given of this earth it seems to be alu- minous, tolerably pure, and in a state of minute di- vision.

MELISSA

Pages 101-101

Balm, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the didynamia clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 42nd order Verticillate. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MELISSUS OF SAMOS

Pages 101-101

a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was the son of Rhagines and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Parmenides; and lived about 440 B.C. He pretended that the universe is infinite, immoveable, and without a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a>. Themistocles was among his pupils.

MELITE

Pages 101-101

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ANCIENT</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">GEOGRAPHY</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>, struck out of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Ionian <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> on account of the arrogance of the people, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a> admitted in lieu of it. The situation not said.

MELITENSIS TERRA

Pages 101-101

the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>: an earth of which there are two very different kinds; the one of which is a loam, the other a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARL">marl</a>. The latter is that known by medical authors under this name; the former is the Malta earth now in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; but both being brought from the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, are confusedly cal- led by the same name. The Maltese marl, which is the terra Melitensis of medical authors, is a loamy, crumbly, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> earth, of unequal and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> texture; and, when exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, soon falls into fine soft powder: but when preserved and dried, it becomes a loamy, light <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, of a dirty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, with a greyish <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a>; it is rough to the touch, adheres firmly to the tongue, is very easily crumbled to pow- der between the fingers, and stains the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. Thrown into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, it swells, and afterwards moulders a- way into a fine powder. It ferments very violently with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>. Both kinds are found in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Malta, and the latter has been much esteemed as a remedy against the bites of venomous animals. The other has supplied its place in the Ger- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> shops; and is used there as a cordial, sudorific, and astringent.

MELITO

Pages 101-101

bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDIS">Sardis</a> in Lydia, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century; remarkable for the apology he presented to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Aurelius, in favour of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; on which Eusebius and the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers bestow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> praises: but that apo- logy and Melito's other works are lost.

MELITUS

Pages 101-101

a Greek orator and poet, the accuser of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>. The Athenians, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of So- <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRATES">crates</a>, discovering the iniquity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> they had passed against that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, put Melitus to death, 420 B.C.

MELLER

Pages 101-101

a lake of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, 80 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and 30 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; on which stands the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a>.

MELLI

Pages 101-102

with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Mundingoes, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. The country formerly called Meli, now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>- ly inhabited by the Mundingoes, who still retain pretty much of the character ascribed to the people of Meli, fes to the south of the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAMBIA">Gambia</a>; on the west it borders on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Kabo; on the south it has Melli, properly so called, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> it from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>; and on the east it extends to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>- dom of Gago. With a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> part of this country we are little acquainted, as is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with regard to most of the inland territories of Africa; but towards the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> this country is a little better known. The first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> we meet with is Kachao, a Portuguese colony, situated on the river of St Do- mingo, which falls into the sea about 26 leagues below this town.—About 26 leagues above Kachao, on th Melilli, where, in the months of October and November, one may trade for about half the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of wax and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> which is traded for at Kachoa. Here are also some slaves to be bought.—Bot is a village near the mouth of the river Gelves, where most of the traders buy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>; which is in great plenty there, and very good.—Gelves is a village on a river of the same name, on which the Portuguese have a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a>. At Gelves one may trade yearly for 250 slaves, 80 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 100 quintals of wax, and as many of ivory. Near the mouth of the river of Gelves is a village called Kurbaldi, where there is a considerable trade for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>; here are also some slaves and ivory. Rio Grande, or the Great River, runs about 10 or 12 leagues to the south of the river of Gelves. About 80 leagues from the mouth of it is a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>, who are considerable traders in ivory, rice, millet, and some flaxes. They are called Anolons. Over against the mouth of Rio Grande is a cluster of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> called Biffago Isles; the most considerable of which is Caffaguet, being about six leagues <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; its <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is very good, and produces millet, rice, and all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, besides <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> and palm trees, and many others. This <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, with those of Carache, Canabac, and La Gallina, are the only ones where the Europeans may trade with some security. They trade, however, sometimes at the other islands, but they must be extremely cautious; and yet after all their precautions, they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be robbed and murdered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they venture to go ashore. The river Nunho runs 16 leagues to the south of Rio Grande; it is very considerable, and comes from a vast distance inland. One may buy here 300 quintals of ivory and 100 slaves a-year. Rice grows here admirably well, and is very cheap. There are everywhere <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> canes which grow naturally; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, which might turn to good account. The trade is carried on here from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> till August. In the river of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIERRA_LEONE">Sierra Leone</a>, the late <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> African <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a> of England had, in the year 1728, two islands; the one, called Taffo, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> flat island, near three leagues in circumference, in which the company's slaves had a good plantation; the rest of the island is covered with wood, among which are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> cotton trees of an unaccountable size. The other island is Benfe, wherein stood a regular fort. It was formerly the residence of one of the English chiefs.

MELMOTH

Pages 102-102

WILLIAM, Esq., a learned member of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>'s Inn, was born in 1666. In conjunction with Mr Peere Williams, Mr Melmoth was the publisher of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VERNON">Vernon</a>'s Reports, under an order of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>. He had once an intention of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> his own Reports; and a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> advertised them at the end of those of his coadjutor Peere Williams, as then actually preparing for the press. They have, however, not yet made their appearance. But the performance for which he justly deserves to be held in perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> is, "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Importance of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">Religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a>?" concerning which it may be mentioned, to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, that notwithstanding many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> editions had before been circulated, 42,000 copies of this useful treatise have been sold in the last 18 years. It is a somewhat singular circumstance, that the real author of this most admirable treatise should never before have been publicly known (it having been <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> attributed to the first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Melmota Egmont, and particularly by Mr Walpole in his Catalogue); which is the more surprising, as the author is plainly pointed out in the following short character prefixed to the book itself: "It may add <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, perhaps, to the reflections contained in the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a>, to inform the reader, that the author's life was one uniform exemplar of those precepts which, with so generous a zeal, and such an elegant and affecting simplicity of style, he endeavours to recommend to general practice. He left others to contend for modes of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, and inflame themselves and the world with endless controversy: it was the wiser purpose of his more ennobled aim, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> up to those clear rules of conduct which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> hath graciously prescribed. He possessed by temper every moral virtue; by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> every Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>. He had a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> that melted at every distress; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> which not only thought no evil, but suspected none. He exercised his profession with a skill and integrity which nothing could equal but the disinterested <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> that animated his labours, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the amiable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> which accompanied all his virtues. He employed his industry, not to gratify his own desires; no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> indulged himself less; not to accumulate useless wealth; no man more disdained so unworthy a pursuit: it was for the decent advancement of his family, for the generous affluence of his friends, for the ready relief of the indigent. How often did he exert his distinguished abilities, yet refuse the reward of them, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the widow, the fatherless, and him that had none to help him! In a word, few have ever passed a more useful, not one a more blameless life; and his whole time was employed either in doing good, or in meditating it. He died on the 6th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of April 1743; and lies buried under the cloister of Lincoln's Inn Chapel. MEM. FAT. OPT. MER. FIL. DIC." The son, by whom this character is drawn, is William Melmoth, Esq., the celebrated translator of Pliny and of Cicero's Letters; and author of those which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> under the name of Sir Thomas Fitzborne.

MELOCHIA

Pages 102-102

JEW'S MALLOW, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the monodelphia clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 37th order, Columiferæ. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MELODUNUM

Pages 102-102

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Cenones in Gallic Celtica, above Lutetia; now <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MELUN">Melun</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of France, on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>.

MELODY

Pages 102-103

in music, a succession of sounds ranged in such a manner, according to the laws of rhythmus and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODULATION">modulation</a>, that it may form a sentiment agreeable to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>. Vocal melody is called singing; and that which is performed upon instruments may be termed symphonic melody. The idea of rhythmus necessarily enters into that of melody. An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is not an air but in proportion as the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> are observed. The same succession of sounds is susceptible of as many different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, as many different kinds of melody, as the various ways by which its emphatic notes, and the quantities of those which intervene, may be diversified; and the change in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of the notes alone, may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> that very succession in such a manner that it cannot be known. Thus, melody in itself is nothing; it is the rhythmus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> measure which determines it, and there can be no air without <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> then we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> measure... measure from both, we cannot compare melody with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>; for to the former it is essential, but not at all to the latter. Melody, according to the manner in which it is considered, has a relation to two different principles. When regarded only as agreeable to the proportions of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> and the rules of modulation, it has its principle in harmony; since it is a harmonical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a>, which exhibits the different gradations of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, the chords peculiar to each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a>, and the laws of modulation, which are the sole elements that compose an air. According to this principle, the whole power of melody is limited to that of pleasing the ear by agreeable sounds, as the eye may be pleased with an agreeable assemblage of suitable colours. But when considered as an imitative art, by which we may affect the mind with various images, excite different emotions in the heart, inflame or soothe the passions; by which, in a word, we produce different effects upon our moral faculties, which are not to be effectuated by the influence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> alone, we must explore another principle for melody: for in our whole internal frame there appears to be no power upon which either harmony alone, or its necessary results, can <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a>, to affect us in such a manner. What then is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> principle? It is as much founded on <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> as the first; but, in order to discover its foundation in nature, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> require a more accurate though simpler observation, and a more exquisite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> in the observer. This principle is the same which varies the tone of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, when we speak; according as we are interested in what we say, and according to the different emotions which we feel in expressing it. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCENT">accent</a> of languages which determines the melody of every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; it is the accent which determines us to employ the emphasis of speaking while we sing, and to speak with more or less energy according as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> which we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is more or less accented. That language whose accents are the most sensible, ought to produce a more passionate and more lively melody; that which has little accentuation, or none at all, can only produce a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and languid melody, without character and without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>. These are the true principles: in proportion as we depart from them, when we speak of the power of music upon the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> heart, we shall become unintelligible to ourselves and others: our words will be without meaning. If music does not impress the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> with images but by melody, if from thence it obtains its whole power, it must follow, that all musical sounds which are not pleasing by themselves alone, however agreeable to harmony they may be, is not an imitative music; and, being incapable, even with its most beautiful chords, either to present the images of things, or to excite the finer feelings, very soon cloy the ear, and leaves always the heart in cold indifference.
