It follows likewise, that notwithstanding the parts which harmony has introduced, and which the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of music so wantonly abuses, wherever two different melodies are heard at the same time, they counteract each other, and destroy the effects of both, however beautiful each may be when performed alone: from whence it may be judged with what degree of taste the French composers have introduced in their operas the miserable practice of accompanying one air with another, as well in singing, which is the native expression of pathos and sentiment, as in instrumental performances; which is the same thing as if whimsical orators should take it in their heads to recite two orations at the same time, that the elegance of each might derive more force from the other. So much for Rousseau. The translator, however, has reason to fear, that the causes by which national melody is diversified and characterized, are more profound and permanent than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> accentuation of language. This indeed may have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> influence in determining the nature of the rhythmus, and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of emphatic notes; but very little in regulating the nature of the emphasis and expression themselves. If Rousseau's principle be true in its full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, he must of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> acknowledge, that an air which was never set or intended for words, however melodious, cannot be imitative; he must likewise confess, that what is imitative in one nation cannot be such in another: nor can it be denied, upon his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, that the recitative, which is formed upon the mode of speaking, is the most forcible of all melodies; which is absurd. His other observations are at once judicious and profound. Though it is impossible to exhibit the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and variety of harmony by playing the same melody at the same time upon different keys, admitting those keys to form among themselves a perfect chord, which will of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> preserve all the subsequent notes in the same intervals; yet this perfect harmony would by no means be uniformly pleasing to the ear. We must therefore of necessity introduce less perfect chords to vary and increase the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and these chords in any complex system of music must of necessity produce dissonances. It then becomes the business of the composer to be careful that these dissonances may arise as naturally from, and return as naturally to perfect harmony as possible. All these causes must inevitably vary the melody of the different parts; but still, amidst all these difficulties, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> ought to be zealous in preserving the melody of each as homogeneous with the others as possible, that the result of the whole may be in some measure uniform. Otherwise, by counteracting each other, the parts will reciprocally destroy the effects one of another.

MELOE

Pages 103-103

a genus of insects of the order of coleoptera. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MELON

Pages 103-103

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of cucumis, in the Linnæan system. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">Water</a> Melon. See Anguria, Botany Index.

MELOS

Pages 103-103

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> between <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a> and Peloponnese, about 24 miles from Syllaum. It is about 60 miles in circumference, and of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. It enjoyed its independence for about 700 years before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Peloponnesian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. This island was originally peopled by a Lacedemonian colony, 1116 years before the Christian era. For this reason the inhabitants refused to join the rest of the island and the Athenians against the Peloponnesians. This refusal was severely punished. The Athenians took Melos, and put to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> all such as were able to bear arms. The women and children were made slaves, and the island left desolate. An Athenian colony repeopled it, till Lygander reconquered it and re-established the original inhabitants in their possessions.

MELOTHRIA

Pages 103-104

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the triandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 34th order, Cucurbitaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MELPOMENE

Pages 104-104

in Fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and Mnemosyne. She presided over tragedy. Horace has addressed the finest of his odes to her, as to the patroness of lyric <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. She was generally represented as a young woman with a serious countenance. Her garments were splendid; she wore a bulkin, and held a dagger in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and in the other a sceptre and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>.

MELROSE

Pages 104-104

a town of Scotland, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Selkirk, and on the confines of Tweedale, seated on the south side of the river Tweed; with an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, now in ruins. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, 2. 32. N. Lat. 55° 32'. This abbey was founded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> I. in 1136. He peopled it with Cistercians brought from Rievaulx abbey in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, and dedicated it to the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>. At the reformation James Douglas was appointed commendator, who took <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> much of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, in order to furnish materials for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> to himself, which still remains, and is dated 1590. Nothing is left of the abbey excepting a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the cloister walls elegantly carved; but the ruins of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> are of most uncommon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. Part is at present used for divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, the rest uncovered; but every part does <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a>.—Alexander II. was buried beneath the great altar, and it is also the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERMENT">interment</a> of the Douglases and other potent families.—Its situation is extremely pleasant. MELT OF FISHES. In the melt of a living cod there are such numbers of those animacules said to be found in the semen of all <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> animals, that in a drop of its juice no larger than a grain of sand, there are contained more than 12,000 of them; and considering how many such quantities there are in the whole melt of one such fish, it is not incredible, that there are more animals in one melt of it than there are living men at one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. However strange and romantic such a conjecture must appear, a serious consideration and calculation <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> make it very evident. An hundred such grains of sand as those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned will make about an inch in length; therefore in a cubic inch there will be a million of such sands; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there be 10,000 animals in each of those quantities, there must be in the whole 150,000 millions, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> vastly exceeding that of mankind, even supposing the whole as populous as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>.

MELTING CONE

Pages 104-104

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSAYING">assaying</a>, an hollow cone of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, into which melted metallic substances are thrown, in order to free them from their fusible. When a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is melted, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be sufficient to rub the inside of the cone with grease; but when the quantity is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, especially <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it contains any thing sulphurous, this caution of allowing the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a> is not sufficient. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the assayer has recourse to a lute reduced to thin pap with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which effectually prevents any injury to the cone.

MELTON MOWBRAY

Pages 104-104

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a>, 108 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> well-built <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, in a fertile <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>; with a market on Tuesday, the most considerable for cattle of any in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. It is almost encompassed with a little river called the Eye, over which it has two fine bridges; and has a large handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, with a free school. Here are frequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> races, and three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> in the year.

MELVIL

Pages 104-104

SIR JAMES, descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> Scots family, being the third son of the laird of Kaeth, was born about the middle of the 16th century. He went to France very young, in the capacity of page to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, then married to the dauphin; and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of her husband, followed her to Scotland, where he was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of her chamber, and admitted a privy counsellor. She employed him in her most important concerns, till her unhappy confinement in Lochleven, all which he discharged with the utmost fidelity; and, from his own accounts, there is reason to conclude, that, had she taken his advice, she might have avoided many of her misfortunes. When she was prisoner in England, she recommended him strongly to her son James; with whom he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in favour and employment until the death of Queen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>; James would then have taken him to England; but Melvil, now grown old, was desirous of retiring from business, and in his retirement he drew up the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of his past <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his son. These Memoirs were accidentally found in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> castle in the year 1662, though nobody knew how they came to be deposited there; and were published in folio in 1683.

MEMBER

Pages 104-104

is also used to denote some particular order <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in a state or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>: thus we say, "member of a corporation, member of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, member of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, &c."

MEMBERS

Pages 104-104

in Anatomy, the exterior parts, arising from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> body of an animal, like the boughs from the trunk of a tree.

MEMBRANE

Pages 104-104

Membrana, in Anatomy, a similar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of an animal body; being a thin, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>, expanded skin, formed of several sorts of fibres interwoven together, and serving to cover <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wrap up certain parts of the body. See ANATOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MEMEL

Pages 104-104
or Memmel; a town of Prussia, situated on the northern extremity of the Curische Haf, an inlet of the sea about 70 miles in length, which is here joined to the Baltic by a narrow strait.—It is an ill built town, with narrow dirty streets; but remarkable for its extensive commerce, being provided with the finest harbour in the Baltic. In 1784, 996 ships, amongst which were 500 English, arrived here. The imports chiefly are, salt, iron, and salted herrings; the exports, which greatly exceed the imports, are amber, corn, hemp, flax, and particularly timber. An English consul resides here. The trade is daily increasing, on account of the high duties which the court of Russia has laid on the imports of Riga.

MEMNON

Pages 104-105

in Fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Ethiopia, son of Tithonus and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AURORA">Aurora</a>. He came with a body of 10,000 men to assist his uncle Priam, during the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. He behaved with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> courage, and killed Antilochus, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NESTOR">Nestor</a>'s son. The aged father challenged lenged the Ethiopian monarch; but Mennon refused it on account of the venerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of Nestor, and accepted that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>. He was killed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>, in the fight of the Grecian and Trojan armies. Aurora prayed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> her son such honours as might distinguish him from other mortals. The god consented; and immediately a numerous flight of birds issued from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> pile on which the body was laid, and dividing themselves into two separate bodies, fought with such fury, that above half of them fell <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in the fire as victims to appease the manes of Mennon. These birds were called Memnonides; and it has been observed by some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, that they never failed to return yearly to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of Mennon in Troas, and repeat the same bloody engagement in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> from whom they received their name. The Ethiopians <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Egyptians, over whom Mennon reigned, erected a celebrated statue to the honour of their monarch. This statue had the wonderful <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of uttering a melodious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> at sunrise, like that which is heard at the breaking of the string of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a> when it is wound up. This was effected by the rays of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> when they fell upon it. At the setting of the sun, and in the night, the sound was lugubrious. This is supported by the testimony of the geographer Strabo, who confesses himself ignorant whether it proceeded from the basis of the statue, or the people that were then around it. This celebrated statue was dismantled by order of Cambyses when he conquered <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>; and its ruins still astonish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> travellers by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. Mennon of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, one of the generals of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> king of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, advised that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> to lay waste the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, in order to deprive Alexander the Great's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of support, and afterwards to attack Macedon; but this counsel was disapproved by Darius's other generals. Mennon behaved at the passage of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANICUS">Granicus</a> like an experienced general. He afterwards defended the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Miletum with great courage; seized the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIO">Chio</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LESBOS">Lesbos</a>; spread terror throughout all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; and would have put a stop to the conquests of Alexander, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had not been prevented by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Barina, Mennon's widow, was taken prisoner with Darius's wife, and Alexander had a son by her named <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>.

MEMOIRS

Pages 105-105

in matters of literature, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, written by persons who had some share in the transactions they relate; answering to what the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> called Commentarius.—The journals of the proceedings of a literary <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a collection of matters transferred therein, are likewise called Memoirs.

MEMORY

Pages 105-105

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of the mind, which presents to us <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> notions of what is past accompanied with a persuasion that the things themselves were formerly real and present. What we distinctly remember to have perceived, we as firmly believe to have happened, as what is now present to our senses.

MEMPHIS

Pages 107-108

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence of the kings in the Higher <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>; distant from the Delta to the south 15 miles, according to Pliny. Called also Moph, and Noph, in scripture. Though this city is now so completely ruined, that authors greatly disagree concerning its situation; yet Strabo informs us that in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it was the most magnificent in Egypt, next to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>. It was called the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and there was an entire temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APIS">Apis</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sacred ox was kept and worshipped. In the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was an apartment of the mother of the ox; a very magnificent temple of Vulcan; a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a> or space for fighting bulls; and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> colossus in the middle of the city, which was thrown <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. There was likewise a temple of Venus, and a Serapium in a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> place, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> heaps up hills of sand very dangerous to travellers; together with a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of sphinxes, the heads of some of them only being visible, the others covered up to the middle of their body. The same author likewise informs us, that in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the city there were many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>; and that it contained a number of palaces, at that time in ruins. These buildings, he said, formerly stood upon an eminence; they lay along the side of the hill, stretching down to the lakes and groves, 40 stadia from the city. There was likewise a mountain in the neighbourhood, on which were a great number of pyramids, with the sepulchres of the kings, among which were three remarkable, and two of them accounted wonders of the world. From this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, Mr Bruce concludes that the celebrated capital of Egypt stood in the place where the villages of Metrahenny are now situated; in opposition to Dr Shaw's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, who thinks it was situated at Geeza or Gifa. M. Savary has also shown, that Gifa was not the situation of the ancient Memphis. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, he says, on the western <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, on the spot where the village of Memph now stands, which still preserves the name. Large heaps of rubbish are still to be seen there; but the Arabs have transported to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a> the columns and remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, which they have disposed, without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and without order, in their mosques and public buildings. This city extended as far as Saccara; and was almost wholly encompassed by lakes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of which are still subsiding. It was necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> them to convey the dead to the sepulchre of their fathers. The tombs, hewn out of the rock, were closed up with stones of a proportionable size, and covered with sand. These bodies embalmed with so much care, preserved with so much respect, are torn from the monuments they repose in, and sold without decency to strangers by the inhabitants of Saccara. This place is called the plain of mummies. There too we find the well of the birds, into which one descends by means of a rope. It leads to subterranean galleries, filled with earthen vases containing the sacred birds. They are rarely met with entire, because the Arabs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> them in hopes of finding idols of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. They do not conduct travellers into the places where they have found more precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. They even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> them up carefully, referring to themselves some secret <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> by which they defend. In a journey into Egypt made by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENANDER">Menander</a> de Chaulnes, he advanced very far into these winding labyrinths, sometimes crawling, and sometimes scrambling on his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>. Informed by Mr Edward Worley Montague, who has carefully visited Egypt, he arrived at one of those passages which had an opening shut up from without by branches of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> tree interwoven, and covered with sand. He remarked there some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a> in relief, executed in the highest perfection. But the Arabs refused every offer he made them to permit him to take drawings of them, or to mould them, in order to preserve their form. The duke de Chaulnes is of opinion that these hieroglyphics, sculptured with so much art that the objects they represent may be discovered at the first sight, might possibly furnish the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a> of the others, whose contours are simply expressed, and form a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a> of this unintelligible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. Several pyramids are distinguishable along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which bound Saccara on the west, the greatest part of which appear as lofty as those of Gifa. See PYRAMIDS.

MENAGE

Pages 108-108

denotes a collection of animals; whence we have derived the word menagerie.

MENANDER

Pages 108-108

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greek poet, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> in the same year with Epicurus, which was the third of the 109th Olympiad. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> in introducing the new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>, and refining an art which had been so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> and licentious in former times, quickly spread his name over the world. Pliny informs us, that the kings of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> and Macedon gave a noble testimony of his merit, by sending ambassadors to invite him to their courts, and even fleets to bring him over; but that Menander was so much of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, as to prefer the free enjoyment of his studies to the promised favours of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. Of his works, which amounted to above 100 comedies, we have had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> loss, the originals being not only vanished, but the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of them, when copied by Terence, having unfortunately perished by shipwreck before they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> Rome. Yet the four plays which Terence borrowed from him before that accident happened, are still preserved in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>; and it is chiefly from Terence that most people form their judgement of Menander, the fragments that remain of him not being sufficient to enable them to do it. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> have paid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> things of Menander; and we find the old masters of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> recommending his works as the true patterns of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> of public speaking. Quintilian declares, that a careful <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of Menander only, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> satisfy all the rules he has laid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in his institutions. It is in Menander that he would have his orator search for a copiousness of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, for a happy elegance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, and especially for that universal genius which is able to accommodate itself to persons, things, and affections.—But Julius Caesar has left the loftiest as well as the justest praise of Menander's works, when he calls Terence only a Half-Menander. For while the virtues of the Latin poet are so deservedly admired, it is impossible we should raise a higher notion of excellency than to conceive the great original still shining with half its lustre unreflected, and preserving an equal part of its graces, above the power of the best copier in the world. Menander died in the 3d year of the 122d Olympiad.

MENANDRIANS

Pages 108-109

the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> branch of Gnostics; thus called from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENANDER">Menander</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, said by some, without sufficient foundation, to have been a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Simon Magus, and himself a reputed magician. He taught, that no person could be saved, unless he were baptised in his name; and he conferred a peculiar sort of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, which would render those who received it immortal in the next world: exhibiting himself to the world, with the phrasery of a lunatic more than the founder of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, as a promised favourer. For it appears by the testimonies of Irenaeus, Justin, and Tertullian, that he pretended to be one of the sons sent from the pleroma, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> regions, to succour the souls that lay groaning under bodily oppression and servitude; and to maintain them against the violence and stratagems of the demons that hold the reins of empire in this sublunary world. As this doctrine was built upon the same foundation with that of Simon Magus, the ancient writers looked upon him as the instructor of Menander. See SIMONIANS.

MENASSEH BEN ISRAEL

Pages 109-109

a celebrated rabbi, born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> about the year 1604, was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Ben Israel, and followed his father into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. Here he was educated by Rabbi <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Uziel, under whom he in a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> made such progress in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> tongue, that at 18 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> he succeeded him in the synagogue of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> several years, and married Rachel of the family of the Abarbanels, whom the Jews imagine to be descended from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>. He afterwards went to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Ephraim, a rich merchant, who had settled at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>; by whose advice he entered into trade. Some time after, the hopes of a more agreeable settlement induced him to come into England, under the protectorship of Cromwell; who gave him a very favourable reception, and one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> entertained him at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> with several other learned divines. However, he soon after passed into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>; and died at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDDLEBURG">Middleburg</a>, about the year 1657. The Jews at Amsterdam obtained his body, and interred it at their expense. He was of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARISEES">Pharisees</a>; had a lively <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> judgement, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning, and all the virtues that can adorn private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He wrote many works in Hebrew, Latin, Spanish, and English. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of those published in Latin, are: 1. His Concilior; a learned and curious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, in which he reconciles those <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of Scripture which seem to contradict each other. 2. De resurrectione mortuorum. 3. De termino vitae. 4. Dissertatio de fragilitate humana, ex lafis Adami, deque Divino in bono opere Mendel-auxilio. 5. Spes Israël. Dr Thomas Pococke has written ten life in English.

MENDELSON

Pages 109-109

MOSES, that is, Moses the son of Mendel, a Jew of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, and one of the most celebrated writers in Germany, died there in the year 1785 at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 57. His fourth attempt as an author was soon after 1767, by a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> entitled <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>; in which, besides other bold and unjustifiable opinions, he maintains, that the Jews have a revealed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> but not a revealed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; that opinions are not subjects of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a>; and that the only religion of the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> is that of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. He acquired <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> by his Phaedon, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> "Discourses on the Immateriality and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">Immortality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">Soul</a>," translated into the French 1773, 8vo; in which he unfolds this important <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, the great foundation of all morality, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of an enlightened <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and the charms of an elegant writer. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this excellent work, he was styled the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> by some of the periodical writers; but he wanted the firmness and courage of the Grecian philosopher. His timidity, and even pusillanimity, defects too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> men, prevented him from being of any essential <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to his nation; of which he might have become the benefactor by being the reformer. The pliancy of his character, his soft, modest, and obliging disposition, gained him the esteem alike of the superstitious and of the incredulous. After all, he could never procure admission to the Berlin <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, or to the conveivation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>. At his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> he received from his nation those honours which are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> paid to their first rabbins. Contrary to an imprudent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> prevalent among the Jews of burying their dead before sunset, his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERMENT">interment</a> was delayed till 24 hours after he expired. Though Mendelsion was descended from a respectable family, he was very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. In early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he entered into a counting-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of his own nation, wherein he greatly recommended himself by his capacity and integrity in business: But <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and literature soon became his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> occupation; and to the famous Lessing he was indebted for counsels which, without diverting his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> from those pursuits that were necessary to his subsistence, accelerated his progress in his literary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a>. Even after the death of his benefactor, Mendelsion retained for him the sincerest regard and the most lively <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>. Notwithstanding the very strict regimen which he observed, he survived him only a few years; for his feeble frame and weak <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> were gradually and insensibly undermined by intense application to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>.

MENDEZ PINTO

Pages 109-110

FERDINAND, was born at Montemor-o-Velho in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, and was at first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> to a Portuguese <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of making a fortune, he embarked for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> in 1537. His vessel being taken by the Turks on his passage, he was carried to Mocka, and sold to a Greek renegade, and afterwards to a Jew, in whose possession he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till he was redeemed by the governor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORMUS">Ormus</a>, a Portuguese fort. The governor procured him an opportunity of going out to India, agreeable to his first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. During a residence of twenty-one years in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he was witness to very important transactions, and experienced many singular adventures. He returned to Portugal in 1558, where he enjoyed the reward <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a> of his labours, after having been thirteen times a slave and sixteen times sold. A very curious account of his travels was written by himself, and published at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>, A.D. 1614, in folio. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was translated into French by Bernard Figuier, a Portuguese gentleman, and printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> 1645, in 4to. It is written in a very interesting manner, and in a style more elegant than might have been expected from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> whose whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was spent in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> and in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>. It elucidates a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of particulars relating to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, and manners of the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEGU">Pegu</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a>, Achem, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>, &c. Many of his facts appeared fabulous, but their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> has since been ascertained. M. de Surgi compiled an interesting history from the most singular facts in Mendez Pinto's relation, which he published in the Vicissitudes de la Fortune, Paris, 2 vols. 8vo.

MENDICANTS

Pages 110-111
or BEGGING FRIARS, several orders of religious in Popish countries, who having no settled revenues, are supported by the charitable contributions they receive from others. This sort of society began in the 13th century; and the members of it, by the tenor of their institution, were to remain entirely destitute of all fixed revenues and possessions; though in process of time their number became a heavy tax upon the people. Innocent III. was the first of the popes who perceived the necessity of instituting such an order; and accordingly he gave such monastic societies, as made a pretension of poverty, the most distinguishing marks of his protection and favour. They were also encouraged and patronized by the succeeding pontiffs, when experience had demonstrated their public and extensive usefulness. But when it became generally known, that they had such a peculiar place in the esteem and protection of the rulers of the church, their number grew to such an enormous and unwieldy multitude, and swarmed so prodigiously in all the European provinces, that they became a burden, not only to the people, but to the church itself. The great inconvenience that arose from the excessive multiplication of the mendicant orders was remedied by Gregory X. in a general council, which he assembled at Lyons in 1272. For here all the religious orders that had sprung up after the council held at Rome in 1215, under the pontificate of Innocent III. were suppressed; and the extravagant multitude of mendicants, as Gregory called them, were reduced to a smaller number, and confined to the four following societies or denominations, viz. the Dominicans, the Franciscans, the Carmelites, and the Augustins or hermits of St. Augustine. As the pontiffs allowed these four mendicant orders the liberty of travelling wherever they thought proper, of conversing with persons of every rank, of instructing the youth and multitude wherever they went; and as those monks exhibited, in their outward appearance and manner of life, more striking marks of gravity and holiness than were observable in the other monastic societies, they rose all at once to the very summit of fame, and were regarded with the utmost esteem and veneration through all the countries of Europe. The enthusiastic attachment to these sanctimonious beggars went so far, that, as we learn from the most authentic records, several cities were divided or cantoned out into four parts, with a view to these four orders; the first part being assigned to the Dominicans, the second to the Franciscans, the third to the Carmelites, and the fourth to the Augustins. The people were unwilling to receive the sacraments from any other hands than those of the mendicants, to whose churches they crowded to perform their devotions, while living, and were extremely delirious to depose there also their remains after death: nor did the influence and credit of the mendicants end here; for we find in the history of this and of the succeeding ages, that they were employed, not only in spiritual matters, but also in temporal and political affairs of the greatest consequence, in composing the differences of princes, concluding treaties of peace, concerting alliances, presiding in cabinet councils, governing courts, levying taxes, and other occupations, not only remote from, but absolutely inconsistent with, the monastic character and profession. However, the power of the Dominicans and Franciscans greatly surpassed that of the other two orders: in much that these two orders were, before the Reformation, what the Jesuits have been since that happy and glorious period, the very soul of the hierarchy, the engines of the state, the secret springs of all the motions of the one and the other, and the authors and directors of every great and important event, both in the religious and political world. By very quick progression their pride and confidence arrived at such a pitch, that they had the presumption to declare publicly, that they had a divine impulse and commission to illustrate and maintain the religion of Jesus; they treated with the utmost insolence and contempt all the different orders of the priesthood; they affirmed, without a blush, that the true method of obtaining salvation was revealed to them alone; proclaimed, with ostentation, the superior efficacy and virtue of their indulgencies; and vaunted beyond measure their interest at the court of heaven, and their familiar connexions with the Supreme Being, the Virgin Mary, and the saints in glory. By these impious wiles, they so deluded and captivated the miserable, and blinded the multitude, that they would not intrust any other but the mendicants with the care of their souls. They retained their credit and influence to such a degree, towards the close of the 14th century, that great numbers of both sexes, some in health, others in a state of infirmity, and others at the point of death, earnestly desired to be admitted into the mendicant order, which they looked upon as a sure and infallible method of rendering heaven propitious. Many made it an essential part of their last wills, that their bodies after death should be wrapped in old ragged Dominican or Franciscan habits, and interred among the mendicants. For such was the barbarous superstition and wretched ignorance of this age, that people universally believed they should readily obtain mercy from Christ, at the day of judgement, if they appeared before his tribunal associated with the mendicant friars. About this time, however, they fell under an universal odium; but being resolutely protected against all opposition, whether open or secret, by the popes, who regarded them as their best friends and most effectual supports, they suffered little or nothing from the efforts of their numerous adversaries. In the 15th century, century, besides their arrogance, which was excessive, a quarrelsome and litigious spirit prevailed among them, and drew upon them justly the displeasure and indignation of many. By affording refuge at this time to the Beguins in their order, they became offensive to the bishops, and were hereby involved in difficulties and perplexities of various kinds. They lost their credit in the 16th century by their rustic impudence, their ridiculous superstitions, their ignorance, cruelty, and brutish manners. They discovered the most barbarous aversion to the arts and sciences, and expressed a like abhorrence of certain eminent and learned men, who endeavoured to open the paths of science to the pursuits of the studious youth, recommended the culture of the mind, and attacked the barbarism of the age in their writings and discourses. Their general character, together with other circumstances, concurred to render a reformation desirable, and to accomplish this happy event. Among the number of mendicants are also ranked the Capuchins, Recollets, Minims, and others, who are branches or derivations from the former. Buchanan tells us, the mendicants in Scotland, under an appearance of beggary, lived a very luxurious life; whence one wittily called them, not Mendicant but Monducati friars.

MENECRATES

Pages 111-111

a physician of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a>, who flourished about 365 B.C. is famous for his skill in his profession, but much more for his vanity. He would always be followed by some of the patients he had cured, and with whom he previously stipulated that they should follow him wherever he went. One appeared with the attributes of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, another with those of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, and others again with those of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Æsculapius; while he, clad in a purple robe, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> on his head, and a sceptre in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, presented himself, to the admiration of the public, under the name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, and travelled through different countries escorted by these counterfeit deities. He once wrote the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Macedon: Menecrates Jupiter to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, greeting. Thou reignest in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, and I in medicine; thou givest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> to those who are in good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, I restore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to the sick; thy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> is composed of Macedonians; the gods themselves constitute mine." Philip answered him in a word, that he wished him restored to reason. Learning some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after that he was in Macedon, Philip sent for him, and invited him to an entertainment. Menecrates and his companions were placed on rich and lofty couches; before which was an altar, covered with the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>; and whilst an excellent repast was served up to the other guests, perfumes and libations only were offered to these new gods, who, unable to endure the affront, hastily left the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, in which they never more made their appearance.

MENEDEMUS

Pages 111-111

a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, born at Erythreum, was the son of Callichenes, and one of Phedo's followers. He was in the greatest esteem, and enjoyed several important posts in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. He several times defended Erythreum with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> bravery, and died of grief when Antigonus became <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of it. A person one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> saying to him, "It is a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> to have what we desire," he replied, "It is a much greater to desire nothing but what we have." He flourished about 300 B.C.

MENELAUS

Pages 111-111

the son of Atreus, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Agamemnon, reigned at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>, when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> deprived him of his wife Helen. This <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">rape</a> occasioned the famous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>. See Helen. Menelaus, a mathematician in the reign of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Trajan, wrote three books on the Sphere, which have been published by Father Marleme.

MENES

Pages 111-111

born at This, a town of Thebais in Upper <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, was the founder of the Egyptian empire. He had three sons, viz. Athotis, who ruled after him, at This and Thebes; Curudes, who in Lower Egypt founded the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELIOPOLIS">Heliopolis</a>, which afterward was the kingdom of Diospoli; and Necherophes, who reigned at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMPHIS">Memphis</a>. It is thought this Menes reigned 117 years after the birth of Phaleg, son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBER">Heber</a>, which was the very year of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a> of the people throughout the whole <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> Memphis, he stopped the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a> near it, by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of a caufeway 100 furlongs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and caused it to run through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>.

MENIALS

Pages 111-111
domestic or household servants, who live under their lord or master's roof.

MENINGES

Pages 111-111
or MENYNGES, in Anatomy, a name given to the dura and pia mater of the brain. See Anatomy, No 129.

MENIPPEAN

Pages 111-111

a kind of satire consisting of prose and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> intermixed. It is thus called from Menippus a cynic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> who delighted in composing satirical letters, &c. In <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of him, Varro also wrote satires under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Satire Menippae: whence this sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> is also denominated Varronian satire. Among the moderns there is a famous piece under this title first published in 1594, against the chiefs of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a>, called also the Catholicon of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. It is esteemed a masterpiece for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>.

MENIPPUS

Pages 111-111

a cynic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> of Phoenicia. He was originally a slave, but obtained his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> with a sum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and became one of the greatest orators at Thebes. He grew so desperate from the continual reproaches and insults to which he was daily exposed on account of his meanness, that he destroyed himself. He wrote 13 books of satires, which have been lost.

MENISCUS

Pages 111-111

in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, a glass <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENS">lens</a>, concave on one side and convex on the other; sometimes also called lunula. See Optics.

MENISPERMUM

Pages 111-111

moonseed, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dicotyledon class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 11th order, Serrantaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MENIXN

Pages 111-111

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Mediterranean, to the west of the Syrtis <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>. Supposed by Strabo and Polybius to be <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOTOPHAGI">Lotophagi</a>; and hence <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> and Eratothenes denominate the island Lotophagitis, with a cognominal town Meninx. It was the country of Vibius <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLUS">Gallus</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, and of Volusianus. Now called Gerbi and Zarbi.

MENNONITES

Pages 111-113

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> in the United Provinces, in most respects the same with those in other places called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANABAPTISTS">Anabaptists</a>. They had their rise in 1536, when Menno Simon, a native of Friesland, who had been a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, and a notorious profligate, resigned his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and office in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and publicly embraced the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> of the Anabaptists. Menno was born at Witmarsum, a village in the neighbourhood of Bolsward in Friesland, in the year 1505, and died in 1561 in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a>, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> seat of a certain nobleman not far from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Oldenlooe, who, moved with compassion by a view of the perils to which Menno was exposed, and the snares that were daily laid for his ruin, took him with certain of his associates into his protection, and gave him an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a>. The writings of Menno, which are almost all composed in the Dutch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, were published in folio at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> in the year 1651. About the year 1627, Menno was earnestly solicited by many of the sect with which he connected himself, to assume among them the rank and functions of a public teacher; and as he looked upon the persons who made this proposal to be exempt from the fanatical frenzy of their brethren at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a> (though according to other accounts they were originally of the same stamp, only rendered somewhat wiser by their sufferings), he yielded to their entreaties. From this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> to the end of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he travelled from one country to another with his wife and children, exercising his ministry, under persecutions and calamities of various kinds, that succeeded each other without interruption, and constantly exposed to the danger of falling a victim to the severity of the laws. East and West Friesland, together with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRONINGEN">Groningen</a>, were first visited by this zealous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> of the Anabaptists; from whence he directed his course into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, Guelderland, Brabant, and Westphalia, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> it through the German provinces that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> on the coasts of the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and penetrated as far as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>. In all these places his ministerial labours were attended with remarkable success, and added to his sect a prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of followers. Hence he is deservedly considered as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of almost all the Anabaptists, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> of the sect that still subsists under that denomination. Menno was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of genius, undirected by a very <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> judgment; he possessed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and persuasive eloquence, and such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of learning as made him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> for an oracle in the estimation of the multitude. He appears, moreover, to have been a man of probity, of a meek and tractable spirit, gentle in his manners, pliable and obsequious in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with persons of all ranks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, and extremely zealous in promoting practical <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and virtue, which he recommended by his example as well as by his precepts. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of doctrine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> drawn up by Menno was of a much more mild and moderate <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> than that of the furious and fanatical Anabaptists, whose tumultuous proceedings have been recited under that article, but somewhat more severe, though more clear and confident, than the doctrine of the wiser branches of that sect, who aimed at nothing more than the restoration of the Christian church to its primitive purity. Accordingly he condemned the plan of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> discipline that was founded on the prospect of a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, to be miraculously established by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ on the ruins of civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> and the destruction of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> rulers, and which had been the fatal and pestilential source of such dreadful commotions, such execrable rebellions, and such enormous crimes. He declared publicly his dislike of that doctrine, which pointed out the approach of a marvellous reformation in the church by the means of a new and extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EFFUSION">effusion</a> of the Holy Spirit. He expressed his abhorrence of the licentious tenets, which several of the Anabaptists had maintained, with respect to the unlawfulness of polygamy and divorce; and finally, considered as unworthy of toleration those fanatics who were of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the Holy Ghost continued to descend into the minds of many chosen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEVERS">believers</a>, in as extraordinary a manner as he did at the first establishment of the Christian church, and that he testified this peculiar presence to several of the faithful by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>, predictions, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a>, and visions of various kinds. He retained indeed the doctrines <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> received among the Anabaptists, in relation to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MILLENNIUM">millennium</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 1000 years reign of Christ upon <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of magistrates from the Christian church, the abolition of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and the prohibition of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> enjoined by our Saviour, and the vanity as well as the pernicious effects of human science. But while Menno retained these doctrines in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, he explained and modified them in such a manner as made them resemble the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> tenets that were universally received in the Protestant churches; and this rendered them agreeable to many, and made them appear inoffensive even to numbers who had no inclination to embrace them. It however so happened, that the nature of the doctrines considered in themselves, the eloquence of Menno which set them off to such advantage, and the circumstances of the times, gave a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> degree of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to the religious system of this famous teacher among the Anabaptists, so that it made a rapid progress in that sect. And thus it was in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the ministry of Menno, that the different sorts of Anabaptists agreed together in excluding from their communion the fanatics that dishonoured it, and in renouncing all tenets that were detrimental to the authority of civil government, and by an unexpected coalition formed themselves into one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>. Though the Mennonites usually pass for a sect of Anabaptists, yet M. Herman Schyn, a Mennonite minister, who has published their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and apology, maintains, that they are not Anabaptists either in principle or by origin. However, nothing can be more certain than this fact, viz. that the first Mennonite congregations were composed of the different sorts of Anabaptists, of those who had been always inoffensive and upright, and of those who, before their conversion by the ministry of Menno, had been factious fanatics; besides, it is alleged, that the Mennonites, MEN The Mennonites do actually retain, at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, some of their opinions and doctrines, which led the sedulous and turbulent Anabaptists of old to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of so many and such enormous crimes; such particularly is the doctrine concerning the nature of Christ's kingdom, or of the church of the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, though modified in such a manner as to have lost its noxious qualities, and to be no longer pernicious in its influence. The Mennonites are subdivided into several sects; whereof the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> are the Flandrians or Flemings, and the Waterlandians. The opinions, says Molheim, that are held in common by the Mennonites, seem to be all derived from this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> principle, that the kingdom which Christ established upon earth is a visible church or community, into which the holy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> alone are to be admitted, and which is consequently exempt from all those institutions and rules of discipline that have been invented by human <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, for the correction and reformation of the wicked. This principle, indeed, was avowed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Mennonites, but it is now almost wholly renounced: nevertheless, from this ancient doctrine, many of the religious opinions that distinguish the Mennonites from all other Christian communities, seem to be derived: in consequence of this doctrine, they admit none to the sacrament of baptism but persons that are come to the full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of their reason; they neither admit civil rulers into their communion, nor allow any of their members to perform the functions of magistracy; they deny the lawfulness of repelling force by force, and consider war, in all its shapes, as unchristian and unjust; they entertain the utmost aversion to the execution of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and more especially to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> punishments; and they also refuse to confirm their testimony by an oath. The particular sentiments that divided the more considerable <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of the Mennonites are the following: The rigid Mennonites, called the Flemings, maintain with various degrees of rigour, the opinions of their founder Menno, as to the human nature of Christ, alleging that it was produced in the womb of the Virgin by the creating power of the Holy Ghost; the obligation that binds us to wash the feet of strangers, in consequence of our Saviour's command; the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of excommunicating and avoiding, as one would do the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>, not only avowed sinners, but also all those who depart, even in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> instances pertaining to dress, &c., from the simplicity of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>; the contempt due to human learning, and other matters of less moment. However this austere system declines, and the rigid Mennonites are gradually approaching towards the opinions and discipline of the more moderate or Waterlandians. The first settlement of the Mennonites, in the United Provinces, was granted them by William <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the 16th century; but it was not before the following century that their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> and tranquillity were fixed upon <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> foundations, when, by a confession of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> published in the year 1626, they cleared themselves from the imputations of those pernicious and detestable errors that had been laid to their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. In order to appease their intestine discords, a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Anabaptists of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, Germany, and Friesland, concluded their debates in a conference held at Amsterdam, in the year 1630, and entered into the bonds of fraternal communion, each referring to themselves a liberty of retaining certain opinions. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> was renewed and confirmed by new resolutions, in the year 1649; in consequence of which the rigorous laws of Menno and his successors were, in various respects, mitigated and corrected.

MENOLOGY

Pages 113-113

MENOLOGIUM, (from μήν, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, and ἀγορά, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>), is much the same as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARTYROLOGY">martyrology</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a>, in the Latin. The Greek menologium is divided into the several months in the year; and contains an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">abridgment</a> of the lives of the saints, with a bare enumeration of the names of such whose lives were never written. The Greeks have various menologies; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> tax them with inserting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> heretics in their menologies as saints.—Baillet treats of them at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>.

MENSA

Pages 113-113

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> books, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> that includes in it all patrimony, and necessaries for livelihood.

MENSALS

Pages 113-113

MENSALIA, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, such livings as were formerly united to the tables of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses, and hence called mensal benefices. See the article BENEFICE.

MENSES

Pages 113-113

CATAMENIA, in Medicine, the monthly evacuations from the uterus of women not with child <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not giving suck. They are so called from mensis "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>," the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> wherein they return. They are also called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, courses, &c. By the Jewish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> a woman was unclean while the menstrual blood flowed; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who touched her, or the moveables she had touched, was declared unclean.—Lev. xv. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MIDWIFERY">MIDWIFERY</a> and MEDICINE.

MENSORES

Pages 113-113

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, were harbingers, whose business it was to go before the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, and fix upon lodgings for him when he travelled into any of the provinces. They also marked out encampments, and assigned every regiment its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>. Menfors were also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>-surveyors, architects, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> appraisers of houses and public buildings. The distributors of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> were called menfors frumentarii. And menfors was also an appellation given to servants who waited at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>.

MENTZEL

Pages 139-139

CHRISTIAN, born at Frustenwall in the Mittel-mark, is celebrated for his skill in medicine and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, in pursuit of which he travelled through many countries. He had correspondents in the most distant parts of the world. He died A.D. 1701, about the 79th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He was a member of the academy des Curieux de la <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a>. His works are: 1. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a> nominum plantarum, printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a> in folio, 1696; and reprinted with additions in 1715, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Lexicon plantarum polyglotton universale. 2. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, in German, printed at Berlin 1696 in 4to. The following <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> are preserved in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> library at Berlin. 1. Sur l'Histoire Naturelle du Brésil, in four volumes folio. 2. Sur les Fleurs et les Plantes du Japon, with coloured plates, two vols folio.

MENUS

Pages 139-139

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a river of Germany; now the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>, rising in Franconia, and running from east to west into the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>.

MENUTHIAS

Pages 139-139
