in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> adjoining to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of the promontory Prafum of Ethiopia beyond <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. Some take it to be Madagascar, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the island St Laurence. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Vossius <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it to be Zanzibar; Madagascar being at a greater distance from the continent than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> ever sailed to, whereas Menuthias was nearer: yet though Zanzibar be nearer the continent, it is however nearer the equator than <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>'s Menuthias, placed in fourth latitude 12° degrees.

MENYANTHES

Pages 139-139

MARSH-TREFOIL, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Bogbean; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria clasps; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 21st order, Precise. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MENZIKOFF

Pages 139-140

ALEXANDER, was originally an apprentice to a pastry-cook near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a>; but by a fortunate circumstance was drawn from that situation in early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and placed in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>. Having made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of several languages, and being formed for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> and for business, he first rendered himself agreeable, and afterwards became necessary, to his master. He assisted Peter in all his projects; and was rewarded for his services with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Ingria, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>-general. He signalized himself in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a> in 1708 and 1709; but in 1713 he was accused of embezzling the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and fined in 300,000 crowns. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CZAR">czar</a> remitted the fine; and having restored him to favour, gave him the command of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in the Ukraine in 1719, and sent him as his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> into Poland in 1722. Constantly employed about the means of preserving his influence after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his master, who was then evidently on the decline, Menzikoff discovered the person to whom the czar intended to leave the succession. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> was highly offended, and his penetration cost him the principality of Pleckoff. Under the czarina Catherine, however, he was higher in favour than ever; because, on the death of the czar in 1725, he was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> in bringing different parties in Russia to agree to her succession. This princess was not ungrateful. In appointing her son-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> Peter II. to be her successor, she commanded him to marry the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Menzikoff, and gave the czar's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILLET">fillet</a> to his son. The parties were actually betrothed: and Menzikoff was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Cozel and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> to the czar. But this summit of elevation was the prelude to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. The Dolgoroukis, favourites of the czar, had influence enough to procure his banishment, together with that of his family, to one of his own estates at the distance of 250 leagues from Moscow. He had the imprudence to leave the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> with the splendour and magnificence of a governor going to take possession of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. His enemies took advantage of this circumstance to inflame the indignation of the czar. At some distance from Moscow he was overtaken by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. The officer who commanded them made him alight from his chariot, which he sent back to Moscow; and placed him and his whole family in covered waggons, to be conducted into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of peasants. When he arrived at the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his destination, he was presented with cows and sheep big with young, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, without knowing from whom he received the favour. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was a simple cottage; and his employment was to cultivate the ground, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to superintend its cultivation. New causes of sorrow were added to the sufferings of exile. His wife died in the journey; he had the misfortune to lose... MENZINI one of his daughters by the smallpox; and his other two children were seized with the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, but recovered. He sunk under his misfortunes, November 2, 1729; and was buried beside his daughter, in a little chapel which he had built. His misfortunes had inspired him with sentiments of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, which, amid the splendor of his former situation, he had altogether neglected. His two surviving children enjoyed greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> after the death of their father. The officer permitted them to attend public worship on Sundays by turns. One <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> when his daughter was returning from the village, she heard herself accosted by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a> from the window of a cottage, and, to her great surprize, recognized in this peasant the persecutor of her family, Dolgorouki; who, in his turn, had fallen a sacrifice to the intrigues of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. She communicated this intelligence to her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, who could not behold, without <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a>, this new instance of the vanity and instability of honours and power. Young Menzikooff and his sister were soon after recalled to Moscow by the czarina <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNA">Anna</a>; and left Dolgorouki in possession of their cottage. He was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of the guards, and received the fifth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his father's possessions. His sister was appointed maid of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to the empress, and afterwards married to great advantage.

MENZINI

Pages 140-140

BENEDICT, a celebrated Italian poet, born at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, was professor of eloquence at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> Della Sapienza at Rome, where he died in 1704. He wrote, 1. The art of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. 2. Satires, elegies, hymns, and the Lamentations of Jeremiah. 3. Academia Tusculana, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> and prose, which passes for his masterpiece.

MEOTIS

Pages 140-140
or PALUS MEOTIS, a sea of Turkey, which divides Europe from Asia; extending from Crim Tartary to the mouth of the river Don or Tana.

MEPHITIC

Pages 140-140

a name expressing any kind of noxious vapour; but generally applied to that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of vapour called fixed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. See CARBONIC ACID, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">CHEMISTRY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MEPHITIS FANUM

Pages 140-140

a temple erected to the goddefs Mephitis, near Lacus Amianthi; who was worshipped also at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREMONA">Cremona</a>. Figuratively, Mephitis denotes a noisome <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pestilential exhalation, (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>).

MEQUINEZ

Pages 140-140
or MIQUENEZ, the northern capital of the Morocco empire, stands at the extremity of the province of Beni Hassen, 80 leagues north from the city of Morocco (which is the southern imperial city), and 20 to the east of Salée and the ocean. Maknassia, its founder, built it first at the bottom of a valley; but Muley Idriss extended it considerably over the plain that lies to the west of the valley. It is surrounded with well cultivated fields and hills, adorned with gardens and olive plantations, and abundantly watered with rivulets. Accordingly, fruits and kitchen stuffs thrive here exceedingly, and even the superior urbanity of the inhabitants announces the temperature of the climate. The winter indeed is very inconvenient, on account of the dirtiness of the town, the streets not being paved, and the soil being slimy. Mequinez is surrounded with walls; the palace itself is fortified with two battions, on which formerly some small guns were mounted. Muley Idriss, and Muley Abdallah, often in this city resisted the efforts of the Berbes, the sworn enemies of their tyranny. To the west are seen some walls of circumvallation, five feet in height, which were probably mere intrenchments for the infantry; the attacks of the Berbes being only sudden and momentary inroads, which did not require a long defence. There is at Mequinez, as well as at Morocco, a walled and guarded suburb for the Jews. The housetops are neater here than at Morocco. The Jews here are more numerous; and they can turn their industry to greater account, because the Moors in this city are more polished, and (being nearer to Europe) more civilized, than those in the Southern parts. Near the Jewry, there is another enclosed and separate quarter, called the Negro town. It was built by Muley Idriss, for the accommodation of those black families which composed his soldiery. This town is now uninhabited, as are all those destined for the same use through the rest of the empire. At the south-east extremity of the city stands the palace of the emperor, which was built by Muley Idriss. The space occupied by this palace is very great; it includes several gardens, elegantly disposed, and well watered. There is a large garden in the centre, surrounded by a vast and pretty regular gallery, resting on columns, which communicates with the apartments. Those of the women are very spacious, and have a communication with a large chamber which looks into the garden. As you pass from one apartment to another, you find at intervals regular courts paved with square pieces of black and white marble; in the middle of these courts is a marble basin, from the centre of which rises a jet d'eau, and the water falls down into this basin. These fountains are numerous in the palace; they are useful for domestic purposes, and they serve for the ablutions, which the scruples of the Mahometans have exceedingly multiplied. The palaces of the Moorish kings are large, because they are composed only of one range of apartments; these are long and narrow, from 18 to 20 feet high; they have few ornaments, and receive the light by two large folding doors, which are opened more or less as occasion requires. The rooms are always lighted from a square court in the centre, which is generally encompassed with a colonnade. The Moors here are more courteous than those in the southern parts; they are civil to strangers, and invite them into their gardens, which are very neat. The women in this part of the empire are beautiful; they have a fair complexion, with fine black eyes, and white teeth. I have sometimes seen them taking the air on the terraces; they do not hide themselves from Europeans, but retire very quickly on the appearance of a Moor.

MERA-DE-ASTA

Pages 140-140

formerly a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, seated on the river Guadalata, between Arcos and Xeres de la Frontera; but now only a large heap of ruins. Here the Arabs conquered Roderick the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, and by that victory became masters of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> in 713.

MERCATOR

Pages 140-141

GERARD, one of the most celebrated geographers of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was born at Ruremonde in 1512. He applied himself with such industry to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, that he is said to have frequently forgot to eat and drink. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. had a particular esteem for him, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Juliers made him his cosmographer. He Mercator composed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>, some geographical tables, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATLAS">atlas</a>, &c.; engraving and colouring the maps himself. He died in 1594. His method of laying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTS">charts</a> is still used, and bears the name of Mercator's charts. Mercator, Nicholas, an eminent mathematician in the 17th century, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>; and came to England about the time of the restoration, where he lived many years. He was fellow of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>; and endeavoured to reduce astrology to rational principles, as appeared from a MS. of his in the possession of William Jones, Esq. He published several works, particularly Cosmographia. He gave the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRATURE">quadrature</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYPERBOLA">hyperbola</a> by an infinite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a>; which was the first appearance in the learned world of a series of this sort drawn from the particular <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the curve, and that in a manner very new and abstracted. Mercator's Sailing, that performed by Mercator's chart. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>.

MERCATORUM FESTUM

Pages 141-141

was a festival kept by the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> on the 15th of May, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, who presided over merchandise. A sow was sacrificed on the occasion, and the people present sprinkled themselves with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> fetched from the fountain called <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUA">aqua</a> Mercurii; the whole concluding with prayers to the god for the prosperity of trade.

MERCHANT

Pages 141-141

a person who buys and sells commodities in grots, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> deals in exchanges; or that trades in the way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, either by importation or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>. Formerly every one who was a buyer or seller in the retail way was called a merchant, as they still are both in France and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; but here shopkeepers, or those who attend <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>, have lost that appellation. Previous to a person's engaging in a general trade; and becoming an universal dealer, he ought to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> up such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of useful knowledge as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> enable him to carry it on with ease to himself, and without risking such losses as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ill-concerted undertakings would naturally expose him to. A merchant should therefore be acquainted with the following parts of commercial learning: 1. He should write properly and correctly. 2. Understand all the rules of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a> that have any relation to commerce. 3. Know how to keep books of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> and single entry, as journals, a leger, &c. 4. Be expert in the forms of invoices, accounts of sales, policies of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSURANCE">insurance</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>-parties, bills of lading, and bills of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>. 5. Know the agreement between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, weights, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of all parts. 6. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, woollen, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, he ought to know the places where these different sorts of merchandises are manufactured, in what manner they are made, what are the materials of which they are composed, and from whence they come, the preparations of these materials before working up, and the places to which they are sent after their fabrication. 7. He ought to know the lengths and breadths which silk, woollen, or hair stuffs, linen, cottons, fustians, &c., ought to have according to the several statutes and regulations of the places where they are manufactured, with their different prices, according to the times and seasons; and if he can add to his knowledge the different dyes and ingredients which form the various colours, it will not be useless. 8. If he confines his trade to that of oils, wines, &c., he ought to inform himself particularly of the appearances of the succeeding crops, in order to regulate his disposing of what he has on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; and to learn as exactly as he can what they have produced when got in, for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> in making the necessary purchases and engagements. 9. He ought to be acquainted with the sorts of merchandise found more in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> than another, those which are scarce, their different <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> and qualities, and the properest method for bringing them to a good market either by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. 10. To know which are the merchandises permitted or prohibited, as well on entering as going out of the kingdoms or states where they are made. 11. To be acquainted with the price of exchange, according to the course of different places, and what is the cause of its rise and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. 12. To know the customs due on importation or exportation of merchandises, according to the usage, the tariffs, and regulations, of the places to which he trades. 13. To know the best manner of folding up, embaling, or tumbling, the merchandises for their preservation. 14. To understand the price and condition of freighting and insuring ships and merchandise. 15. To be acquainted with the goodness and value of all necessaries for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> and repairs of shipping, the different manner of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; what the wood, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, cordage, cannons, sails, and all requisites, may cost. 16. To know the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> given to the captains, officers, and sailors, and the manner of engaging with them. 17. He ought to understand the foreign languages, or at least as many of them as he can attain to; these may be reduced to four, viz. the Spanish, which is used not only in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> but on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANARIES">Canaries</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope; the Italian, which is understood on all the coasts of the Mediterranean, and in many parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>; the German, which is understood in almost all the northern countries; and the French, which is now become almost universally current. 18. He ought to be acquainted with the consular jurisdiction, with the laws, customs, and usages of the different countries he does or may trade to; and in general all the ordinances and regulations both at home and abroad that have any relation to commerce. 19. Though it is not necessary for a merchant to be very learned, it is proper that he should know something of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, particularly that of his own country; <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, hydrography, or the science of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>; and that he be acquainted with the discoveries of the countries in which trade is established, in what manner it is settled, of the companies formed to support these establishments, and of the colonies they have sent out. All these branches of knowledge are of great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to a merchant who carries on an extensive commerce; but if his trade and his views are more limited, his learning and knowledge may be so too; but a material requisite for forming a merchant is, his having on all occasions a strict regard to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and his avoiding fraud and deceit as corroding cankers that must inevitably destroy his reputation and fortune. Trade is a thing of so universal a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, that it is impossible for the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, or of any other <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, to determine all the affairs relating to it; therefore

MERCIA

Pages 141-143

the name of one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> kingdoms founded in England by the Saxons. Though the latest formed, it was the largest of them all, and grew by degrees to be by far the most powerful. On the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> it was bounded by the Humber and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MERSEY">Mersey</a>, which separated it from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>; on the east by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and the territories of the East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">Angles</a> and Saxons; on the south by the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>; and on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEE">Dee</a>. It comprehended well nigh 17 of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> counties, being equal in size to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a> in France; very little, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> at all, less than the kingdom of Arragon in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; and superior in size to that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a> in Germany. Penda is regarded as its first monarch; and the kingdom is thought to derive its name from the Saxon word *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a>*, which signifies "a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, bound, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> limit," because the other kingdoms bordered upon it on every side; and not from the river Mersey, as some would persuade us. Penda assumed the regal <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> A.D. 626, and was of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 50 at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his accession; after which he reigned near 30 years. He was of a most furious and turbulent temper, breaking at different times with almost all his neighbours, calling in the Britons to his assistance, and shedding more Saxon blood than had been hitherto spilled in all their intestine quarrels. He killed two kings of Northumberland, three of the East Angles, and compelled Kenwalh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the West Saxons to quit his dominions. He was at length slain, with most of the princes of his family, and a multitude of his subjects, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought not far from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEEDS">Leeds</a>, by Oswy king of Northumberland. This battle, which the Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONICLE">chronicle</a> tells us was fought at Winnidfield, A.D. 655, made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> change in the Saxon affairs, which the unbridled fury of Penda had thrown into great confusion. He had the year before killed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNA">Anna</a> king of the East Angles in battle, whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ETHELRED">Ethelred</a> notwithstanding took <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> with Penda. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, Penda the eldest son of Penda, to whom his father had given the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> kingdom of the Mid Angles, had two years before married the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of King Oswy, and had been baptized at his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. At that time it should seem that Oswy and Penda were upon good terms; but after the latter had conquered the East Angles, he resolved to turn his arms against the kingdom of Northumberland. Oswy by no means had provoked this rupture; on the contrary, Bede tells us that he offered <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sums of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and jewels of great value, to purchase peace: these offers being rejected, he was reduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of deciding the quarrel by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. The river near which the battle was fought overflowing, there were more drowned than killed. Amongst these, as the Saxon chronicle says, there were 35 princes of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> line, some of whom bore the title of kings; and also Ethelred king of the East Angles, who fought on the side of Penda against his family and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. His son Penda, who married the daughter of that conqueror, became a Christian, and was not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> after murdered, as is said, by the malice of his mother. His brother Wolfher becoming king of Mercia, embraced in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of time the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of the gospel, and proved a very victorious and potent monarch; and is, with no fewer than seven of his immediate successors, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> styled king of the Anglo-Saxons, though none of them are owned in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> by the Saxon chronicle. But though possibly none of them might enjoy this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, they were undoubtedly very illustrious princes, maintaining great wars, and obtaining many advantages over the sovereigns of other Saxon states, and especially the East Angles, whom they reduced. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the Mercian territories was so ample as to admit, and so situated as to require, the constituting subordinate rulers in several provinces; to whom, especially if they were of the royal line, they gave the title of kings; which occasions some confusion in their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. Besides the establishing episcopal sees and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, the Saxon monarchs took other methods for improving and adorning their dominions; and as Mercia was the largest, so these methods were most conspicuous therein. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVENTRY">Coventry</a>, as being situated in the centre, was usually, but not always, the royal residence. Penda, who was almost continually in a state of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, lived as his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> operations directed, in some great town on the frontiers. Wolfher built a castle or fortified <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> for his own residence, which bore his name.—Offa kept his court at Sutton Walls near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEREFORD">Hereford</a>. In each of the provinces there resided a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>; and if he was of the royal blood, had usually the title of king. Penda, at the time he married Oswy's daughter, had the title of king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a>.—Ethelred Mercurial. Ethelred made his brother Morwald king of Hereford; who, dying without issue, bequeathed it to his younger brother Mercelm. The like honours were sometimes conferred upon the princesses; and hence, in Mercia especially, we occasionally read of vice-queens. By these means the laws were better executed, the obedience of the subjects more effectually secured, and the splendor of their residences constantly kept up and augmented. At length, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> devolving sometimes on minors and sometimes on weak princes, intestine factions also prevailing, the force of this hitherto mighty kingdom began sensibly to decline. This falling out in the days of Egbert, the most prudent as well as the most potent monarch of the West Saxons, he took advantage of these circumstances; and having encouraged the East Angles to make an attempt for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of their independence, he, in a conjecture every way favourable to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, broke with the Mercians, and after a short war obliged them to submit. But this was not an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> conquest, the kings of Mercia being allowed by him and his successors to retain their titles and dominions, till the invasion of the Danes put an end to their rule, when this kingdom had subsisted above 250 years; and when the Danes were afterwards expelled by the West Saxons, it sunk into a province, or rather was divided into many.

MERCURIALIS

Pages 143-143

DOGS <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">MERCURY</a>; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dioecia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 38th order, Tricocceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MERCURIFICATION

Pages 143-143

in metallurgic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, the obtaining the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> from metallic minerals in its fluid form. See Chemistry and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MERCURY

Pages 144-144

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLAZONING">blazoning</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, for the purple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> used in the arms of sovereign princes.

MERCY

Pages 144-144

a virtue that inspires us with compassion for our brethren, and which inclines us to give them assistance in their necessities. Mercy is also taken for those favours and benefits that we receive either from God <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, particularly in the way of forgiveness of injuries or of debts. Nothing can be more beautiful than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of mercy given us by Shakespeare, in the pleading between Portia and the Jew: Por. Then must the Jew be merciful. Shy. On what compulsion must I? tell me that. Por. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of mercy is not strain'd; It droppeth as the gentle <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> from heav'n Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> beneath. It is twice blest: It blest him that gives, and him that takes. 'Tis mightiest in the mightiest; it becomes The throned monarch better than his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>: The sceptre shows the force of temporal power, The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> to awe and majesty, Wherein doth sit the dread and fear of kings; But mercy is above this scepter'd sway, It is enthroned in the hearts of kings; It is an attribute to God himself, And earthly power doth then show likest God's, When mercy seasons <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. Therefore, Jew, Though justice be thy <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a>, consider this, That in the course of justice none of us Should see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a>. We do pray for mercy; And that same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> doth teach us all to render The deeds of mercy. Merchant of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> iv.

MERCY-SEAT

Pages 144-144
or PROPITIATORY, in Jewish antiquity, the covering of the ark of the covenant.—The Hebrew name of this cover, which we translate mercy-seat, is Capporeth (Exod. xxv. 17, 22.), from Cappor, which signifies to cover, to shut up, to expiate, to pay. This cover was of gold, and at its two ends were fixed the two cherubims of the same metal, which by their wings extended forwards, seemed to form a throne for the majesty of God, who in scripture is represented to us as sitting between the cherubims, and the ark itself was as it were his footstool. It was from hence that God gave his oracles to Moses, or to the high priest that consulted him, Exod. xxv. 22. Numb. vii. §9.)

MERETRIX

Pages 144-144

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, differed from the profibula. The profibulae were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> courteans, with bills over their doors, signifying their profession, and were ready at all times to entertain customers; whereas the meretrices entertained none but at night.—The meretrices differed in their dress from the matrons; the former wore the toga and short tunics, like those of the men: the latter wore the pallia and the stola of such a length as to reach to their feet. MERGANSER. See Mergus.

MERGUS

Pages 144-144

a genus of birds of the order of anseres. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MERIAN

Pages 144-144
MARIA SIBYLLA, a celebrated painter, born at Frankfort in 1647, was the daughter of Matthias Merian, a noted engraver and geographer.—As she showed a very early fondness for painting, she was instructed by Abraham Mignon; from whom she learned great neatness of handling and delicacy of colour. Her genius particularly led her to paint reptiles, flowers, and insects, which she designed after nature, and studied every object with a most curious and inquisitive observation; so that her works rose every day more and more into reputation. Frequently she painted her subjects in water colours on vellum, and finished an astonishing number of designs, as she was equally indefatigable in her work and in her inquiries into the curiosities of nature. She drew the flies and caterpillars in all the variety of changes and forms in which they successively appear from their quiescent state till they become butterflies; and also drew frogs, toads, serpents, ants, and spiders, after nature, with extraordinary exactness and truth. She even undertook a voyage to Surinam, to paint those insects and reptiles which were peculiar to that climate; and at her return to her own country published two volumes of engravings after her designs, which are well known to the curious. She died in 1717. Her daughter Dorothea Henrietta Graff, who painted in the same style, and had accompanied her mother to Surinam, published a third volume collected from the designs of Sibylla; which complete work has been always admired by the learned, as well as by the professors of painting.

MERIDA

Pages 144-144

a town of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>, seated in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> abounding with all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, 130 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PAMPLONA">Pamplona</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 71. 0. N. Lat. 8. 30.

MERIDEN

Pages 144-145
or MIREDEN, a town of Warwickshire, 97 miles from London on the London road, near Coventry. It is pleasantly situated, though in a wet clayey situation, and is not ill built. The church stands on an elevated spot, and contains some good monuments. There is an inn here, about half way from Meridian from St Clement's forest to Coventry, one of the finest in this part of England, being built like a nobleman's seat. **Meridian**, in Geography, a great circle supposed to be drawn through any part on the surface of the earth, and the two poles; and to which the sun is always perpendicular at noon. See Geography. In astronomy, this circle is supposed to be in the heavens, and exactly perpendicular to the terrestrial one. See Astronomy. **Meridiani**, in antiquity, a name which the Romans gave to a kind of gladiators who entered the arena about noon after the bellfarii (who fought in the morning against beasts) had finished. They were thus called from meridiæ, i.e., noon, the time when they exhibited their shows. The meridiani were a sort of artless combatants, who fought man with man, sword in hand. Hence Seneca takes occasion to observe, that the combats of the morning were full of humanity compared with those which followed. **Meridional distance**, in Navigation, the same with departure, or ealing and welling; being the difference of longitude between the meridian under which the ship now is, and any other meridian which she was under before. **Meridional parts**, miles, or minutes, in Navigation, are the parts by which the meridians in a Mercator's chart do increase, as the parallels of latitude decrease. **Merionethshire**, a county of North Wales, is bounded on the north by Caernarvonshire and Denbighshire; on the east by Montgomeryshire; on the west by St George's channel, or the Irish sea; and on the south by the river Dyfi, which parts it from Cardiganshire; extending 40 miles in length and 36 in breadth. It is divided into six hundreds, in which are four market towns, 37 parishes, about 5787 houses, and 29,506 inhabitants in 1801. It lies in the diocese of Bangor, and sends one member to parliament. The air is very sharp in winter, on account of its many high barren mountains; and the soil is as bad as any in Wales, it being very rocky and mountainous. However, this county feeds large flocks of sheep, many goats, and large herds of horned cattle, which find pretty good pasture in the valleys. Besides these, among their other commodities may be reckoned Welch cotton, deer, fowl, fish, and especially herrings, which are often taken on this coast in great plenty. **Merit**, signifies desert. This term is more particularly applied to signify the moral goodness of the actions of men, and the rewards to which those actions entitle them. **Merlin**, Ambrose, a famous English poet and reputed prophet, flourished at the end of the 5th century. Many surprising and ridiculous things are related of him. Several English authors have represented him as the son of an incubus, and as transporting from Ireland to England the great stones which form Stonehenge on Salisbury plain. Extravagant prophecies and other works are also attributed to him, on which some authors have even written commentaries. **Merlin**. See Falco, Ornithology Index. **Merlon**, in Fortification, is that part of a parapet which is terminated by two embrasures of a battery. --- **Merlucius**, the Hake. See Gadus, Ichthy-Ornithology Index. **Mermaid**, or **Merman**, a sea-creature frequently talked of, supposed half human and half a fish. However naturalists may doubt of the reality of mermen or mermaids, we have testimony enough to establish it; though, how far these testimonies may be authentic, we cannot take upon us to say. In the year 1187, as Lary informs us, such a monster was fished up in the county of Suffolk, and kept by the governor for six months. It bore so near a conformity with man, that nothing seemed wanting to it but speech. One day it took the opportunity of making its escape; and plunging into the sea, was never more heard of. Hist. de Angleterre, P. I. p. 403. In the year 1430, after a huge tempest, which broke down the dikes in Holland, and made way for the sea into the meadows, &c., some girls of the town of Edam in West Friesland, going in a boat to milk their cows, perceived a mermaid embarrassed in the mud, with a very little water. They took it into their boat, and brought it with them to Edam, dressed it in woman's apparel, and taught it to spin. It fed like one of them, but could never be brought to offer at speech. Some time afterwards it was brought to Haarlem, where it lived for some years, though still showing an inclination to the water. Parival relates, that they had given it some notion of a Deity, and that it made its reverences very devoutly whenever it paused by a crucifix. Delices de Hollande. In the year 1560, near the island of Manaar, on the western coast of the island of Ceylon, some fishermen brought up, at one draught of a net, seven mermen and mermaids; of which several Jesuits, and among the rest F. Hen. Henriques and Dimas Roquez, physicians to the viceroy of Goa, were witnesses. The physician, who examined them with a great deal of care, and made dissection thereof, affirms, that all the parts both internal and external were found perfectly conformable to those of men. See the Hist. de la compagnie de Jesus, P. II. T. iv. No 276, where the relation is given at length. We have another account of a merman, seen near the great rock called Diamond, on the coast of Martinico. The persons who saw it, gave in a precise description of it before a notary. They affirmed that they saw it wipe its hand over its face, and even heard it blow its nose. Another creature of the same species was caught in the Baltic in the year 1531, and sent as a present to Sigismund king of Poland, with whom it lived three days, and was seen by all the court. Another very young one was taken near Rocca de Sintra, as related by Damian Goes. The king of Portugal and the grand master of the order of St James, are said to have had a suit at law to determine which party these monsters belong to. In Pontopidan's href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural History of Norway, also, we have accounts of mermaids; but not more remarkable or any way better attested than the above, to which we have given a place, merely to shew how far the folly and extravagance of credulity have been carried by weak minds.

MERNIS

Pages 145-146

Mearns, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Kingardineshire, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Scotland. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINCARDINESHIRE">Kincardineshire</a>. MERODACH was an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, who was placed among the gods, and worshipped by the Babylonians. Jeremiah (chap. 1. 2.), speaking of the ruin of Babylon, says, "Babylon is taken, Bel is confounded, Merodach is broken in pieces; her idols are confounded, her images are broken in pieces." We find certain kings of Babylon, in whose names that of Merodach is contained: for example, Evil-merodach and Merodach-baladan. Evil-merodach was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEBUCHADNEZZAR">Nebuchadnezzar</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, and had for his successor the wicked Belihazzar. Merodach-baladan, son of Baladan king of Babylon, having heard that Hezekiah had been cured miraculously (Isa. xxxix.), and that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> had gone backwards to give him an assurance of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a>, sent him presents, and made him compliments upon the recovery of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> calls him Mardoc-empadus; and says, that he began to reign at Babylon 26 years after the beginning of the era of Nabonassar, that is, in the year of the world 2283.

MEROE

Pages 146-146

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Ethiopia beyond <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>; with a cognominal town, the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of the Ethiopians. The Jesuits have endeavoured to prove, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Gojam in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a> is the Meroë of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; but this is strongly contested by Mr Bruce, who is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that it must be looked for somewhere between the source of the Nile and its union with the Athbara. The latter, he thinks, is very plainly the Atlaboras of the ancients; and Pliny says, that this stream encloses the left side of Meroë as the Nile does the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> we must suppose him looking southward from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, otherwise the words would not apply. We are told by Diodorus Siculus, that Meroë had its name from a sister of Cambyses' <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, who died there in the expedition undertaken by that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> against the Ethiopians. His <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> perished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a> and thirst in the deserts beyond Meroë, which could not have happened <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had reached Gojam, the latter being one of the most plentiful countries in the world. A further <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that Gojam cannot be the ancient Meroë, is, that the latter was enclosed between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Nile and Atlaboras, while Gojam is almost entirely surrounded by the Nile. If the ancients were acquainted with Gojam, they must also have been acquainted with the fountains of the Nile, which we certainly know they were not. Pliny says that Meroë, the most considerable of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of the Nile, was called Atlaboras, from the name of its left channel, which cannot be supposed any other than the junction of the Nile and Athbara. He informs us moreover, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> was vertical twice in the year, viz. when proceeding northward he entered the 18th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of Taurus, and when returning he came to the 14th degree of Leo; but this could never be the case with Gojam, which lies in about 10 degrees <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. Again, the poet Lucan describes Meroë by two circumstances which cannot apply to any other than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of Athbara. One is, that the inhabitants were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; which was the case with the Gymnosophists and first inhabitants, and which has been the case with all the rest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the Saracen conquest: but the inhabitants of Gojam, as well as the other Abyssinians, are fair, at least greatly different in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> from the blacks; they are also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>-haired, and nobody imagined that they ever had philosophers <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> science among them, which was eminently the case with the ancient inhabitants of Meroë. The other circumstance is, that the ebony tree grew in the island of Meroë, which at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> grows plentifully in the peninsula of Athbara, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the province of Kuara, but not in Gojam, where the tree could not subsist on account of the violent rains which take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> during six months of the year. Mr Bruce mentions another circumstance quoted from the poet Lucan, which likewise tends to prove the identity of Meroë and Athbara; viz. that though there are many trees in it, they afford no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>. This our traveller found by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, when returning from Abyssinia through Athbara. "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> (says he) is flat, and has very little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The forests, though thick, afforded no sort of shade, the hunters for the sake of their sport, and the Arabs for destroying the flies, having set fire to all the dry grass and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>; which falling with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> rapidity in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> from east to west, though it had not <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to destroy the trees, did yet wither, and occasion every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> that was upon them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, unless in those spaces where villages had been, and where water was. In such spots a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> spreading trees remained full of foliage; which, from their great height and being cleared of underwood, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in full verdure, loaded with large, projecting, and exuberant branches. But even here the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> that their shade afforded was very temporary, so as to allow us no time for enjoyment. The sun, so near the zenith, changed his azimuth so rapidly, that every few minutes I was obliged to change the carpet on which I lay, round the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of the tree to which I had fled for shelter; and though I lay down to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> perfectly screened by the trunk or branches, I was presently awakened by the violent rays of a scorching sun, the shade having passed beyond me. In all other places, though we had travelled constantly in a forest, we never met with a tree that could shade us for a moment, the fire having deprived them of all their leaves." The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of Athbara is excessive, the thermometer having been observed at 119°: two of Mr Bruce's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> died of thirst, or at least of the consequences of drinking after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> thirst. The inhabitants live in the greatest misery, and are continually in danger from the neighbouring Arabs, who, by destroying and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> their corn, are able to reduce them to a starving condition. Notwithstanding all their disadvantages, however, they have a manufacture of coarse cotton towels, of a size <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> sufficient to go round the waist, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> current as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> throughout the whole country.

MEROM

Pages 146-147

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>. The waters of Merom, at which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> Jabin and the other confederate kings met to fight Joshua (xi. 5.), are generally supposed by the learned to be the lake Semechon, which lies between the head of the river Jordan and the lake Gennaret; since it is agreed on all <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> Hazor, where Jabin reigned, was situated upon this lake. But others think, that the waters of Merom <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Merome were somewhere about the brook Kishon, since there is a place of that name mentioned in the account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> against Sifera (Judg. v. 21.) And it is more rational to think, that the confederate kings advanced Merope advanced as far as the brook Kition, and to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> which led into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, to hinder Joshua from penetrating it; or even to attack him in the country where he himself lay encamped, than to imagine that they waited for him in the midst of their own country; leaving all Galilee at his mercy, and the whole tract from the brook Kition to the lake Semechon.

MEROPE

Pages 147-147

in *Fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>*, one of the Atlantides. She married <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SISYPHUS">Sisyphus</a> the son of Æolus, and like her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a> was changed into a constellation after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. It is said that in the constellation of the Pleiades the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> of Merope appears more dim and obscure than the rest, because she, as the poets observe, married a mortal, while her sisters married some of the gods <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> their descendants.

MEROPS

Pages 147-147

a genus of birds belonging to the order of picus. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MEROVINGIAN CHARACTER

Pages 147-147

derives its name from Merouée, the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of France of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, which reigned 333 years, from Pharamond to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES_MARTEL"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Martel. This race is said by some to have terminated in Childeric III. A.D. 751. There are many MSS. in the French <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> still extant in this character.

MEROZ

Pages 147-147

in *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>*, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the neighbourhood of the brook Kition, whose inhabitants refusing to come to the assistance of their brethren when they fought with Sifera, were put under an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANATHEMA">anathema</a> (Judges v. 23.) "Curse ye Meroz, says the angel of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>; curse ye bitterly the inhabitants thereof: because," &c. Some have thought that Meroz is the same as Merus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Merom; and this F. Calmet thinks the most probable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. Others <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it, that Meroz was a mighty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, who dwelt near the Kition, and not caring to come to the assistance of Barak and Deborah, was excommunicated by the angel of the Lord by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of 400 trumpets. The angel of the Lord, according to some, was Barak, the general of the Lord's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; but according to others he was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> being, or a prophet.

MERSA

Pages 147-147

a town of Barbary, pleasantly situated about 11 miles from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>, and two from Melcha the site of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>. The bey has here two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> houses, one of them very costly <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, built by Hafian Bey named the Good. From these are <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> gardens reaching almost to the seashore; on the edge of which is a famous well of sweet <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, esteemed the best and lightest in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">Close</a> to this is a coffeehouse, whither numbers of people from the neighbouring places <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> to drink coffee, and a glass of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> so peculiarly enjoyed in the eastern countries. In the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> mulberry tree, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of which they sit and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> and play at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESS">chess</a>; inhaling the comfortable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> breeze that refreshes this delightful spot. The water is drawn up by a camel with the Persian wheel. There are the remains of an ancient port, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cophon, (supposed to be an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> one), built by the Carthaginians after Scipio had blocked up the old port, nothing but the turret or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LIGHTHOUSE">lighthouse</a> being left. **MERS** or **<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MERSE">MERSE</a>**, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Scotland, called also <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol4.html#article-BERWICKSHIRE">Berwickshire</a>. This last name it derives from the town of Berwick, which was the head of the shire before it fell into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the English, and obtained the appellation of Mers or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, because it was one of the borders towards England. See Berwick, County of.

MERSENNE

Pages 147-147

Marin, in Latin *Merseanus*, a learned French author, born at Oyé, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>, anno 1638. He studied at La Fleche at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> with Des Cartes; with whom he contracted a strict friendship, which lasted till <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. He afterwards went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and studied at the Sorbonne; and in 1611 entered himself among the Minims. He became well skilled in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>. He was of a tranquil, sincere, and engaging temper; and was universally esteemed by persons illustrious for their birth, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and their learning. He taught philosophy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> in the convent of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEVERS">Nevers</a>, and at length became superior of the convent; but being willing to apply himself to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> with more freedom, he resigned all the posts he enjoyed in his order, and travelled into Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of excellent works; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are, 1. *Questiones celeberrima in Genesim*. 2. *Harmoniconum libri*. 3. *De sonorum natura, causis, et effectibus*. 4. *Cogitata phyisco-mathematica*. 5. *La verité des Sciences*. 6. *Les questions inutiles*. He died at Paris in 1648. He had the reputation of being one of the best men of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. No person was more curious in penetrating into the secrets of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and carrying all the arts and sciences to their utmost perfection. He was in a manner the centre of all the men of learning, by the mutual correspondence which he managed between them. He omitted no means to engage them to publish their works; and the world is obliged to him for several excellent discoveries, which, had it not been for him, would perhaps have been lost.

MERSUS

Pages 147-148

in *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>*, a mountain of the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, hanging over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> Nyssa, built by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, and situated between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Cophen and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDUS">Indus</a>. The name, denoting the thigh, gave rise to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of Bacchus being inferred into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>'s thigh, and... Mesaraic being born twice; because in this mountain he and his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> are said to have been preserved, when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> and pestilence raged in the plains below.

MERSY

Pages 147-147

a river of England, which runs through the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, and empties itself into the Irish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVERPOOL">Liverpool</a>. By means of inland <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, it has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEE">Dee</a>, Ribble, Ouse, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, Darwent, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, Humber, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, Avon, &c.; which navigation, including its windings, extends above 500 miles, in the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a>, York, Lancaster, Westmorland, Chester, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORD">Stafford</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICK">Warwick</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTERSHIRE">Worcestershire</a>, &c. **Messer <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>**, an island of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, at the mouth of the Coln, south of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLCHESTER">Colchester</a>. It was seized by the Danes in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Alfred, for their winter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. It had eight parishes, now reduced to two, viz. East and West <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MERSEY">Mersey</a>. There was formerly a blockhouse on the island.

MESARAIC VESSELS

Pages 148-148

in the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, are the same with **MESENTERIC**. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, mesaraic is more frequently applied to the veins, and mesenteric to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a>, of the mesentery. See **ANATOMY**.

MESCHED

Pages 148-148

a considerable town of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Chorasan; fortified with several towers, and famous for the magnificent sepulchre of Iman Rifa, of the family of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALI">Ali</a>, to whom the Persians pay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. It is seated on a mountain near this town, in which are fine turquoise <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 59° 25'. N. Lat. 37° 0'.

MESEMBRYANTHEMUM

Pages 148-148

Fig-marigold, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICOSANDRIA">icosandria</a> clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 13th order, Succulentae. See **<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">INDEX</a>**.

MESENTERIC

Pages 148-148
or **MESARAIC**, an epithet given to two arteries arising from the descending aorta, and proceeding to the mesentery. See **MESENTERY**.

MESENTERY

Pages 148-148

**MESENTERIUM**, (formed of *mesos*, middle, and *stereon*, intestine), in anatomy, a fatty membranous body, thus called as being placed in the middle of the intestines, which it connects to one another. See **ANATOMY**, No. 94.

MESN

Pages 148-148
or **MESNE**, a term in law, signifying him who is lord of a manor, and so hath tenants holding of him; yet he himself holds of a superior lord. The word is properly derived from *mesne*, quasi minor natu; because his tenure is derived from another, from whom he holds. **MESN** also denotes a writ, which lieth where there is lord mesn and tenant; and the tenant is disfrained for services due from the mesn to the superior lord. This is in the nature of a writ of right; and in this case the tenant shall have judgement to be acquitted or indemnified by the mesne lord; and if he makes default therein, or does not appear originally to the tenant's writ, he shall be forejudged of his mesnalty, and the tenant shall hold immediately of the lord paramount himself.

MESOCHRI

Pages 148-148

were musicians among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, who presided in concerts, and by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> a wooden desk regularly with their feet, directed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of the music. For the purpose of beating <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, they wore wooden clogs, called by the ancients *crupesia*, which occasioned the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> to be better heard.

MESOCOLON

Pages 148-148

in Anatomy, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the mesentery, which, having reached the extremity of the ileum, contracts and changes its name. See **ANATOMY**, No. 94.

MESOLOGARITHMS

Pages 148-148

according to Kepler, are the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOGARITHMS">logarithms</a> of the co-sines and co-tangents; the former of which were called by Baron Napier anti-logarithms, and the latter differentials.

MESOPORPHYRON

Pages 157-157

a name given by the Greeks to the Roman laetivlae; because that garment, being edged on each side, where it opened before, with purple, appeared when clothed with two purple stripes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the middle. The same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> was also applied to the angustulae.

MESOPOTAMIA

Pages 148-148

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> name of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Diarbeck, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. It is situated between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> and Tigris; having Af. Meopotery, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> on the east, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, Syria on the west, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Deferta with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a> on the south. The Hebrews called it *Padan aram*, (Gen. xxviii. 2, &c.), and *Aram Naharaim* (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Psa. lx.) <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Aram of the two rivers, because it was first peopled by Aram father of the Syrians, and is situated between the two rivers already mentioned. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is much celebrated in Scripture, as being the first dwelling of men both before and after the deluge; and because it gave birth to Phaleg, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBER">Heber</a>, Terah, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>, Nahor, Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Leah, and to the sons of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a> was in the ancient Mesopotamia, till, by vast labour and industry, the two rivers of the Tigris and Euphrates were united into one channel. The plains of Shinar were in the same country. Often they gave it the name of Mesopotamia (Deut. xxiii. 4. &c.) and sometimes that of Syria, (Hosea xii. 12.). Balama son of Beor was of Mesopotamia, Deut. xxxiii. 4. Chuthan-rilhathaim <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Mesopotamia kept the Hebrews in subjection some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Joshua, Judg. iii. 8.

MESOPTERYGIUS

Pages 148-148

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to such fishes as have only one back-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIN">fin</a>, which is situated in the middle of the back.

MESPILLUS

Pages 148-148

the Medlar, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICOSANDRIA">icosandria</a> clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 56th order, Pomaceae. See **<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">INDEX</a>**.

MESSALINA

Pages 148-148

Valeria, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Messala Barbatus. She married the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Claudius, and disgraced herself by her cruelties and incontinence. Her husband's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> was not the only seat of her licentiousness, but she prostituted herself in the public streets, and few men there were at Rome who could not boast of having enjoyed the favours of the impure Messalina. Her extravagances at last irritated her husband, who commanded her to appear and answer all the accusations which were brought against her: upon which she attempted to destroy herself; and when her courage failed, one of the tribunes who had been sent to her dispatched her with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. It is in speaking of her debaucheries and lewdness that Juvenal says, > Et laffata viris, necdum satiata, recessit. Her name has become a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> appellation to denote a woman of shameless and inordinate lust.

MESSANA

Pages 148-152
