in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the first town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> on crossing over from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, situated on the strait now called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FARO">Faro</a>, (Italicus). Anciently called Zancle, according to Diodorus Siculo, from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Zanclus; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to others, from the Sicilian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> Zanclon, denoting a fickle, alluding to the curvity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>; a name appropriated by the poets; and hence Zanclon, the people, (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, Paulianas). The other name Messenia is from the Messenii of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, (Strabo.) <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a> ascribes its origin to Anaxilas the Messenian, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> of Régium, who received all comers, calling the town after the name of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The Greeks always call it Messene; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> Messene constantly, to distinguish it from Messene of Peloponnesus. Now Messina, lately ruined by earthquakes. Messenia, or Messene, an inland town, and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Messenia, a country of Peloponnesus; erroneously replaced by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> on the coast. It was built by Epaminondas, who called all the Messenian exiles, and gave the town the name of Messene. A <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> vying in point of strength and situation with Corinth, according to Strabo; and therefore Demetrius Phalereus advised <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, father of Perseus, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he wanted to have Peloponnesus in his power, he should make himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of these two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, as thus he would have the ox by both horns. Messengers, are certain officers chiefly employed under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the secretaries of state, and always in readiness to be sent with all kinds of dispatches foreign and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a>. By virtue of the secretaries warrants, they also take up persons for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, or other offences against the state. The prisoners they apprehend are usually kept at their own houses, for each of which they are allowed 6s. 8d. per <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; and when they are sent abroad, they have a stated allowance for their journey, viz. 30l. for going to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>; 25l. for going to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; and to other places in the same proportion; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> is advanced for the expense of their journey. Their standing salary is 45l. per annum; and their posts, if purchased, are esteemed worth 300l. But these sums have now probably been increased. The messengers wait 20 at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, monthly, and are distributed as follows, viz. four at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, five at one secretary's office, five at another, two at the third for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, three at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> office, and one at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> chamberlain's of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>. Messengers, in Scotland. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, Part III. Messengers of the Exchequer, are four officers who attend the exchequer, in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of pursuivants, and carry the lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>'s letters, precepts, &c. Messenger of the Press, a person who, by order of the court, searches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>-houses, bookellers' shops, &c., in order to discover the printers or publishers of seditious books, pamphlets, &c. Messenia, a country in the south of Peloponnesus, mostly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a>, situated between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELEA">Elea</a> to the west, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACONIA">Laconia</a> to the east. Anciently a part of Laconia under Menelaus, and called Messene by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>; interpreted by the scholiast, Messenica Regia. Messenii, the people, reduced to a state of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> and subjection by the Spartans; Messenius, the epithet. This country is famous in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, on account of the resistance made by the Messenians against the Spartans, and the exploits of their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> Arilomenes. The first hostilities commenced about the year 652 B.C. on what occasion is uncertain. Though the Messenians were inferior in the knowledge of the art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> to the Spartans; yet, by keeping for some time on the defensive, they improved so much, that in three years time they found themselves in a capacity of giving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> to their enemies in the open Messenia field; nor did they appear to be in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> inferior either in courage or conduct: the war was therefore protracted, with various success, on both sides. At last, both consulted the oracle at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a>; and received for answer, "that whoever should first dedicate 100 tripods in the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> at Ithome, a strong hold of the Messenians, should be masters of the country." The inhabitants of Messenia, on hearing this, having no money to make the tripods of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, fell to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> them out in wood; but before this could be accomplished, a Spartan having got into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> by stratagem, dedicated 100 little tripods of clay; which threw the Messenians into such despair, that they at last submitted to the Spartans. The new subjects of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a> were treated with the utmost barbarity by these cruel tyrants; so that a new war commenced under Arilomenes, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of unconquerable valour, and enthusiastically fond of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. He perceived that the Argives and Arcadians, who were called the allies of the Lacedemonians, adhered to them only through fear of their power; but that in reality they hated them, and wished to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> the injuries they had done them. To these Arilomenes applied; and receiving an answer conformable to his wishes, he engaged his countrymen unanimously to take up arms. About a year after the revolt began, and before either party had received any auxiliaries, the Spartans and Messenians met at a village called Derca, where an obstinate engagement ensued. Arilomenes was conceived to have performed more than mortal achievements: in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> therefore, respect being also had to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, his countrymen unanimously saluted him king; which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> he modestly waved, alleging, that he took up arms to set them free, and not to make himself <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>; he consented, however, to accept the title of general, with a power of doing whatsoever he thought requisite for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the public. Knowing well the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> in which he lived, he resolved to intimidate the Spartans, by showing them what he was sure they would take for an ill <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OMEN">omen</a>. Disguising himself therefore, he went privately to the city, where, in the night, he hung up a shield on the wall of the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, with this inscription: Arilomenes dedicates this, out of the spoils of the Spartans, to the gods. It was easily perceived that this war would be both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and bloody; the Lacedemonians therefore sent deputies to Delphi, to inquire of the oracle concerning its event: the answer they received was, That it behoved the Spartans to seek a leader from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. The Athenians naturally envious of the Spartans, granted their request indeed, but in such a manner as manifested their spite; for they sent them for a general Tyrtaeus, a schoolmaster and poet, lame of one foot, and who was suspected to be a little out of his wits. But here their skill failed them; for this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>, notwithstanding his despicable appearance, proved of great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to Sparta, teaching them how to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> good, and how to bear up under ill fortune. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, Arilomenes had drawn together a mighty <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, the Eleans, Argives, Sicyonians, and Arcadians, having sent troops to his assistance; the Spartans in this, as in the former war, having no ally but Corinth. The Spartan kings, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, custom of their city, no sooner took the field, than, notwithstanding their inferiority in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, they offered the enemy battle, which Aristomenes readily accepted. It was long, obstinate, and bloody; but in the end the Messenians were victorious, and the Lacedemonians put to flight with a great slaughter. It is scarce to be conceived how much the Spartans were struck with this defeat: they grew weary of the war, dissatisfied with their kings, dissident of their own power, and in a word sunk into a state of general uneasiness and want of spirit. It was now that the Athenian general convinced them, that he was capable of fulfilling all the promises of the oracle; he encouraged them by his poems, directed them by his counsels, and recruited their broken armies with chosen men from among the Helotes. Aristomenes, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, acted with no less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and vigour. He thought it not enough to restore the reputation of the Messenians, if he did not also restore their wealth and power: he therefore taught them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> offensively against their enemies; and, entering the territories of Sparta, he took and plundered Phaëte, a considerable borough in Laconia, putting all such as made any resistance to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, carrying off at the same time an immense booty. This, however, was an injury which the Spartans could not brook with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>; they therefore sent immediately a body of forces to overtake the Messenians, which accordingly they did: but Aristomenes routed these pursuers, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to make a mighty slaughter of them, till such time as he was disabled by having a spear thrust in his side, which occasioned his being carried out of the battle. His cure, which took up some time, being finished, he resolved to carry the war even to the gates of Sparta; and to that purpose raised a very great army: but, whether he found his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> impracticable, or was really diverted by some dream, he gave out, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASTOR">Castor</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLLUX">Pollux</a>, with their sister Helena, had appeared to him, and commanded him to desist. A short time after this retreat, going with a small party to make an incursion, and attempting to take prisoners some women who were celebrating <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> near Egila, a village in Laconia, those zealous matrons fell upon him and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> with such fury, that they put them to flight, and took him prisoner: however, he soon afterwards made his escape, and rejoined his forces. In the third year of the war, the Spartans with a great force entered Messenia, whither Arifocrates king of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a> was come, with a great body of troops, to the assistance of his allies: Aristomenes therefore made no difficulty of fighting when the Spartans approached; but they entering privately into a negociation with Arifocrates, engaged him with bribes and promises to betray his confederates. When the battle began, the deceitful Arcadian represented to the forces under his command the mighty danger they were in, and the great difficulty there would be of retreating into their own country, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the battle should be lost: he then pretended, that the sacrifices were ominous; and, having terrified his Arcadians into the disposition of mind fitted to serve his purpose, he not only drew them off from both wings, but, in his flight, forced through the Messenian ranks, and put them too in confusion. Aristomenes and his troops, however, drew themselves into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> order, that they might defend themselves the best they could: and Messenia indeed they had need of all their valour and skill; for the Lacedemonians, who expected this event, immediately attacked and surrounded them on all sides. Fortune was, on this occasion, too powerful either for the courage or the conduct of the Messenians; so that, notwithstanding their utmost efforts, most of their army were cut to pieces, and amongst them the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. Aristomenes, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> remains of his shattered forces, retired as well as he could; and, perceiving that it was now impossible to maintain the war against the Lacedemonians upon equal terms, he exhorted his countrymen to fortify Mount Era, and to make the best dispositions possible for a long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. He likewise placed garrisons in Pylus and Methone on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> coasts; and to these three places he gathered all the inhabitants, leaving the rest of Messenia to the mercy of the Spartans. They, on the other hand, looked on the war as now in a manner finished; for which reason they divided the lands among their citizens, and caused them to be carefully cultivated, while they besieged Era. But Arifomenes quickly convinced them that the war was far from being over: he chose out of all the Messenians 300 men, with whom he ravaged all the adjacent country: carried off a prodigious booty; and, when Messenia could no longer supply the wants of his garrison, penetrated into Laconia, and bore away corn, wine, cattle, and whatever else was necessary to the subsistence of his countrymen shut up in Era: so that at last the Spartans were constrained to issue a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a>, forbidding the cultivation, not only of the Messenian territory in their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, but also of Laconia in its vicinity; whereby they distressed themselves more than their enemies, inducing at last a famine in Sparta itself, which brought with it its usual attendant, sedition. Here again all things had gone wrong, if the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of the poet Tyrtæus had not supported the Spartan courage; nor was it without much difficulty that he influenced them to continue the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCKADE">blockade</a> of Era, and to maintain a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> for the security of the country. Aristomenes, in spite of all these precautions, committed terrible depredations with his small corps of 300 men. Amongst other places which he plundered, the city of Amyclæ was one; from whence he carried not only a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, but also many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> laden with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. The kings of Sparta lying with their troops in its neighbourhood, as soon as they heard of this expedition, marched after Aristomenes with the utmost diligence; and, as the Messenians were encumbered with their booty, came up with them before they could reach Era. In this situation of things, Aristomenes, prompted rather by despair than prudence, disposed his troops in order of battle; and, notwithstanding they were so few, made a long and vigorous resistance against the whole Lacedemonian army. At length, however, numbers prevailed: the greatest part of the Messenians were slain on the spot; and Aristomenes, with about 50 of his men who survived the slaughter, were taken prisoners; that chief having received so many wounds, that he was senseless when they carried him away. The Lacedemonians expressed the loudest joy at the sight of this illustrious captive; who for so many years, by his single abilities, had Mes Messenia had enabled his exhausted country to defend itself against the whole force of Sparta. When he was recovered from his wounds, they decreed him and all his fellow prisoners to be thrown together into a deep cavern, which was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of the lowest kind of offenders. This judgement was executed with the utmost severity, excepting that Ariftomenes had leave to put on his armour. Three days he continued in this dismal place, lying upon and covered over with dead bodies. The third day, he was almost famished through want of food, and almost poisoned with the stench of corrupted carcases, when he heard a fox gnawing a body near him. Upon this he uncovered his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>, and perceiving the fox <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> by him, he with one hand seized one of its hind legs, and with the other defended his face, by catching hold of its jaw when it attempted to bite him. Following as well as he could his struggling guide, the fox at last thrust his head into a little hole; and Ariftomenes then letting go his leg, he soon forced his way through, and opened a passage to the welcome rays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, from which the noble Messenian had been so long debarred. Feeble as he was, Ariftomenes wrought himself an outlet with his nails; and travelling by night with all the expedition he could, at length arrived safe at Era, to the great joy and amazement of his countrymen. When this news was first blazed abroad, the Spartans would have had it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> for a fiction; but Ariftomenes soon put the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of it out of doubt, by falling on the pots of the Corinthians, who, as allies of the Spartans, had a considerable body of troops before Era. Most of their officers, with a multitude of private men, he slew; pillaged their camp; and, in short, did so much mischief, that the Spartans, under the pretence of an approaching festival, agreed to a cessation of arms for 40 days, that they might have time to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a> their dead. On this occasion, Ariftomenes for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time celebrated the hetaeromphonia, or the sacrifice appointed for those who had killed 100 of the enemy with their own hands. He had performed the same before and after his second battle; and he lived to do it a third time: which must appear wonderful to the reader, when he is informed, that notwithstanding this truce, certain Cretan archers in the service of the Spartans seized Ariftomenes as he was walking without the walls, and carried him away a prisoner. There were <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> of them in all; two of them immediately flew with the news to Sparta, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> remained to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>, whom they bound, and conducted to a lone cottage inhabited only by a widow and her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>. It fell out, that the young woman dreamed the night before, that she <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a lion without claws, bound, and dragged along by wolves; and that she having loosed his bonds, and given him claws, he immediately tore the wolves to pieces. As soon as Ariftomenes came into the cottage, and her mother, who knew him, had told her who he was, she instantly concluded that her dream was fulfilled; and therefore plied the Cretans with drink, and, when they were asleep, took a poniard from one of them, cut the thongs with which Ariftomenes was bound, and then put it into his hands. He presently verified her vision, by putting all his guards to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; and then carried her and her mother to Era, where, as a reward for her service, he married the young woman to his son Gorgus, then about 18 years of age. When Era had held out near eleven years, it fell into the hands of Sparta by an accident: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> of one Empiramus, a Spartan commander, driving his master's cattle to drink at the river Neda, met frequently with the wife of a Messenian, whom he engaged in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMOUR">amour</a>. This woman gave him notice, that her husband's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was without the wall; so that he could come to it without danger, when the good man was abroad; and she likewise gave him intelligence when her husband was upon duty in the garrison. The Spartan failed not to come at the time appointed; but they had not been long in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> before the husband returned, which put the house into great confusion: the woman, however, secured her gallant; and then let in her husband, whom she received in appearance with great joy, inquiring again and again by what excess of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> she was blest with his return. The innocent Messenian told her, that Ariftomenes being detained in his bed by a wound, the soldiers knowing that he could not walk the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROUNDS">rounds</a>, had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> to retire to their houses, to avoid the inclemency of the season. The Spartan no sooner heard this, than he crept softly out of doors, and hastened away to carry the news to his master. It happened, that the kings were at this time absent from the camp, and Empiramus had the chief command of the army. As soon as he received this information, he ordered his army to begin its <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, though it rained excessively, and there was no moonlight. The fellow guided them to the ford, and managed matters so well that they seized all the Messenian pots: yet, after all, they were afraid to engage; darkness, and high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, heavy <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, together with the dread of Ariftomenes, keeping them quiet in the places they had seized. As soon as it was light, the attack began; and Era had been quickly taken, if only the men had defended it; but the women fought with such fury, and by their mingling in the fray, brought such an accession of numbers, as made the event doubtful. Three days and two nights this desperate engagement lasted: at last, all hopes of preserving the city being lost, Ariftomenes drew off his wearied troops. Early in the fourth morning, he disposed the women and children in the centre, the Messenian youth in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> and rear, the least able men in the main body: himself commanded the van; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REAR_GUARD">rear-guard</a> was brought up by Gorgus and Manticlus, the former the son of Ariftomenes, the latter of Theocles, a Messenian of great merit, who fell with much <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> in this attack, fighting valiantly in the cause of his country. When all things were ready, Ariftomenes caused the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> to be thrown open; and, brandishing his spear, marched directly towards the Spartan troops, in order to force a passage. Empiramus, perceiving his intent, ordered his men to open to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and left, and fairly gave them a passage; so that Ariftomenes marched off in triumph, as it were, to Arcadia. The Arcadians, when they heard that Era was taken, were very desirous of succouring their old confederates in this deep distress: they therefore treated their king Ariftocrates to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> them into Messenia. But he, corrupted by the Lacedemonians, persuaded them that it was too late; that the Messenians were all cut off; and that such a step would only expose them to the fury of the conquerors. When the thing appeared to be otherwise, and it was known that Arictomenes was on the frontiers of Arcadia, they went in crowds to carry him provisions, and to testify their readiness to assist him and those under his command all the affluence in their power. Arictomenes desired to be heard before a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>; which being accordingly convoked, he there opened one of the boldest and best laid schemes recorded in history: he said, that he had yet 500 undaunted soldiers, who, at his command, would undertake anything; that it was very probable most of the Spartans were employed in pillaging Eria, and that therefore he determined to march and surprise Sparta; which appeared so sensible, that all the assembly loudly commended his great capacity and unshaken courage. Arictocrates, however, took care to betray him; having, by various pretences, retarded the execution of the project. The Arcadians, who began to suspect him, waited for and surprized the messengers as they came back. They took the letters from them, and read them openly in the assembly. The purport of them was, that they acknowledged his great kindness both now and in the battle; and promised, that the Lacedemonians would be grateful. As soon as the letters were read, the Arcadians fell to stoning their king, frequently calling upon the Messenians to assist them; which, however, they did not, waiting for Arictomenes's orders; who, far from triumphing in this spectacle, stood still, with his eyes fixed on the ground, which he wet with his tears, his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> pierced with sorrow to see a crowned head so shamefully and so deservedly put to death. The Arcadians afterwards erected a monument over him, with an inscription to perpetuate his infamy. As for the Messenians under the command of Gorgus and Manticlus, they passed over into Sicily; where they founded the city of Messene, one of the most famous in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. Arictomenes remained, however, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; where he married all his daughters, except the youngest, to persons of great <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, inquiring of the oracle at Delphi whom he should espouse, that his subjects might be happy under his prosperity, was directed to marry the daughter of the most worthy of the Greeks; which answer was immediately understood to point at the virgin daughter of Arictomenes. Her therefore he demanded, and received; Arictomenes accompanying him back to his dominions, where he formed a scheme of uniting the Lydians and Medes against the Spartans, resolving with this view to go into Media, and to the court of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDIS">Sardis</a>; but while he meditated these great things, death surprized him, and thereby freed Lacedemon from the most formidable enemy she ever had.

MESSIAH

Pages 152-153

a word signifying one anointed, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> installed into an office by unction. It was usual among the Jews to anoint kings, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> priests, and sometimes prophets, at the consecration or installment of them, to signify emblematically the mental qualifications necessary for discharging these offices. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, and Joab, kings of Judah, received the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> unction. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a> and his sons received the sacerdotal, and Elisha the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Elijah received the prophetic unction.—The name MESSIAH, Anointed or Christ (Χριστός), was given to the kings and high-priests of the Jews. The patriarchs and prophets are also called by the name of Messiah, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s anointed. See 1 Sam. xii. 3, 5; 1 Chron. xvi. 22; Ps. cv. 15. But this name Messiah was principally and by way of eminence given by the Jews to their expected <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Deliverer, whose coming they still vainly wait; and is a name the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> apply to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, in whom the prophecies relating to the Messiah were accomplished. The sum of these prophecies is, That there should be a glorious person named Messiah, descended from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>, who should be born at Bethlehem, of a virgin of the family of David, then in its decline, before the Jews ceased to be a people, while the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> temple was standing, and about 500 years after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EZRA">Ezra</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; who, though appearing in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> circumstances, should be introduced by a remarkable forerunner, whose business it should be to awaken the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of the people. That this illustrious person called Messiah should himself be eminent for the piety, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, and benevolence of his character, and the miraculous works he should perform: yet that, notwithstanding all this, he should be rejected and put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by the Jews; but should afterwards be raised from the dead, and exalted to a glorious throne, on which he should through all generations continue to rule, at the same time making intercession for sinners. That great calamities should for the present be brought on the Jews for rejecting him: whereas the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of God should by his means be erected among the Gentiles, and disperse itself even unto the ends of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; wherever it came, destroying idolatry, and establishing true <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and righteousness. In a word, That this glorious person should be regarded by all who believed in him as a divine teacher, an atoning sacrifice, and a royal governor: by means of whom God would make a covenant with his people, very different from that made with Israel of old; in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which they should be restored to, and established in, the divine favour, and fixed in a state of perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>. See Jesus Christ, and Christianity. The Jews, as was already observed, still wait for the coming of the Messiah, being impressed with the notion of a temporal Messiah, who is to be a mighty conqueror, and to subdue all the world. Most of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> rabbins, according to Buxtorf, believe that the Messiah is already come, but that he keeps himself concealed, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not manifest himself because of the sins of the Jews. Some of the Jews, however, in order to reconcile these prophecies that seem to contradict each other as to the character and condition of the Messiah, have had recourse to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> of two Messiahs, who are yet to succeed each other; one in a state of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMILIATION">humiliation</a> and suffering; the other of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, splendor, and power. The first, they say, is to proceed from the tribe of Ephraim, who is to fight against Gog, and to be slain by Amnillus, Zech. xii. 10. The second is to be of the tribe of Judah, and and lineage of David, who is to conquer and kill An- nillus, and restore the kingdom of Israel, reigning over it in the highest glory and felicity. Jesus Christ affirms himself the Messiah. In St John iv. 25, the Samaritan woman says to Jesus, I know that when Messiah comes, who is called the Christ, he will tell us all things. Jesus answered her, I that speak to thee am he. There are several impostors, who have endeavoured to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> for Messiahs, as Christ himself predicted. J. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">Lent</a>, a Dutchman, has written a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> De Pseudo- messiahs, "Of False Messiahs." The first he mentions was one Barcochab, who appeared under the empire of Adrian. The last was Rabbi Mordecai, who began to be talked of in 1682. A little before him, viz. in 1666, appeared Siobethai Sebi, who was taken by the Turks, and turned Mahometan.

MESSINA

Pages 153-153

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, handsome, and strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, and in the Val di Demona, with a cita- del, several forts, a fine spacious harbour, and an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>- bishop's see. It is seated on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> side, 110 miles east of Palermo, 260 south by east of Rome, and 180 south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 15° 50'. N. Lat. 38° 10'. The public buildings and the monasteries were numer- ous and magnificent, and it contained about 60,000 inhabitants; the harbour is one of the safest in the Mediterranean, and extremely deep; the viceroy of Sicily resides here six months in the year; and it was a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, fruit, corn, and excel- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">lent</a> wine, especially since it was declared a free port. This city in the beginning of the year 1783 suffered most dreadfully by the earthquakes which shook great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a> and Sicily to their foundations, over- turned many rich and populous <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and buried thousands in their ruins; (see CALABRIA, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">EARTH</a>-

MESSUAGE

Pages 157-157

MESSUAGUM, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a dwelling-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, with some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> adjoining assigned for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. By the name of messuage may a garden, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THORN">thorn</a>, mill, cottage, chamber, cellar, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>.—In Scotland, messuage denotes what is called in England the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>-house, viz. the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> dwelling-house within any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARONY">barony</a>.

META

Pages 157-157

in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a>, was a pile of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of a pyramidal form, intended as a boundary of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADIUM">stadium</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> chariot course.—When the meta was passed the seventh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> was concluded. The greatest art and management were required in avoiding the meta, and yet going as near it as possible. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> they went too near, they were in the greatest danger of breaking the chariot to pieces; and if they took too <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> a circuit in the turn, they gave their rivals an opportunity of getting within them, besides losing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of ground. The boundary of the Grecian stadium, or course, was called τρίποδα, τρίποδα, γεγυμνα and αγωγή γεγυμνα; to which last name Horace probably alludes, in calling <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> "ultima linea verum." The meta at Rome were first of wood, afterwards of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Claudius made them of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, or rather gilded them. In the Roman circus there were two meta, one at the entrance of the course, and the other at the end of it. An <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a> was placed upon the top of the meta.

METACARPUS

Pages 157-157
or METACARPIUM, (from μετά, behind, and κάρπη, hand), in Anatomy, that part of the hand between the wrist and the fingers. See ANATOMY, No. 55.

METAGITNION

Pages 157-157

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of the Athenian year, answering to the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> and...

METAL

Pages 158-158

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>. There are two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> used in heraldry, by way of colours, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver, in blazon called <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> and argent. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> of arms these metals are represented by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, which are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> colours of those metals. In engraving, gold is expressed by dotting the coat, &c. all over; and silver, by leaving it quite blank. It is a general rule in heraldry, never to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> metal upon metal, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> upon colour: so that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the field be of one of the metals, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> must be of some colour; and if the field be of any colour, the bearing must be one of the metals. METALEPSIS. See Oratory, No. 59.

METALLISATION

Pages 158-158

is defined to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> by which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> are formed in the bowels of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>.

METALLURGY

Pages 158-158

in a more general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, comprehends the whole art of working <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, from the state of ore to the utensil; and in this sense, effaying, smelting, refining, parting, smithery, gilding, &c. are only branches of metallurgy. But in a more limited sense it includes only the operations which are followed in separating metals from their ores. For an account of these processes, see <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>; and for the practical branches, see Gilding, Parting, Purifying, Refining, Smithery.

METAMORPHOSIS

Pages 158-158

in general, denotes the changing of something into a different form; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it includes the transformation of insects, as well as the mythological changes related by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets. Mythological metamorphoses were held to be of two kinds, apparent and real: thus, that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> into a bull, was only apparent; whereas that of Lycaon into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>, was supposed to be real. Most of the ancient metamorphoses include some allegorical meaning, relating either to physics <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> morality; some authors are even of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ancient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> is couched under them; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a> and Dr Hooke have attempted to unriddle several of them.

METAPHOR

Pages 158-171

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>. See Oratory, No. 54. Metaphor and Allegory, in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>.—A metaphor differs from a simile, in form only, not in substance: in a simile the two subjects are kept distinct in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, as well as in the thought; in a metaphor, the two subjects are kept distinct in the thought only, not in the expression. A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> resembles a lion, and upon that resemblance many similes have been raised by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> and other poets. But instead of resembling a lion, let us take the aid of the imagination, and feign <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> the hero to be a lion; by that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> the simile is converted into a metaphor; which is carried on by describing all the qualities of a lion that resemble those of the hero. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> here, that of resemblance, belongs to the thought. An additional pleasure arises from the expression: the poet, by figuring his hero to be a lion, goes on to describe the lion in appearance, but in reality the hero; and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> is peculiarly beautiful, by expressing the virtues and qualities of the hero in new terms, which, properly speaking, belong not to him, but to the lion. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> better be understood by examples. A family connected with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>, resembles a tree, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> and branches of which are connected with a common root; but let us suppose, that a family is figured, not barely to be like a tree, but to be a tree; and then the simile will be converted into a metaphor, in the following manner: Edward's sev'n sons, whereof thyself art one, Were sev'n fair branches, springing from one root; Some of these branches by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>'s cut: But Thomas, my dear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, my Gloster, One flourishing branch of his most <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> root, Is hack'd <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> leaves all faded, By Envy's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">Murder</a>'s bloody axe. Richard II. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> i. sc. 3. Figuring <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> life to be a voyage at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. There is a tide in the affairs of men, Which, taken at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, leads on to Fortune: Omitted, all the voyage of their life Is bound in shallows and in miseries. On such a full sea are we now afloat; And we must take the current when it serves, Or lose our ventures. Julius Caesar, act iv. sc. 5. Figuring <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to be a garland of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>: Hastur. Wou'd to heav'n, Thy name in arms were now as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> as mine! Pr. Henry. I'll make it greater ere I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> from thee; And all the budding honours on thy crest I'll crop, to make a garland for my head. First Part of Henry IV. act v. sc. 9. Figuring a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who hath acquired great reputation and honour to be a tree full of fruit: Oh, boys, this story The world may read in me; my body's mark'd With Roman words; and my report was once First with the best of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. Cymbeline lov'd me; And when a soldier was the theme, my name Was not far off; then was I as a tree, Whose boughs did <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> with fruit. But in one night, A storm or robbery, call it what you will, Shook down my mellow hangings, nay, my leaves; And left me bare to wither. Cymbeline, act iii. sc. 3. "Blest by thy <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, thou <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of shells, said Swaran of the dark-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> shield. In peace, thou art the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALE">gale</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>; in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, the mountain-storm. Take now my hand in friendship, thou noble king of Morven." Fingal. "Thou dwellest in the foul of Malvina, son of mighty Offian. My sighs arise with the beam of the east; my tears descend with the drops of night. I was a lovely tree in thy presence, Oscar, with all my branches round me: but thy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> came like a blast from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>," An allegory differs from a metaphor; and a figure of speech differs from both. A metaphor is defined above to be an act of the imagination, figuring one thing to be another. An allegory requires no such operation, nor is one thing figured to be another: it confuses in choosing a subject having properties or circumstances resembling those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> subject: and the former is described in such a manner as to represent the latter: the subject thus represented is kept out of view: we are left to discover it by reflection; and we are pleased with the discovery, because it is our own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. (See the word ALLEGORY.) Quintilian gives the following instance of an allegory. O navis, referent in mare te <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVI">novi</a> Fluctus. O quid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGIS">agis</a>? fortiter occupa portum. Horat. Lib. i. ode 14. and explains it elegantly in the following words: "Totaque ille Horatii locus, quo navim pro republica, fluctuum tempestatibus pro bellis civilibus, portum pro pace atque <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCORDIA">concordia</a>," dicit. In a figure of speech, there is no fiction of the imagination employed, as in a metaphor; nor a representative subject introduced, as in an allegory. This figure, as its name implies, regards the expression only, not the thought; and it may be defined, the using a word in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> different from what is proper to it. Thus youth, or the beginning of life, is expressed figuratively by morning of life: morning is the beginning of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and in that view it is employed to signify the beginning of any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a>, life especially, the progress of which is reckoned by days. See Figure of Speech. Metaphor and allegory are so much connected, that it seemed proper to handle them together: the rules particularly for distinguishing the good from the bad, are common to both. We shall therefore proceed to these rules, after adding some examples to illustrate the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of an allegory, which, with a view to this article, was but slightly illustrated under its proper name. Horace, speaking of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> to Pyrrha, which was now extinguished, expressed himself thus: Me tabula facer Votivae paries indicat uvida Suspendisse potenti Vellimenta maris Deo. Carm. lib. i. ode 5. Again: Phocbus volentem praelia me loqui, Violas et urbes, increpuit, lyra Ne parva Tyrrhenum per aquor Vela darem. Carm. lib. iv. ode 15. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>. Great lords, wise men ne'er sit and wail their loss, But cheerly seek how to redress their harms. What though the mast be now blown overboard, The cable broke, the holding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> lost, And half our sailors swallowed in the flood! Yet lives our pilot still. Is't meet that he Should leave the helm, and, like a fearful lad, With tearful eyes add <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to the sea, And give more strength to that which hath too much; While in his moan the ship spits on the rock, Which industry and courage might have fav'd? Ah, what a shame! ah, what a fault were this! Third Part of Henry VI. act v. sc. 5. Oroonoko. Ha! thou hast rous'd The lion in his den; he stalks abroad, And the wide forest trembles at his roar. I find the danger now. Oroonoko, act iii. sc. 2: "My well beloved hath a vineyard in a very fruitful hill. He fenced it, gathered out the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> thereof, planted it with the choicest vine, built a tower in the midst of it, and also made a wine press therein; he looked that it should bring forth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, and it brought forth wild grapes. And now, O inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, and men of Judah, judge, I pray you, betwixt me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my vineyard, that I have not done? Wherefore, when I looked that it should bring forth grapes, brought it forth wild grapes? And now go to, I will tell you what I will do to my vineyard: I will take away the hedge thereof, and it shall be eaten up; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> down the wall thereof, and it shall be trodden down. And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged, but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> that they <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> no rain upon it. For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant." Isaiah v. 1. The rules that govern metaphors and allegories are of two kinds. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of these figures comes under the first kind: the propriety or impropriety of introduction comes under the other.—To begin with rules of the first kind; some of which coincide with those already given for similes; some are peculiar to metaphors and allegories. In the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, it has been observed, that a simile cannot be agreeable where the resemblance is either too strong or too faint. This holds equally in metaphor and allegory; and the reason is the same in all. In the following instances, the resemblance is too faint to be agreeable. Malcolm. ———— But there's no bottom, none, In my voluptuousness: your wives, your daughters, Your matrons, and your maids, could not fill up The cistern of my lust. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACBETH">Macbeth</a>, act iv. sc. 4. The best way to judge of this metaphor, is to convert it into a simile: which would be bad, because there is scarce any resemblance between lust and a cistern, or betwixt enormous lust and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> cistern. Again: He cannot buckle his distemper'd cause Within the belt of rule. Macbeth, act v. sc. 2. There is no resemblance between a distempered cause and any body that can be confined within a belt. Again: Steep me in poverty to the very lips. Othello, act iv. sc. 9. Poverty Metaphor Poverty here must be conceived a fluid, which it resembles not in any manner. Speaking to Bolingbroke banish'd for six years: The sullen passage of thy weary steps, Esteem a foil, wherein thou art to set The precious <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JEWEL">jewel</a> of thy home-return. Richard II. act ii. sc. 6. Again: Here is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, lady, And every word in it a gaping wound Issuing life-blood. Merchant of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, act iii. sc. 3. Tante molis erat Romanam condere gentem. Æneid. i. 37. The following metaphor is strained beyond all endurance: Timur-bec, known to us by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAMERLANE">Tamerlane</a> the Great, writes to Bojazet <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of the Ottomans in the following terms: "Where is the monarch who <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DARES">dares</a> resist us? where is the potentate who doth not glory in being numbered among our attendants? As for thee, descended from a Turcoman sailor, since the vessel of thy unbounded ambition hath been wreck'd in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of thy self-love, it would be proper, that thou shouldest take in the fails of thy temerity, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> the anchor of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a> in the port of sincerity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, which is the port of safety; lest the tempest of our vengeance make thee perish in the sea of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> thou deservest." Such strained figures, as observed above, are not unfrequent in the first dawn of refinement; the mind in a new enjoyment knows no bounds, and is generally carried to excess, till <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> discover the proper limits. Secondly, Whatever resemblance subjects may have, it is wrong to put one for another, where they bear no mutual proportion. Upon comparing a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> to a very low subject, the simile takes on an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURLESQUE">burlesque</a>; and the same will be the effect where the one is imagined to be the other, as in a metaphor; or made to represent the other, as in an allegory. Thirdly, These figures, a metaphor especially, ought not to be crowded with many minute circumstances; for in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> it is scarcely possible to avoid obscurity. A metaphor above all ought to be short: it is difficult, for any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, to support a lively image of a thing being what we know it is not; and for that reason, a metaphor drawn out to any length, instead of illusrating or enlivening the principal subject, becomes disagreeable by overtraining the mind. Here Cowley is extremely licentious. Take the following instance. Great and wise conqueror, who where'er Thou com'st, dost fortify, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> there! Who canst defend as well as get; And never hadst one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> up yet; Now thou art in, thou ne'er wilt part With one inch of my vanquished heart; For since thou took'st it by assault from me 'Tis garrison's so strong with thoughts of thee, It fears no beauteous enemy. For the same reason, however agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> allegories may at first be by their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a>, they never afford any lasting pleasure: witness the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAIRY">Fairy</a> Queen, which with great power of expression, variety of images, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a> of versification, is scarce ever read a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time. In the fourth place, The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> carried on in a simile, being in a metaphor sunk by imagining the principal subject to be that very thing which it only resembles; an opportunity is furnished to describe it in terms taken strictly or literally with respect to its imagined nature. This suggests another rule, That in constructing a metaphor, the writer ought to make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of such words only as are applicable literally to the imagined nature of his subject: figurative words ought carefully to be avoided; for such complicated figures, instead of setting the principal subject in a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, involve it in a cloud, and it is well <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the reader, without rejecting by the lump, endeavour patiently to gather the plain meaning, regardless of the figures: A stubborn and unconquerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> Creeps in his veins, and drinks the streams of life. Lady Jane Gray, act i. sc. i. Copied from Ovid: Sorbent avidæ praecordia flammæ. Metamorph. lib. ix. 172. Let us analyze this expression. That a fever may be imagined a flame, we admit: though more than one step is necessary to come at the resemblance: a fever, by heating the body, resembles fire; and it is no stretch to imagine a fever to be a fire: again, by a figure of speech, flame may be put for fire, because they are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> conjoined; and therefore a fever may be termed a flame. But now admitting a fever to be a flame, its effects ought to be explained in words that agree literally to a flame. This rule is not observed here; for a flame drinks figuratively only, not properly. King Henry to his son <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Henry: Thou hid'st a thousand daggers in thy thoughts, Which thou hast whetted on thy stony heart To stab at half an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of my frail life. Second Part Henry IV. act iv. sc. ii. Such faulty metaphors are pleasantly ridiculed in the Rehearsal: "Physician. Sir, to conclude, the place you fill has more than amply exacted the talents of a wary pilot; and all these threatening storms, which, like impregnate clouds, hover o'er our heads, will, when they once are grasped but by the eye of reason, melt into fruitful showers of blessings on the people." "Bayer. Pray mark that allegory. Is not that good." "Johnson. Yes, that grasping of a storm with the eye is admirable." Act ii. sc. i. Fifthly, The jumbling different metaphors in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, beginning with one metaphor and ending with another, commonly called a mix metaphor, ought never to be indulged. K. Henry. K. Henry. ——Will you again unknit This churlish knot of all-abhorred war, And move in that obedient orb again, Where you did give a fair and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> light? First Part Henry VI. act v. sc. 1. Whether 'tis nobler in the mind, to suffer The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune; Or to take arms against a sea of troubles, And by opposing end them. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMLET">Hamlet</a>, act iii. sc. 2. In the sixth place, It is unpleasent to join different metaphors in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, even where they are preserved distinct: for when the subject is imagined to be first one thing and then another in the same period without <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a>, the mind is diffracted by the rapid transition; and when the imagination is put on such hard duty, its images are too faint to produce any good effect: At <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol0.html#article-REGINA">regina</a> gravi jamdudum faucia cura, Vulnus alti venis, et caeco carpitur igni. Æneid. iv. 1. Est mollis flamma medullas Interea, et tacitum vivit sub pechore vulnus. Æneid. iv. 66. Motum ex Metello consule civicum, Bellique causas, et vitia, et modos, Ludumque fortunæ, graveque Principum anicitiæ, et arma Nondum expiatis uncta cruribus, Periculose plenum opus aleæ, Tractas, et incendis per ignes Subpositos cineri dolofæ. Horat. Carm. lib. ii. ode 1. In the last place, It is still worse to jumble together metaphorical and natural expression, so as that the period must be understood in part metaphorically, in part literally; for the imagination cannot follow with sufficient ease changes so sudden and unprepared: a metaphor begun and not carried on, hath no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>; and instead of light, there is nothing but obscurity and confusion. Instances of such incorrect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> are without <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>: we shall, for a specimen, select a few from different authors. Speaking of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, This precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> set in the sea, Which serves it in the office of a wall, Or as a most defensive to a house, Against the envy of less happier lands. Richard II. act ii. sc. 1. In the first line Britain is figured to be a precious stone: in the following line, Britain, divested of her metaphorical dress, is presented to the reader in her natural appearance. These growing feathers pluck'd from Cæsar's wing, Will make him fly an ordinary pitch, Who else would soar above the view of men, And keep us all in fervile fearfulness. Julius Cæsar, act i. sc. 1. Rebus angustis animosus atque Fortis adpare: sapienter idem Contrahas vento nimum secundo Turgida vela. Hor. Carm. lib. ii. ode 10. The following is a miserable jumble of expressions, arising from an unsteady view of the subject, between its figurative and natural appearance: But now from gathering clouds destruction pours, Which ruins with mad rage our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALCYON">halcyon</a> hours: <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">Mills</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> jealousies the tempest form, Whilst late divisions reinforce the storm. Dijonfary, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTO">canto</a> iii. To thee the world its present homage pays, The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> early, but mature the praise. Pope's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">Imitation</a> of Horace, book ii. Oui, sa pudeur ne s'est que franche grimace, Qu'une <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OMBRE">ombre</a> de vertu qui garde mal la place, Et qui s'évanouit, comme l'on peut favorir, Aux rayons du soleil qu'une bourre vait voir. Molière, L'Étourdi, act iii. sc. 2. Et son feu, de pourvû de fente et de lecture, S'éteint à chaque pas, faut de nourriture. Boileau, L'Art Poétique, chant. iii. l. 319. Dryden, in his dedication of the translation of Æneid, says, "When thus, as I may say, before the use of the loadstone, or knowledge of the compass, I was sailing in a vast ocean, without other help than the pole-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, and the rules of the French stage among the moderns," &c. "There is a time when factions, by the vehemence of their own <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>, stun and disable one another." Bolingbroke. This fault of jumbling the figure and plain expression into one confused <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, is not less common in allegory than in metaphor. Take the following examples: Heu! quoties fidelis, Mutatoque Deos flebit, et alpera Nigris aquora ventis Emirabitur infolens, Qui nunc te fruatur credulus aurea; Qui semper vacuam, semper amabilem Sperat, nec sius auræ Fallacis. Horat. Carm. lib. i. ode 5. Pour moi sur <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CETTE">cette</a> mer, qu'ici bas nous courons, Je songe à me pourvoir d'équipet et d'avirons, À régler mes desirs, à prévenir l'orage, Et sauver, s'il se peut, ma Raison du naufrage. Boileau, epitre 5. Lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a>, speaking of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> fabulists: "They (says he) wrote in signs, and spoke in parables: all their fables carry a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> meaning: the story is one, and entire; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> the same throughout; not broken or changed, and always conformable to the nature of the creature they introduce. They never tell you, that the dog which snapped at a shadow, lost his troop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>; that would be unintelligible. This is Metaphor. His (Dryden's new way of telling a story, and confounding the moral and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> together.) After insisting from the Hind and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PANTHER">Panther</a>, he goes on thus: "What relation has the hind to our Saviour? or what notion have we of a panther's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">bible</a>? If you say he means the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, how does the church feed on lawns, or range in the forest? Let it be always a church, or always a cloven-footed beast; for we cannot bear his shifting the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> every line." A few words more upon allegory. Nothing gives greater pleasure than this figure, when the representative subject bears a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a>, in all its circumstances, to that which is represented: but the choice is seldom so lucky; the analogy being generally too faint and obscure, as to puzzle and not please. An allegory is still more difficult in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> than in poetry; the former can show no resemblance but what appears to the eye; the latter hath many other resources for showing the resemblance. And therefore, with respect to what the abbe du <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOS">Bos</a> terms mixt allegorical compositions, these may do in poetry; because, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, the allegory can easily be distinguished from the historical part: no person, for example, mistakes <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>'s Fame for a real being. But such a mixture in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> is intolerable; because in a picture the objects must appear all of the same kind, wholly real or wholly emblematical. For this reason, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> de Medicis, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of Luxembourg, painted by Rubens, is unpleasing by a perpetual jumble of real and allegorical personages, which produce a discordance of parts, and an obscurity upon the whole: witness, in particular, the tablature representing the arrival of Mary de Medicis at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a>; where, together with the real personages, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEREIDS">Nereids</a> and Tritons appear founding their shells: such a mixture of fiction and reality in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROUP">group</a> is strangely absurd. The picture of Alexander and Roxana, described by Lucian, is gay and fanciful; but it suffers by the allegorical figures. It is not in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> of man to invent an allegorical representation deviating farther from any shadow of resemblance, than one exhibited by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. anno 1664; in which an enormous chariot, intended to represent that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, is dragged along, surrounded with men and women, representing the four ages of the world, the celestial signs, the seasons, the hours, &c. a monstrous composition, and yet scarcely more absurd than Guido's tablature of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AURORA">Aurora</a>. In an allegory, as well as in a metaphor, terms ought to be chosen that properly and literally, are applicable to the representative subject; nor ought any circumstance to be added that is not proper to the representative subject, however justly it may be applicable properly or figuratively to the principal. The following allegory is therefore faulty: Ferus et Cupido, Semper ardentes acuens sagittas. Cote cruenta. Horat. lib. ii, ode 8. For though blood may suggest the cruelty of love, it is an improper or immaterial circumstance in the representative subject: water, not blood, is proper for a whetstone. We proceed to the next head, which is, to examine in what circumstances these figures are proper, in what improper. This inquiry is not altogether superseded by what is said upon the same subject in the article Comparison; because, upon <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, it will be found, that a short metaphor or allegory may be proper, where a simile, drawn out to a greater length, and in its nature more solemn, would scarcely be relished. And, in the first place, A metaphor, like a simile, is excluded from common conversation, and from the description of ordinary incidents. Secondly, In expressing any severe <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> that totally occupies the mind, metaphor is unnatural. The following example, of deep despair, beside the highly figurative style, has more the air of raving than of sense: Califa. Is it the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>, or my father? Madness! confusion! let the storm come on, Let the tumultuous roar drive all upon me, Dahr my devoted bark; ye surges, break it; 'Tis for my ruin that the tempest rises. When I am lost, sunk to the bottom low, Peace shall return, and all be calm again. Fair Penitent, act v. The following metaphor is sweet and lively; but it suits not the fiery temper of Chamont, inflamed with passion: parables are not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of wrath venting itself without restraint: Chamont. You took her up a little tender flow'r, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">Just</a> sprouted on a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, which the next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROST">frost</a> Had nipp'd; and with a careful loving hand, Transplanted her into your own fair garden, Where the sun always shines: there long she flourish'd, Grew sweet to sense, and lovely to the eye; Till at the last a cruel spoiler came, Cropt this fair rose, and riled all its sweetness, Then cast it like a loathsome weed away. Orphan, act iv. The following speech, full of imagery, is not natural in grief and dejection of mind. Gonfalone. O my son! from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> dotage Of a father's fondness these ills arose, For thee I've been ambitious, base, and bloody: For thee I've plung'd into this sea of sin; Stemming the tide with only one weak hand, While o'ther bore the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> (to wreath thy brow), Whose <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> has sunk me ere I reach'd the shore. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">Mourning</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDE">Bride</a>, act v. sc. 6. There is an enchanting picture of deep distress in Macbeth, where Macduff is represented lamenting his wife and children, inhumanly murdered by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>. Stung to the heart with the news, he questions the messenger over and over: not that he doubted the fact, but that his heart revolted against so cruel a misfortune. After struggling some time with his grief, he turns from his wife and children to their <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a>: and then gives vent to his resentment, but still with manliness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>: O, I could play the woman with mine eyes, And braggart with my tongue. But, gentle Heav'n!
