From hence it happens, that nothing is more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> than to see the old father and mother reduced to the utmost indigence, and even begging about the streets, while their unnatural daughters are in affluence; and we ourselves have frequently been shown the eldest daughter parading it through the town in the greatest splendour, while her mother and sister followed her as servants, and made a melancholy part of her attendant train. "The sons, as soon as they are of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> a livelihood, are turned out of the family, sometimes with a small present or portion, but more frequently without anything to support them; and thus reduced, they either endeavour to live by their labour, or, which is more usual, go on board some trading vessel as sailors or as servants, remaining abroad till they have got together some competency, and then return home to marry and to be hanged. Some few there are who, taking advantage of the Turkish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> through this whimsical custom, who marry their calogrias, and retain to themselves a competent provision: but these are accounted men of a singular and even criminal disposition, and are hated and despised as conformists to Turkish manners, and deserters of their native customs; so that we may suppose they are few indeed who have the boldness to depart from the manners of their country, to adopt the customs of their detested masters, and to brave the contempt, the derision, and the hatred, of their neighbours and fellow-citizens. "Of all these extraordinary particulars I was informed by the French <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>, a man of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> and of indisputable veracity, who had resided in this island for several years, and who solemnly assured me that every circumstance was true: but indeed our own observation left us without the least room for doubt, and the singular appearance and deportment of the ladies fully evinced the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of our friend's relation. In walking through the town, it is easy to perceive, from the whimsical manners of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> passengers, that the women, according to the vulgar phrase, wear the breeches. They frequently stopped us in the streets, examined our dress, interrogated us with a bold and manly air, laughed at our foreign garb and appearance; and showed so little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to that decent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> which is or ought to be the true characteristic of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, that there is every reason to suppose they would, in spite of their haughtiness, be the kindest ladies upon <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, if they were not strictly watched by the Turks, who are here very numerous, and would be ready to punish any transgression of their ungallant laws with arbitrary fines. But <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and native manners will often baffle the efforts even of tyranny. In all their customs these manly ladies seem to have changed sexes with the men. The woman rides astride, the man sits sideways upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>; nay, I have been assured that the husband's distinguishing appellation is his wife's family name. The women have town and country houses, in the management of which the husband never <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DARES">dares</a> interfere. Their gardens, their servants, are all their own; and the husband, from every circumstance of his behaviour, appears to be no other than his wife's first domestic, perpetually bound to her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, and slave to her caprice. Hence it is that a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> obtains in the country, that this island was formerly inhabited by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMAZONS">Amazons</a>; a tradition, however, founded upon no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> that I know of. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAPPHO">Sappho</a> indeed, the most renowned female that this island has ever produced, is said to have had manly inclinations; in which, as Lucian informs us, she did but conform with the singular manners of her countrywomen: but I do not find that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> in which the choice to show these inclinations is imitated by the present female inhabitants, who seem perfectly content with the dear prerogative of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> sway, without endeavouring in any other particular to change the course of nature; yet will this circumstance serve to show, that the women of Lesbos had always something peculiar, and even peculiarly masculine, in their manners and propensities. But be this as it may, it is certain that no country whatsoever can afford a more perfect idea of an Amazonian commonwealth, or better serve to render probable those ancient relations which our manners would induce us to esteem incredible, than this island of Metelin. These lordly ladies are for the most part very handsome in spite of their dress, which is singular and disadvantageous. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">Down</a> to the girdle, which as in the old Grecian garb is raised far above what we usually call the waist, they wear nothing but a shift of thin and transparent <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAUZE">gauze</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, green, or brown, through which everything is visible, their breasts only excepted, which they cover with a sort of handkerchief; and this, as we were informed, the Turks have obliged them to wear, while they look upon it as an encumbrance, and as no inconsiderable portion of Turkish tyranny. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a> sleeves of the same thin material perfectly show their arms even to the shoulder. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> ornaments are chains of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a>, to which they hang small pieces of gold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>. Their eyes are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and fine; and the nose, which we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> Grecian, usually prevails among them, as it does indeed among the women of all these islands. Their complexions are naturally fine; but they spoil them by paint, of which they make abundant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; and they disfigure their pretty faces by shaving the hinder part of the eyebrow, and replacing it with a straight line of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> neatly applied with some sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a>, the brow being thus <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in a straight and narrow line till it joins the hair on each side of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>. They are well made, of the middle size, and for the most part plump; but they are distinguished by nothing so much and so universally as by a haughty, disdainful, and supercilious air, with which they seem to look down upon all mankind as creatures of an inferior nature, born for their service, and doomed to be their slaves; neither does this peculiarity of countenance in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> diminish their natural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, but rather adds to it that sort of bewitching <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> which the French call piquant." His lordship has been at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pains to investigate the origin of such a singular custom; but is unable to find any other example in history than that of the Lycians, who called themselves by the names of their mothers, and not of their fathers. When asked by their neighbours who they were? they described themselves by their maternal genealogy. If a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> should marry a slave, the children by that marriage were accounted noble; but though the first man among them marry a foreign woman, the children would be accounted ignoble. This custom is mentioned by several ancient authors. A difficulty of no little magnitude occurs, however, in accounting for the derivation of the inhabitants of Lesbos from the Lycians. This is solved in the following manner: In times of the most remote antiquity, the island of Lesbos was peopled by the Pelasgi, who, under their leader Xanthus, the son of Triopas <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a>, first inhabited Lesbos; previous to that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they had dwelt in a certain part of Metellus Lycia which they had conquered; and in this country we may suppose they had learned the custom in question.

METELLUS

Pages 296-296

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of the family of the Caecilii at Rome, the most known of whom were —A general who defeated the Achaeans, took Thebes, and invaded <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, &c.—Q. Caecilius, who rendered himself illustrious by his successes against Jugurtha the Numidian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, from which he was surnamed Numidicus. Another who saved from the flames the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALLADIUM">palladium</a>, when Vejla's temple was on fire. He was then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>. He lost his sight and one of his arms in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, to reward his zeal and piety, permitted him always to be drawn to the senate <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in a chariot, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> which no one had ever before enjoyed. He also gained a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> victory over the Carthaginians, &c. Q. Caecilius Celer, another who distinguished himself by his spirited exertions against Catiline. He married the sister of Clodius, who disgraced him by her inconstancy and lasciviousness. He died 57 years before Christ. He was greatly lamented by Cicero, who shed tears at the loss of one of his most faithful and valuable friends. L. Caecilius, a tribune in the civil wars of J. Caesar and Pompey. He favoured the cause of Pompey, and opposed Caesar when he entered Rome with a victorious <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. He refused to open the gates of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>'s temple, in which were deposited great treasures; upon which they were broke open by Caesar, and Metellus retired when threatened with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Q. Caecilius, a warlike general who conquered <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a> and Macedonia, and was surnamed Macedonicus. He had four sons, of whom three were consuls, and the other obtained a triumph, all during their father's lifetime. A general of the Roman armies against the Sicilians and Carthaginians. Before he marched, he offered sacrifices to all the gods except Vejla; for which neglect the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> was so incensed, that she demanded the blood of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Metella. When Metella was going to be immolated, the goddess placed a heifer in her <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and carried her to a temple at Lanuvium, of which she became the priestess. Another, surnamed Dalmaticus from his conquest over <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, A. U. C. 634.—Cimber, one of the conspirators against J. Caesar. It was he who gave the signal to attack and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTATOR">dictator</a> in the senate house. —Pius, a general in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, against Sertorius, on whose head he fed a price of 100 talents and 20,000 acres of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>.

METEMPSYCHOSIS

Pages 296-297

(formed of μετά "beyond," and ψυχή "I animate <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> enliven"); in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, the passage or transmigration of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, into the body of some other animal. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a> and his followers held, that after death men's souls passed into other bodies, of this or that kind, according to the manner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> they had led. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> they had been vicious, they were imprisoned in the bodies of miserable beasts, there to do <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a> for several ages: at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> whereof, they returned refreshed to animate men. But, if they lived virtuously, some happier brute, or even a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> creature, was to be their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>. What led Pythagoras into this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> was, the persuasion Metempsychosis he had that the soul was not of a perishable <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; whence he concluded that it must remove into some other body upon its abandoning this. Lucan treats this doctrine as a kind of officious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a>, contrived to mitigate the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of death, by persuading men that they only changed their lodging, and only ceased to live to begin a new life. Reuchlin denies this doctrine; and maintains that the metempsychosis of Pythagoras implied nothing more than a similitude of manners, desires, and studies, formerly existing in some person deceased, and now revived in another alive. Thus when it was said that Euphorbus was revived in Pythagoras, no more was meant than that the martial virtue which had shone in Euphorbus at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, was now, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, revived in Pythagoras, by reason of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> respect he bore the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATHLETE">athlete</a>. For those people wondering how a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> should be so much taken with men of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, he palliated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, by saying, that the soul of Euphorbus, i.e., his genius, disposition, and inclinations, were revived in him. And this gave occasion to the report, that Euphorbus's soul, who perished in the Trojan war, had transmigrated into Pythagoras. Ficinus affirms, that what <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> speaks of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIGRATION">migration</a> of a human soul into a brute, is intended allegorically, and is to be understood only of the manners, affections, and habits, degenerated into a beastly nature by vice. Serranus, though he allows some force to this interpretation, yet inclines rather to understand the metempsychosis of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a>. Pythagoras is said to have borrowed the notion of a metempsychosis from the Egyptians; others say, from the ancient Brahmins. It is still retained among the Banians and other idolaters of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>; and makes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> foundation of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. So extremely are they bigotted to it, that they not only forbear eating any thing that has life, but many of them even refuse to defend themselves from wild beasts. They burn no wood, lest some little animalcule should be in it; and are so very charitable, that they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> redeem from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of strangers any animals that they find ready to be killed. See Pythagoreans. **METEMPSYCHOSIS** (from μετα ποθη, and πνευμα ειδος "I fail,") a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>, expressing the solar equation, necessary to prevent the new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> from happening a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> too late. By which it stands contradistinguished from proempsyphos, which signifies the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> equation, necessary to prevent the new moon from happening a day too soon. The new moons running a little backwards, that is, coming a day too soon at the end of 312 years and a half; by the proempsyphos, a day is added every 300 years, and another every 2400 years: on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, by the metempsyphos, a bifextile is suppressed each 134 years; that is, three times in 400 years. These alterations are never made but at the end of each century; that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> being very remarkable, and rendering the practice of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a> easy. There are three rules for making this addition or suppression of the bifextile day, and, by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, for changing the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> of the epacts. 1. When there is a metempsyphos without a proempsyphos, the next following, or lower index, must be taken. 2. When there is a proempsyphos without a metempsyphos, the next preceding or superior index is to be taken. 3. When there are both a metempsyphos and a proempsyphos, or when there is neither the one nor the other, the same index is preserved. Thus, in 1600, we had D: in 1700, by reason of the metempsyphos, C was taken: in 1800, there was both a proempsyphos and a metempsyphos; so the same index was retained. In 1900, there will be a metempsyphos again, when B will be taken; which will be preserved in 2000, because there will then be neither the one nor the other. This is as far as we need compute for it: But Clavius has calculated a cycle of 301,800 years; at the end of which period, the same indices return in the same order. See **EPACT**.

METEOR

Pages 297-312

(by the Greeks called πτερωξα, q.d. sublima <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> raised;" by the Latins impressiones as making signs or impressions in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>), <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> denotes any bodies in the air that are of a transitory <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. Hence it is extended to the phenomena of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIL">hail</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, snow, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>, &c.; but is most commonly confined to those unusual and fiery appearances named falling stars, ignes fulvi, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-AURORA_BOREALIS"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol3.html#article-AURORA">aurora</a> borealis, &c. See **<a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOROLOGY">METEOROLOGY</a>**. **METEOROLITE.** This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is derived from the Greek πτερωξα, a meteor, and λίθος, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; and denotes a stony substance, exhibiting peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, and whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> is usually accompanied by the appearance and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a> of a fire-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUMINOUS">Luminous</a> meteors have, in all ages, been observed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>. It is also well known that their disappearance has frequently been attended with a loud noise; but that they should moreover terminate in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of one or more <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> bodies to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH_S">earth's</a> surface, is a position so repugnant to our ordinary conceptions of the tenor of physical events, that we cannot admit it as a fact on slight or scanty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>. With due deference, however, to some philosophers of name, we are not prepared to assert, that it implies impossibility. For who has explored the higher regions of the atmosphere? or who knows what may take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> beyond its precincts? <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a solid result from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of two aeriform substances, as muriatic acid and ammonical gases; if <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXYGEN">oxygen</a>, the properties of which are most familiar to us in the state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAS">gas</a>, can undergo <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FIXATION">fixation</a>, and if <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> can <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> into crystalline forms, is it too bold to presume, that the same, or similar processes, effected in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LABORATORY">laboratory</a> of the atmosphere, may be within the range of possible occurrences? At all events, the same Being who called into existence those sublime and countless masses of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> which revolve in space, may, to serve purposes unknown to us, create bodies of dimensions infinitely smaller, and destined to impinge on some planetary orb. The reasoning of an angel may not convince us, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> is greater than the whole, or that the value of two and two is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to five; but a very ordinary logician may prove to our satisfaction, that the contact of particles of matter in portions of space which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> beyond our globe, is no chimerical supposition. Every thing around us proclaims, that matter is subject to incessant change. New forms and new modifications are ever springing into being: and can we doubt, that the same particles, as they may happen to be affected or influenced by various circumstances, may exist in the state of gas, of aqueous vapour, or of a concrete <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>? Again, Again, it surely <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be seriously maintained, that, from the rarity of a phenomenon, we are warranted to infer its nonexistence. The appearance of a comet is rare, but not a fictitious occurrence. Nay, we may safely advance a step farther, and assert, without fear of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFUTATION">confutation</a>, that the existence of a phenomenon, if otherwise well attested, cannot be disproved by our inability to explain it. How multiplied, in fact, are the subjects, even of our daily and hourly observation, which we cannot satisfactorily expound? We cannot say why a small seed should gradually unfold into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tree, why <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> should produce <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, why the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> in immediate subserviency to the will, or why a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTUSION">contusion</a> of the brain should induce stupor, alienation of mind, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. It is one thing to prove a fact, and it is another to account for it. From these premises it follows in course, that we are not entitled to reject the existence of meteoric <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, provided it be established by valid testimony. Should the historical evidence, on a fair and disinterested review, be deemed conclusive, we may afterwards examine the theories which have been propounded for the solution of the appearance. From the Scriptures of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> we are not aware that any passage can be cited in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> corroboration of the descent of stones from the atmosphere. The ingenious and fanciful Mr Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a>, indeed, in his "Remarks concerning stones said to have fallen from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, both in these days, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times," adverts to the 11th <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> of the 18th Psalm.—The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> also thundered out of heaven, and the Highest gave his thunder: hail-stones and coals of fire." This last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> has, no doubt, been conjectured to denote real hard bodies, in a state of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNITION">ignition</a>; and the term ἀβογαστες, employed by the cautious Seventy, rather favours such an interpretation. The same expression, however, occurs in the preceding verse, without admitting this interpretation; and the phrase seems to be only a figurative <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of describing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>. In the sober latitudes of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and even in colloquial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, we talk of balls of fire and thunderbolts, without any reference to solid matter. Mr King likewise quotes the 11th verse of the 10th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of Joshua.—"And it came to pass, as they fled from before Israel, and were in the going <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to Beth-horon, that the Lord <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> down <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> stones from heaven upon them unto Azekah, and they died: they were more which died with hail-stones, than they whom the children of Israel slew with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>." Here, the expression, great stones, is less equivocal than coals of fire; yet the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEXT">context</a> hardly allows us to doubt, that the great stones were really hail-stones, or rather, perhaps, lumps of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a>, consolidated in the atmosphere, such as occasionally fall in hot countries, and such as alarmed the whole of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> and its neighbourhood in 1788. At any rate, the slaughter of the Canaanites is represented as resulting from the special interposition of divine power; and the consideration of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> is irrelevant to our present purpose. If from sacred, we turn to the early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of profane <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, we shall find the annals of public events very copiously interspersed with notices of strange appearances, many of which may be safely ascribed to the ascendancy which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> obtained over the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind. The skepticism of the learned is, however, sometimes not less injudicious and indiscriminate than the credulity of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a>; and he who should resolve every extraordinary event, which is recorded by the writers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> and Rome, into a "cunningly devised <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>," would not be less reprehensible for want of candour, than the untutored rustic, who yields his assent to every alleged miracle, is to be taxed with want of discernment. Although these general positions can scarcely admit of dispute, it becomes extremely difficult, after a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPSE">lapse</a> of many ages, and in the collation of marvellous records, to separate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> from falsehood. In our attempts to prosecute this analytical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, we may sometimes advance a certain length with perfect security, without being able to trace uniformly the precise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of demarcation. Thus, in regard to the topic of our present discussion, we know, that in various periods of the world the vulgar have ascribed a celestial origin to stones of a peculiar configuration, as to certain modifications of pyrites, to belemnites, orthoceratites, &c., which the subsequent observations of naturalists have proved to be of mineral formation, and to the heads of arrows and sharpened flints, which have been fashioned by the hand of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and which, accordingly, we are authorized to exclude from the extra-terrestrial catalogue. But when substances dissimilar from these, and coinciding in any one character or circumstance with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> specimens of atmospheric stone, are reported by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> to have fallen from the clouds, the distance of ages and the lameness of the documents may powerfully affect our appreciation of the reputed evidence. When, therefore, we shortly touch on a few of the many instances which might be quoted from the annals of antiquity, we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> not to vouch for the truth even of these particular instances; but merely to admit their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> which the mention of them may be considered to add to that of subsequent and recent narrations. Through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIST">mist</a> of fable which envelopes the history of the bætuli, we discern some characters which correspond with those of meteorites. Thus, in the Λύκαιος, a poem falsely ascribed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, the εἰδωλονες, which M. Falconet properly classes with the bætuli, is said to be rough, heavy, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>. Damascius, in an extract of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Ibdorus, preserved by Photius, relates that the bætuli fell on Mount Libanus, in a globe of fire. A fragment of Sanchoniathon, preserved in Eusebius, (Præpar. Evangel. i. 10.), moreover informs us, that these stones were fabricated by the god Uranus (or Heaven), one of whose four sons was named Bætulus. May not this mythological genealogy be regarded as merely emblematical of their descent from the upper regions of the atmosphere? In the same chapter we are told that Attarne found a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> which had fallen from heaven, and honoured it with consecration in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a>. The stone denominated "the mother of the gods," if we can believe Appian, Herodian, and Marcellinus, fell from heaven. Aristodemus, cited by the Greek scholiast on <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PINDAR">Pindar</a>, affirms that it fell encircled by fire, on a hill, at the feet of the Theban bard. It is said to have been of a black <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> shape. Herodian (lib. v.) expressly declares, that the Phoenicians had no statue of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, polished by the hand; but only a certain stone, circular below, and terminated. terminated acutely above, in the form of a cone, of a black colour, and that, according to report, it fell from heaven, and was regarded as the image of the sun. Among various instances which might be selected from Livy, is that of a shower of stones on Mount <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBA">Alba</a>, in the reign of Tullus Hostilius, or about six hundred and fifty-two years before the birth of Christ. When the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> were told, that it had rained stones, they doubted the fact, and deputed commissioners to inquire into the particulars. They were then assured, that stones had really fallen, haud alter quam quem grandinem venti glomeratam in terras agunt. On this occasion, the historian mentions, that similar events were celebrated by a festival of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> days. Manjit follemne, ut quando cumque idem prodigium nuntiarent, feriae per novem dies agerentur. But one of the most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> which occurs in the records of antiquity, is that which is mentioned in the 58th chapter of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> book of Pliny's <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> History, of a large stone which fell near Egepolotamos, in Thrace, in the second year of the seventy-eighth Olympiad, or, according to our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>, about four hundred and sixty-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years before the Christian era. Pliny affirms us, that this extraordinary mass was still shewn in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and that it was as large as a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CART">cart</a>, and of a burnt colour. The Greeks pretended that it had fallen from the sun, and that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANAXAGORAS">Anaxagoras</a> had predicted the day of its arrival on the earth's surface. According to Plutarch, in the life of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LYCURGUS">Lycurgus</a>, the inhabitants of the Chersonesus held the Thracian stone in great veneration, and exhibited it as a public show. His account of its first appearance is chiefly extracted from the relation of Daimachus of Platea, and may be thus translated. "During seventy-five successive days before the stone fell, a large fiery body, like a cloud of flame, was observed in the heavens, not fixed to one point, but wandering about with a broken, irregular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. By its violent agitation, several fiery fragments were forced from it, impelled in various directions, and darted with the velocity and brightness of so many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> stars. After this body had fallen on the Chersonesus, and the people had assembled to examine it, they could find no inflammable matter, nor the slightest trace of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBUSTION">combustion</a>, but a real stone, which, though large, by no means corresponded to the dimensions of the flaming globe which they had seen in the sky, but seemed to be only a piece detached from it." Daimachus, it is true, may, on this occasion, have given way to his reputed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of the marvellous; and we can easily believe that the seventy-five continuous days are either an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of the copyist, or an original exaggeration; yet, from the marked coincidence of some of the circumstances with those more fully detailed in the sequel, there arises the presumption that a meteorite really fell at the place and period above assigned. From this period, till near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the fifteenth century, any historical notices which we have been enabled to collect, are so vague and scanty, that, in this abridged view of the subject, we may pass them over in silence. Professor Bantenschoen, of the central school of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLMAR">Colmar</a>, first directed the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of naturalists to some of the old chronicles, which commemorate with much naïveté, and in the true spirit of the times, the fall of the celebrated stone of Ensisheim. The following account accompanied this very singular mass, when it was suspended in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. "In the year of the Lord 1492, on Wednesday, which was Martinmas <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">eve</a>, the 7th of November, there happened a singular miracle: for, between eleven o'clock and noon, there was a loud peal of thunder, and a prolonged confused noise, which was heard to a great distance, and a stone fell from the air, in the jurisdiction of Ensisheim, which weighed 260 pounds, and the confused noise was, moreover, much louder than here. There a child <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> it strike on a field, situated in the upper jurisdiction, towards the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> and Inn, near the district of Giffard, which was sown with wheat, and did it no harm, except that it made a hole there; and then they conveyed it from that spot; and many pieces were broken from it, which the landvogt forbade. They, therefore, caused it to be placed in the church, with the intention of suspending it as a miracle; and many people came hither to see this stone. So there were remarkable conversations about this stone; but the learned said, that they knew not what it was; for it was beyond the ordinary course of nature, that such a large mass should unite the earth from the height of the air; but that it was really a miracle of God; for, before that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, never anything was heard like it, nor seen, nor described. When the people found that stone, it had entered into the earth, to the depth of a man's stature, which every body explained to be the will of God, that it should be found, and the noise of it was heard at Lucerne, at Villing, and in many other places, so loud, that it was believed that houses had been overturned: And as the king (Maximilian) was here, the Monday after St Catherine's day, of the same year, his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> excellence ordered the stone which had fallen to be brought to the castle, and after having conferred a long time about it with the noblemen, he said the people of Ensisheim should take it, and order it to be hung up in the church, and not allow any body to take anything from it. However, his excellency took two pieces of it, of which he kept one, and sent the other to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> Sigismund of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>; and they spoke a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> about this stone, which they suspended in the choir, where it still is; and a great many people came to see it." Trithemius, in his Hirsauigenian Annals, employs language to this effect.—"In the same year, on the 7th day of November, in the village of Suntgaw, near the townlet of Ensisheim, not far from Basle, a city of Germany, a stone, called a thunder-stone, of a prodigious size, for we know from eye-witnesses that it weighed 255 pounds, fell from the heavens. Its fall was so violent, that it broke into two pieces. The most considerable is still exhibited at the door of the church of Ensisheim, suspended by an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> chain, as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the fact which we have mentioned, and to preserve it in the public recollection."—We learn also from Paul Lang that there arose a furious storm on the 7th of November 1492, and that while the thunder roared, and the heavens appeared all on fire, a stone of enormous size fell near Ensisheim. "Its form was that of the Greek delta, with a triangular point. They still show it at Ensisheim as an astonishing phenomenon." It is worthy of observation, that these chroniclers lived at the period which they assign to the descent of the stone; and that, though their names are hastening to oblivion, Tritheimius yielded to few of his contemporaries in labour and learning; while Lang, a German Benedictine as he was, travelled in search of historical monuments, arraigned the licence of the catholic clergy, and applauded the independence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a> and Melanchthon. Of the Ensisheim stone, which has been transported to the national library at Colmar, and which, notwithstanding various dilapidations, still weighs 150 pounds, some interesting specimens may now be seen in the cabinets of the curious. Robert Ferguson, Esq., younger of Raith, has, in the most polite and obliging manner, gratified us with the sight of a small fragment, which belongs to his valuable collection of minerals at Raith <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in Fifehire, Scotland. We are fully aware, that M. Barthold has laboured to convince his readers (Journal de Physique, Ventofe, year 8.) that the far-famed mass of Ensisheim is merely argillo-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRUGINOUS">ferruginous</a>, of secondary formation, detached from an adjacent mountain, and conveyed to the spot on which it was found by some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, we might partially acquiesce; did not the artificers of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> and concurring records militate against it, and had not the more accurate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> of Vauquelin detected the same constituent parts as in the other stony and metallic substances denominated meteoric. "It is certainly composed of silica," observes this celebrated chemist, "of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNESIA">magnesia</a>, of iron, of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NICKEL">nickel</a>, of sulphur, and of a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of lime.—Particular trials have convinced me of the presence of sulphur and nickel in the grains of malleable iron, and in the pyrites, though in different proportions. This stone, then, in every respect, resembles others which have fallen from the atmosphere." In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">Commentary</a> of Surius, a Carthusian monk of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a>, mention is made of a shower of large stones in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LOMBARDY">Lombardy</a>, in 1510. These stones were harder than flint, and smelled of sulphur. The heaviest weighed 120 pounds.—The same event is more particularly related by Cardan, in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> intitled de Rerum Varietate (lib. xiv. c. 72.) According to this author, near the river Adda, not far from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, and at five o'clock in the evening, about 1120 stones fell from the air, one of them weighing 120 pounds and another 60 pounds. Many were presented to the French governor, and his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>. At three o'clock P.M. the sky appeared as if in a general blaze; and the passage, though somewhat ambiguous, would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> us to infer, that the meteor was visible for two hours. Like many of the learned and unlearned of his day, Cardan instantly connects the extraordinary appearance with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> transactions of his district. We next pass to an interesting extract from the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Jehangire, written in Persian, by himself, and translated by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Kirkpatrick, "A.H. 1030, or 16th year of the reign.—The following is among the extraordinary occurrences of this period. "Early on the 30th of Furverdeen of the present year (1629), and in the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the heavens, there arose in one of the villages of the purgannah of Jalindher, such a great and tremendous noise, as had nearly, by its dreadful nature, deprived the inhabitants of the place of their senses. During this noise, a luminous body was observed to fall from above, on the earth, suggesting to the beholders the idea that the firmament was raining fire. In a short time, the noise having subsided, and the inhabitants having recovered from their alarm, a courier was dispatched to Mahomed Syeed, the amil of the aforefaid purgannah, to advertise him of this event. The amil, instantly mounting his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, proceeded to the spot. Here he perceived the earth, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of a dozen yards in length and breadth, to be burned to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that not the least trace of verdure, or a blade of grass remained; nor had the heat yet subsided entirely. "Mahammed Syeed hereupon directed the aforefaid space of ground to be dug up; when the deeper it was dug, the greater was the heat of it found to be. At length a lump of iron made its appearance, the heat of which was so violent, that one might have supposed it to have been taken from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>. After some time it became <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>: when the amil conveyed it to his own habitation, from whence he afterwards dispatched it in a sealed bag to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. "Here I had this substance weighed in my presence. Its weight was 160 tolahs (A). I committed it to a skilful artisan, with orders to make of it a sabre, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, and a dagger. The workman reported, that the substance was not malleable, but shattered into pieces under the hammer. "Upon this I ordered it to be mixed with other iron. Conformably to my orders, three parts of the iron of lightning (B) were mixed with one part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> iron; and from the mixture were made two sabres, one knife, and one dagger." Our limits will not permit us to give the whole of the extract, nor the remarks of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">Right</a> Hon. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Greville and Colonel Kirkpatrick, which were read before the Royal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, on the 27th <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, 1803. We feel, however, no hesitation in attaching to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCUMENT">document</a> something very nearly approaching to direct evidence of the fact in question. The celebrated Gassendi relates, that, on the 27th of November, 1627, about 10 o'clock A.M., during a very clear sky, he saw a flaming stone, of the apparent diameter of four feet, fall on Mount Vaison, an eminence situated between the small <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of Perne and Guillaumes, in Provence. This stone was surrounded by a luminous circle of different colours, nearly resembling the rainbow, and its fall was accompanied with a noise like the discharge of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>. It weighed 59 pounds; and its specific gravity was to that of common marble as 14 to 11. It was of a dark metallic colour, and extremely hard. Though it was not subjected to chemical analysis, and is not now to be found, the circumstances which have been stated by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> are sufficiently (A) A tolah is about 180 grains, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a> weight. (B) This expression is equivalent to our term thunder-bolt. sufficiently minute to operate on the conviction of those who are willing to be convinced. From a curious book printed at Paris in 1672, and now become very scarce, entitled Conversations tirées de l'Académie de M. l'Abbé Bourdelot, contenant diverses recherches et observations physiques, par le Sieur Legallais, we make the ensuing extract. "A member presents a fragment of two stones which fell near <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a>, one of which weighed 300, and the other 200 pounds. These stones," says he, "fell during the night, when the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> was perfectly mild and serene. They seemed to be all on fire, and came from above, but in a slanting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, and with a tremendous noise. This prodigy terribly alarmed 300 or 400 eyewitnesses, who were at a loss what to think of it. These stones fell with such rapidity, that they formed a ditch, in which after the noise had ceased, the spectators ventured to approach them, and examine them more closely. They then sent them to Verona, where they were deposited in the Academy, and that learned body sent fragments of them to different places." That which accompanied the above intimation was of a yellowish hue, very easily pulverized, and smelled of sulphur.—In the course of examining one of these stones, M. Laugier, professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a> at Paris, has recently detected the presence of chrome, by means of the caustic alkali.—The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> of the Verona phenomena, if we have been correctly informed, is 1663. In the Bornian collection there is a substance which is designated Ferrum retractorium, granulis nitentibus, matrice virescenti immixtis (Ferrum vires Lin.), cujus fragmenta <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> unius <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> viginti usque librarum pondus, cortice nigro scoriaco circumdata, ad Plann, prope Tabor, circuli Bechinchens Bohemiae, palum reperturunt. The following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> is subjoined. (Quae fragmenta 3. Iulii anni 1753, inter tonitrura, e celo pluteo creduliores quidam affluerunt.) The expression creduliores quidam, it may be alleged, at once destroys the evidence of this memorandum. It deserves, however, to be noted, that, in regard to our present subject, what was formerly accounted the credulity of the vulgar, may now, on several occasions, be confirmed into probability, if not into matter of fact; and that Mr Greville has found the identical fragment to have the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> with other meteoric stones. Hence, we are compelled either to admit its extra-terrestrial origin, or the existence of a substance, originally belonging to the earth, and yet agreeing in character with those deemed atmospheric. The former part of the alternative is perfectly consonant with well-authenticated facts; whereas of the latter, we are not warranted to pronounce, that a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> has hitherto been established, to the satisfaction of any chemist or mineralogist. But we have now to turn our attention to a report of M. de la Lande, inserted in the Historical <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALMANACK">Almanack</a> of Breffle, for 1756. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of September, 1753, about one o'clock P.M. when the weather was very hot, and very serene, without the least appearance of a cloud, a very loud noise, like the discharge of two or three cannons, was heard within the circumference of six leagues, but was of very short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. This noise was loudest in the neighbourhood of Pont-de-Velle; and at Liponas, a village three leagues from the last-mentioned place, it was even accompanied with a hissing, like that of a cracker. On the same evening there were found at Liponas and at <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">Pin</a>, two blackish masses, of a form nearly circular, but very uneven, which had fallen on ploughed ground, and sunk, by their own weight, to half a foot below the surface. One of them weighed about twenty pounds; and a fragment of one of them weighing 114 lb. was preferred in the cabinet of M. Varenne de Beoff, at Dijon. The basis of these masses resembled a grayish whinstone, and was very refractory; and some ferruginous particles were disseminated in grains, filaments, or minute masses, through the substance of the stone, especially in its fissures. This iron, when subjected to a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> heat, became obedient to the magnet. The black coating on the surface, M. de la Lande attributes to fusion, induced by violent heat. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>'s acknowledged respectability and accuracy of observation, combined with the circumstances which he has adduced, circumstances, too, which, if mistated, lay so open to public <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>, powerfully plead in favour of his testimony. On the 15th of September 1760, according to the abbé Bachelay, about half past four o'clock P.M. there appeared near the chateau de Chevabrie, in the neighbourhood of Lucé, a small town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>, a stormy cloud, from which proceeded a loud peal of thunder, like the discharge of cannon, and followed by a noise which was mistaken by several people for the lowing of oxen. This <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> was heard over a space of about two leagues and a half, but unaccompanied by any perceptible flame. The reapers in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Perigué, about three leagues from Lucé, on hearing the same noise, looked up, and saw an opaque body, which described a curve, and fell on soft turf, on the high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from Mons, near which they were at work. They all quickly ran up to it, and found a sort of stone, nearly half of which was buried in the earth, and the whole so hot that it could not be touched. At first they ran away in a panic; but on returning to the spot some time after, they found the stone precisely in the same situation, and sufficiently cooled to admit of being handled, and narrowly examined. It weighed seven ounces and a half, and was of a triangular form, presenting, as it were, three rounded horns, one of which, at the moment of the fall had entered into the ground, and was of a gray or ash colour, while the rest, which was exposed to the air, was very black. When the abbé presented this stone to the academy, that body appointed three of its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, namely, Messieurs Lavoisier, Fougeroux, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADET">Cadet</a>, to examine and analyse it. This task they performed with more care and accuracy than M. de la Lande had done on the preceding occasion; but their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> was confined to an integral part of the whole, considered as a homogeneous substance, in place of being repeated on each of the constituent parts. The substance was of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> cinereous hue, speckled with an infinite number of small and shining metallic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, visible through a magnifying glass. That part of the outer surface which remained above ground was incrusted with a thin black coating, which seemed to have undergone fusion, and which gave a few sparks when struck with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>. The specific gravity of the mass was 3.335. —Two other stones, nearly of the same characters, the one reported to have fallen at Ajre, in Artois, and the other in the Cotentin, in Normandy, were presented to the academy in the course of the same year by M. Gurlon de Boyaval, honorary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-general of the bailiwick of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIRE">Aire</a>, and the younger M. Morand. According to the academical report, these three stones, when compared, presented no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> to the eye, were of the same colour, and nearly of the same grain, exhibiting metallic and pyritous particles, and covered with a black and ferruginous incrustation. Although the coincidence of facts and circumstances, in three places so remote from one another, did not convince the academy that these stones had been conveyed to the earth by lightning, yet it induced them to invite naturalists to prosecute the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of the subject. On the 20th of November 1768, a stone fell at Mauerkirchen near the Inn, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, that weighed 38lb. was of a triangular form, and only eight inches in thickness. Its fall was accompanied by a hissing noise, and great darkness in the atmosphere. This meteorite penetrated two feet and a half into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. Part of it is now in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a> of the right <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> Charles Greville, and a fragment may be seen in Mr Ferguson's collection quoted above. The next remarkable case on record occurred on the 20th of August 1789, at Barbaton, near Roquefort, in the Landes of Bordeaux, and is thus related by Citizen Lomet, who was known to several members of the institute, and happened to be at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGEN">Agen</a> when the meteor appeared. "It was a very bright fire-ball, luminous as the sun, of the size of an ordinary balloon, and, after inspiring the inhabitants with consternation, burst and disappeared. A few days after, some peasants brought stones, which they said fell from the meteor; but the philosophers to whom they offered them laughed at their assertions as fabulous. The peasants would have now more reason to laugh at the philosophers."—One of these stones broke through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of a cottage, and killed a herdman and some cattle. Vaquelin, who received a process-verbal of the circumstances, also examined one of the specimens. The fragment procured by Mr Ferguson has visibly all the characters of a genuine meteorite. A much more remarkable phenomenon, however, of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, occurred near Agen, on the 24th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1790. An inhabitant of St Severe communicates the following particulars to M. Darcey the chemist, who was then resident at Paris. "Our towns-people were yesterday very much alarmed. About a quarter past nine o'clock, in the evening, there suddenly appeared in the air a fire-ball, dragging a long train, which diffused a very vivid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> over the horizon. This meteor soon disappeared, and seemed to fall at one hundred paces from us. It was quickly followed by an explosion louder than that of cannon or of thunder. Every body dreaded being buried under the ruins of his house, which seemed to give way from the concussion. The same phenomenon was seen, and the report heard, in the neighbouring towns, as Mont de Marfan, Tartas, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAX">Dax</a>. The weather in other respects was very calm, without a breath of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> or a cloud, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> shone in all her brightness." M. Darcey's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, a clergyman in that part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, sent him a small stone, which was picked up on the morning after the explosion, and the history of which he was scrupulously anxious to investigate. Being satisfied with respect to all the particulars, he at length dispatched it to Paris, accompanied with some curious remarks. "When these stones fell," says he, "they had not their present degree of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a>. Some of them fell on straw, bits of which stuck to the stones, and incorporated with them. I have seen one in this predicament. It is at present at la Battele; but I cannot persuade the owner to part with it." Thole which fell on the houses produced a noise, not like that of stones, but rather of a substance which had not yet acquired compactness." We subjoin the process-verbal—a simple but authentic document. "In the year one thousand seven hundred and ninety, and the 30th day of the month of August, we, the Sieur Jean Duby, mayor, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> Maulion, procurator of the commune of the municipality of La Grange de Juillac, and Jean Darmite, resident in the parish of La Grange de Juillac, certify in truth and verity, that, on Saturday the 24th of July last, between nine and ten o'clock in the evening, there passed a great fire, and after it we heard in the air a very loud and extraordinary noise; and, about two minutes after, there fell stones from heaven, but fortunately there fell only a very few, and they fell about ten paces from one another in some places, and in others nearer, and finally, in some other places, farther, and falling, most of them, of the weight of about half a quarter of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> each; some of about half a pound, like that found in our parish of La Grange; and on the borders of the parish of Creon, they were found of a pound weight; and in falling they seemed not to be inflamed, but very hard and black without, and within of the colour of steel; and, thank God, they occasioned no harm to the people, nor the trees, but only to some trees which were broken on the houses; and most of them fell gently, and others fell quickly, with a hissing noise; and some were found which had entered into the earth, but very few. In witness whereof we have written and signed these presents. (Signed) Duby, Mayor—Darmite." Monseigneur Baudin mentions, that, as M. Carris of Barbotan and he were walking in the court of the castle of Mormes about half past nine o'clock, in the evening of the 24th of July 1790, when the air was perfectly calm, and the sky cloudless, they found themselves suddenly surrounded by a pale clear light, which obscured that of the moon, though the latter was nearly full. On looking up, they observed, almost in their zenith, a fireball of a larger apparent diameter than that of the moon, dragging a tail, which seemed to be five or six times longer than the diameter of its body, and which gradually tapered to a point, the latter approaching to blood-red, though the rest of the meteor was of a pale <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>. This luminous body proceeded with great velocity from south to north, and in two seconds split into portions of considerable size, like the fragment of a bursting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOMB">bomb</a>. These fragments became extinguished in the air, and some of them, as they fell, assumed that deep red colour, which had been observed at the point of the tail. Two or three minutes after M. Baudin and his friend heard a dreadful explosion, like the simultaneous firing of several pieces of ordnance; but they were not sensible of any tremulous motion under their feet, though the concus- Meteorite. The phenomenon of the atmosphere shook the windows in their frames, and threw down <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> utensils from their shelves. When these gentlemen removed to the garden, the noise still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, and seemed to be directly over their heads. Some time after it had ceased, they heard a hollow sound rolling in echoes, for fifty miles, along the chain of the Pyrenees, and at the end of about four minutes gradually dying away in distance. At the same time, a strong sulphurous odour was diffused in the atmosphere. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> which occurred between the disruption of the meteor, and the loud report, induced M. Baudin to conjecture, that this fireball must have been at least eight miles from the earth's surface, and that it fell about four miles from Mormes. "The latter part of my conjecture, lays he, was soon confirmed by an account which we received of a great many stones having fallen from the atmosphere at Juillac and in the neighbourhood of Barbotan." It appears, indeed, from the concurring testimony of intelligent persons worthy of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, that the meteor really exploded at a little distance from Juillac, and that its fragments were found lying in an almost circular space, of nearly two miles in diameter. Some of them weighed eighteen or twenty, and a few, it is alleged, even fifty pounds. M. de Carris procured one of 18 lbs. which he transmitted to the Parisian Academy of Sciences. That examined by M. Baudin was small, but heavy in proportion to its size, black on the outside, grayish within, and intermixed with many minute, thinning, metallic particles. These last circumstances perfectly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a> with the fragment of a Barbotan stone preserved in Mr Ferguson's collection. In one of his letters to Professor St Amand, M. Goyon d'Arzaz remarks, that these stones, though generally smooth on the outside, presented some longitudinal cracks, or fissures, while their interior parts exhibited symptoms of metallic veins, especially of a ferruginous-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>. When yet red-hot, and scattered in various directions, they formed that magnificent firework, that shower of flame, which enlightened the horizon over a large tract of country; for this extraordinary meteor was seen at Bayonne, Auch, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAU">Pau</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TARBES">Tarbes</a>, and even at Bordeaux and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOULOUSE">Toulouse</a>. At the last mentioned place it excited little attention, on account of its great distance, and its appearing only a little brighter than a shooting star. It, moreover, deserves to be noted, that the meteorites in question were found on a bare moor, of an extremely thin soil, on which no such stones, or indeed stones of any description, had been observed in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of man. They who are solicitous of additional information on this part of our subject, may consult Nos. 23 and 24 of the Journal des Sciences Utiles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTPELLIER">Montpellier</a>, for 1790, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECADE">Decade</a> Philosophique for February 1796. When all the circumstances of the case are duly considered, we need not be surprised, that they should produce conviction on the minds of many men of science, who, till then, persisted "an evil heart of unbelief." M. de St Amand ingenuously confessed to M. Piélet of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, that he had treated this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVEL">novel</a> topic with unmerited contempt, and that the evidence deduced from the similar characters of the stones should not be rashly rejected. The learned and the unlearned of the district in which the phenomenon is stated to have occurred, attest its existence; the professor of natural history in the central school of Agen renounces his former scepticism; Vauquelin analyses a specimen, and finds it to contain the same chemical substances as other meteorites, and in nearly the same proportions; and shall we be so unreasonable as to withhold our assent, merely because we have not ocular demonstration of the alleged particulars? Our chronological <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of cases has now brought us to the fall of several meteorites near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIENNA">Sienna</a>, the particulars of which, as reported by the late <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a> and Sir William <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a>, are recorded in the first part of the Philosophical Transactions for 1795 (page 103). Mr King, likewise in the tract which we have already quoted, communicates some interesting circumstances relative to this phenomenon, chiefly extracted from an account of it published by Professor Soldani. While we refer our readers to these details, we cannot omit mentioning that, in regard to aspect and composition, the Sienna stones are perfectly analogous to others already noticed, and very different from any that occur in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>. As the meteor from which they were discharged appeared on the morning after a violent eruption of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VESUVIUS">Vesuvius</a>, they were at first supposed to be volcanic, till cool reflection and examination betrayed the extravagance of such a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>. The precise number of stones which were collected on this occasion is not specified, but many of them were small, weighing from a quarter of an ounce to two ounces. A pretty entire specimen occurs in Mr Ferguson's collection.—The date of the Sienna meteor is the 16th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, 1794. On the 13th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> of the following year, about three o'clock in the afternoon, another of these singular stones, weighing 56 pounds, fell near the country house of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Topham, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>. The captain's report, which is inserted in the Gentleman's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a> for 1796, is distinct and satisfactory; while the chemical examination of the mass, detailed in Mr Howard's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, in the Philosophical Transactions for 1802, affords a still more decisive proof of its atmospheric origin. M. de Drée, also, found it to correspond exactly in aspect and character, with fragments of meteor stones from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENARES">Benares</a> and Ville-franche. The original mass is in the possession of Mr Sowerby author of English <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, &c. It is larger than a man's head. Mr Southey, in his letters from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, transcribes the authenticated relation of another instance of the descent of a stone from the clouds on the 19th of February 1796. But we pass to some of the most important details relative to the stone which is affirmed to have fallen near Ville-franche, in the department of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a>, on the 12th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, 1798. When it was transmitted to Professor Sage, member of the National Institute, he considered it at first, as only a pyritous and magnetic ore of iron, although it bore no resemblance to any known <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of ore of that metal, since it contained nickel, silica, magnesia, and native iron, which shone like steel when polished. "It is of an ash gray colour," says M. Sage, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANULATED">granulated</a> and speckled with gray, thinning, and pyritous metallic points. One of its surfaces is covered with a dingy-black enamel, about the third of a line in thickness. This stone acts very powerfully on the magnetic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>. When the senator Chaffet transmitted it to me, it... was accompanied by an historical notice of similar import with that which M. Delivre, of Ville-franche, who saw and described the phenomenon on the spot. At six o'clock in the evening, a round body, which diffused the most vivid light, was observed in the vicinity of Ville-franche, moving westward, and producing a hissing, like that of a bomb which traverses the air. This luminous body, which was seen at the same time at Lyons and on Mont-Cenis, marked its path by a red track of fire, and exploded, about 200 toises from the earth, with a tremendous report and concussion. One of the flaming fragments fell on the vineyard of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Crepier, an inhabitant of Sales. On the spot where this portion of the meteor was seen to fall, and in a fresh opening of about 20 inches in depth, and 18 in width, was found a black mass, 15 inches in diameter, and rounded on one side. An account of the same meteor was published in the Journal de Physique, for Floreal, year 11, by M. de Drée. From his minute and deliberate investigation, it appears that the fire-ball had scarcely fixed the attention of the inhabitants of the Sales and of the adjacent villages, when its rapid approach, accompanied by a terrible whizzing noise, like that of an irregular hollow body, traversing the air with unusual velocity, inspired the whole commune with alarm, especially when they observed it passing over their heads, at an inconsiderable elevation. It left behind a long train of light, and emitted, with an almost unceasing crackling, small vivid flames, like little stars. Its fall was remarked, at the distance of only 50 paces, by three labourers, one of whom, named Montillard, let fall his coat and bundle of sticks that he might run the faster, while the other two, Chardon and Lapoec, fled with equal precipitation to Sales, where the alarm had become general.—These three witnesses attest the astonishing rapidity of the meteor's motion, and the hissing which proceeded from the spot where it fell. So terrified was Crepier at the explosion, that he locked himself up with his family, first in his cellar, and then in his private apartment, not venturing abroad till next morning, when, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of M. Blandel, Chardon, Lapoec, and many others, he repaired to the opening which had been made by the fire-ball. At the bottom of this opening, which was 18 inches deep, including the entire thickness of the mould, they found a large black mass, of an irregularly oval form, having a fanciful resemblance to a calf's head. Though no longer hot, it smelled of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a>-powder and was cracked in several places. When the observers broke it, and discovered nothing but stone, indifference succeeded to curiosity, and they coolly ascribed its appearance to causes more or less whimsical and supernatural. The original weight of this stone was about twenty pounds. Its black vitrified surface gave fire with steel.
